docs.title: Course Description for Course Technology of Robotic Design
Technology of Robotic Design
docs.text:
Title: Technology of Robotic Design

Target Audience: High school

Prerequisites: None

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Technology of Robotic Design introduces high school students to the study of robotic systems and their real-world applications. Students apply the engineering design process while exploring programming, electrical concepts, mechanical concepts, and control systems that together form the foundation of modern robotics.

Through hands-on learning and problem-solving activities, students design, build, and program robotic systems, gaining direct experience with the same processes used by engineers and technicians in robotics, automation, and manufacturing industries. The course blends technical skill-building with professional and employability competencies, preparing students for further study or entry-level work in STEM and advanced manufacturing fields.

Robotics sits at the intersection of some of the fastest-growing career fields today, and this course gives students an early, practical foundation in the technologies driving automation across manufacturing, healthcare, agriculture, and beyond.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
• Robotic systems and their applications
  • The engineering design process
  • Programming
  • Electrical concepts
  • Mechanical concepts
  • Control systems

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Advanced robotics research topics such as machine learning-driven autonomy or computer vision
  • Industrial-scale automation and PLC programming at a professional/certification level
  • Advanced fluid power system design (hydraulics/pneumatics beyond introductory concepts)
  • Professional CNC machining and manufacturing certification
  • Graduate-level control theory (e.g., state-space methods, advanced feedback control mathematics)

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define robotics, automation, and control systems.
  • Identify components of robotic systems.
  • Identify sensors.
  • Identify open and closed loops in control systems.
  • Identify the primary concepts and components of mechanical systems.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain the universal systems model.
  • Describe the concepts of voltage, current, and resistance in electricity.
  • Explain the primary functions of electronic systems components.
  • Describe the purpose of a microcontroller/logic controller.
  • Explain primary concepts and components of a fluid power system.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Demonstrate precision measurement equipment and techniques.
  • Simulate control and automation systems.
  • Simulate electronic circuits.
  • Measure circuit values with a multimeter.
  • Implement basic programming procedures.
  • Demonstrate how sensors are used to control robotic technology.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Research robotic hardware used in various industries.
  • Compare open and proprietary hardware components.
  • Compare analog and digital electronics for control systems.
  • Research the development and future of robotics.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Select the most appropriate programming language or platform for an application.
  • Ensure the security of programs.
  • Compare and judge tradeoffs between hardware and design options for a given application.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design a circuit for a given purpose.
  • Design a mechanical system.
  • Design code for a given purpose.
  • Design a robot.
  • Build a robot.
  • Reengineer the design of an existing robotic system.
  • Capstone project: Design, build, and program a complete robotic system that satisfies a defined set of requirements, then evaluate and document its performance against those requirements.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 14 chapters covering 204 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Identifying Kit Parts and Building Your StarterBot - Hands-on introduction where students identify kit hardware and assemble a complete robot before any theory.
  2. Introduction to Robotics and Systems - Formal vocabulary for the robot just built: robotics, automation, the universal systems model, and robot categories.
  3. Programming Fundamentals - General-purpose programming concepts (algorithms, variables, control structures, functions, debugging) independent of hardware.
  4. Programming Your Robot - Applying programming fundamentals to the robot: microcontrollers, sensors, actuators, and basic control loops.
  5. Designing and Building Custom Parts - The engineering design process applied to manufacturing custom robot parts via additive manufacturing and 3D printing.
  6. Electrical Fundamentals - The electrical theory underlying the robot's power system: voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, and safety.
  7. Electronic Components and Circuit Design - Physical components and circuit-building skills: resistors, transistors, breadboarding, soldering, and circuit design.
  8. Sensors and Measurement - A deeper dive into precision measurement, specific sensor types, calibration, and signal processing.
  9. Mechanical Systems and Simple Machines - The mechanical theory behind the kit's hardware: simple machines, gears, torque, friction, and chassis design.
  10. Fluid Power: Hydraulics and Pneumatics - Hydraulic and pneumatic systems: fluid pressure, cylinders, valves, pumps, and fluid power system design.
  11. Control Systems and Feedback Loops - A deeper dive into control theory: setpoints, error signals, PID basics, stability, and motion/actuator control.
  12. Digital Logic and Computing Fundamentals - What's inside the microcontroller: digital vs. analog electronics, binary numbers, logic gates, and computing components.
  13. Advanced Robot Programming - Teleoperation, motion and path planning, arm/wheeled robot control, calibration, troubleshooting, and safety programming.
  14. Integrating, Testing, and Maintaining a Complete Robotic System - The capstone: component selection, assembly, wiring, system integration, testing, and maintenance.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
This course follows a "build first, then work backwards" approach: you'll identify parts and assemble a complete robot in Chapter 1 before learning any underlying theory. From there, you'll program the robot and design custom parts for it, then circle back through the electrical, mechanical, sensing, control, and computing theory that explains why everything you built actually works. Chapters build on each other in this order, so it's best to work through them sequentially rather than skipping ahead.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Identifying Kit Parts and Building Your StarterBot
Identifying Kit Parts and Building Your StarterBot
Summary
docs.text: This chapter opens the course with a real robot kit in hand: the goBILDA FTC StarterBot Kit. Students first learn to identify the structural hardware, motion components, power/motor parts, and fasteners that make up the kit, then read and follow a guided assembly manual to build a complete robot. By the end of this chapter, students will have a working robot chassis in front of them and firsthand experience with the vocabulary and physical components that every later chapter builds on.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Robot Kit Overview
  2. Kit Parts Identification
  3. Structural Hardware
  4. Motion Hardware Components
  5. Power And Motor Components
  6. Fasteners And Hardware
  7. Assembly Instructions Reading
  8. Guided Robot Assembly
  9. Robot Subassembly Build
  10. Build Verification And Troubleshooting

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

docs.title: Robot Kit Overview
docs.text:
Most robotics courses start with theory: circuits, forces, and code, followed months later by a real machine. This course flips that order. Before you learn why a motor spins or how a program controls a servo, you are going to open a box, spread out the parts, and build a real, drivable robot. The theory will make a lot more sense later once your hands already know what a gear, a shaft, and a chassis feel like.

The kit you will build from is the goBILDA FTC StarterBot Kit (SKU 3200-4008-2627), a robotics kit designed for the preseason of FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC), a national robotics competition for middle and high school teams. Unlike a toy kit with a dozen snap-together pieces, the StarterBot Kit ships with hundreds of individual aluminum, plastic, and metal components, along with a 20-page assembly manual that walks you through 40 numbered build steps. When you finish, you will have a rolling robot chassis with a working drivetrain, a battery mount, and an intake mechanism, the same kind of subsystem an FTC team uses as the backbone of a competition robot.

Every part in the kit falls into one of four broad categories, and learning to sort parts into these categories is the very first skill this chapter teaches:

  • Structural hardware — the aluminum channels, mounts, and plates that form the robot's frame, or "skeleton"
  • Motion hardware — the shafts, hubs, bearings, gears, sprockets, chain, and wheels that let the robot move
  • Power and motor components — the battery, motors, and servos that provide energy and rotational force
  • Fasteners and hardware — the screws, nuts, washers, and hex keys that hold everything together

Tip

Don't worry about memorizing every part name today. This chapter builds your vocabulary the same way a mechanic builds theirs: by handling real parts, matching them to a parts list, and using them right away in a real build.

docs.title: Kit Parts Identification
docs.text:
Before any assembly manual makes sense, you need to be able to identify parts. Every professional assembly guide, from furniture instructions to aircraft maintenance manuals, begins with a Bill of Materials (BOM), a complete list of every part needed, usually shown with a picture, a part name, and a quantity. The StarterBot Kit's BOM lists every U-channel, shaft, gear, motor, and screw that ships in the box, organized by category.

Learning to read a BOM is a transferable skill you will use throughout your career in any technical field: you scan the picture, compare it to the part in your hand, check the quantity, and set it aside in a labeled tray or bag. Skipping this step is the single most common reason first-time builders get stuck at step 15 of a manual, only to discover they used the wrong length of shaft back at step 3.

Instead of memorizing the whole BOM from a page of tiny thumbnail images, it helps to explore an exploded view of the finished robot, where each region of the machine is linked back to its hardware category. Clicking through this kind of exploded diagram lets you build a mental map of "where does this type of part usually go" before you ever pick up a screwdriver.

docs.title: Diagram: StarterBot Exploded Parts Explorer
docs.text:
StarterBot Exploded Parts Explorer

Type: infographic sim-id: starterbot-parts-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students identify the four hardware categories (structural, motion, power/motor, fasteners) by exploring a labeled, exploded-view illustration of the assembled StarterBot chassis.

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) and Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, locate, classify

Learning objective: Given an exploded view of the StarterBot, students will identify which hardware category each visible component belongs to and recall the specific part name.

Layout: A simplified line-art illustration of the StarterBot chassis rendered in an "exploded" style, with component groups pulled slightly apart from the main frame so each group is individually selectable. Four color-coded regions overlay the drawing: frame/channels (silver), drivetrain/wheels (blue), battery/motors (orange), fasteners (gray).

Interactive elements: - Hovering over any region highlights it and displays the category name in a floating label - Clicking a region opens a side panel listing the real part names in that category (for example, clicking the frame region lists "1-Hole U-Channel, 8-Hole U-Channel, 15-Hole U-Channel, Quad Block Mount, Drop-Center Bearing Plate") - A "Show All Labels" toggle button reveals every category label simultaneously for review - A "Quiz Me" button hides the labels and asks the student to click the region that matches a randomly chosen part name, giving immediate right/wrong feedback

Data to be displayed: Four hardware categories mapped to 6-10 real StarterBot part names each, drawn from the kit's actual Bill of Materials.

Color coding: Silver for structural hardware, blue for motion hardware, orange for power/motor components, gray for fasteners. Legend displayed in the corner of the canvas.

Responsive behavior: Illustration and hit regions scale proportionally to the width of the containing iframe; labels reflow to remain readable on narrower screens.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with an SVG-derived line drawing as a background image, clickable polygon hit-regions defined in an array, and a text panel drawn in the remaining canvas space for the infobox.

docs.title: Structural Hardware
docs.text:
Structural hardware refers to the rigid parts that give the robot its shape and hold every other component in a fixed position relative to the rest of the machine. If motion hardware is the robot's muscles and power components are its energy source, structural hardware is its skeleton.

The most common piece of structural hardware in the StarterBot Kit is the U-channel: a length of extruded aluminum bent into a U-shaped cross-section, with a regular pattern of holes drilled along its length for mounting screws. U-channels are named by how many holes run along their length, which also tells you roughly how long the piece is. A 1-Hole U-Channel is a short stub used as a spacer or bracket, while a 15-Hole U-Channel is long enough to form an entire side rail of the chassis.

The following table lists the U-channel sizes used in the StarterBot build, since recognizing these by hole count is a skill you will rely on for every future robotics project, not just this kit.

U-Channel Type Approx. Length Typical Use in the Build 1-Hole U-Channel Shortest Small brackets and spacers 1-Hole Low U-Channel Shortest, shallower profile Tight-clearance brackets 3-Hole Mini U-Channel Short Small mounting brackets 8-Hole U-Channel Medium Cross braces and short rails 10-Hole Low U-Channel Medium, shallower profile Low-profile chassis rails 15-Hole U-Channel Longest Main chassis side rails

Beyond U-channels, the kit includes other structural parts that connect channels to one another or to motion hardware:

  • Quad Block Mount — a block with four screw points, used to join two U-channels at a corner or to mount a bearing
  • Dual Block Mount — a smaller block with two screw points, used for lighter connections
  • Drop-Center Bearing Plate — a flat plate with a lowered center section that holds a bearing in perfect alignment with a shaft passing through the frame

Because structural hardware carries no moving parts of its own, it is the easiest category to identify: if a part is solid aluminum, has a repeating hole pattern, and does not spin or roll, it is almost certainly structural hardware.

docs.title: Motion Hardware Components
docs.text:
Motion hardware is the collection of parts that transmits rotational force from a motor to the wheels, or otherwise allows a part of the robot to move. This is the most mechanically complex category in the kit, because motion hardware parts must fit together with very tight tolerances to spin freely without wobbling.

At the center of the StarterBot's motion system is the 8mm REX Shaft, a precision-ground steel shaft available in several lengths that passes through the frame and carries rotating parts along its length. A shaft alone cannot transmit force to anything; it needs a way to grip a wheel, sprocket, or gear so the two rotate together. That job belongs to hubs: the 8mm REX Sonic Hub and 8mm REX Hyper Hub both clamp onto the shaft and provide a mounting pattern that other motion parts bolt onto.

For a shaft to spin freely through a hole in a U-channel or bearing plate without grinding against the aluminum, it passes through an 8mm REX Bearing, a ring of hardened steel with an inner race that lets the shaft rotate with almost no friction. Builders also use thin 0.5mm shims to fine-tune the spacing between parts on a shaft, and collars to lock a part's exact position on the shaft so it cannot slide side to side.

Once a shaft is supported by bearings and fitted with hubs, it can drive a wheel directly, or it can drive another shaft through a chain-and-sprocket or gear-and-gear connection. The StarterBot Kit uses both approaches:

  1. Chain-and-sprocket drivetrain — a 10-Tooth Sprocket on the motor's output shaft is connected by plastic chain (snapped together from individual links into a closed loop) to a larger sprocket on the wheel shaft, multiplying torque while reducing speed.
  2. Gear-driven mechanisms — the 30-Tooth Gear, 20-Tooth Gear, and 100-Tooth Gear mesh directly, tooth to tooth, to transmit rotation between shafts without the flexibility of a chain, which is useful in the kit's intake roller mechanism.
  3. Wheels — the finished drivetrain rolls on a mix of wheel types: 72mm and 48mm GripForce Gecko Wheels for high-traction driving, Omni Wheels that roll freely sideways for smooth turning, and Hogback Wheels that support the frame without adding drive traction.

Notice the pattern in every motion assembly: a shaft is supported by bearings, positioned with shims and collars, and driven by a hub, gear, or sprocket. Once you can recognize that pattern, every motion subassembly in the manual, and in future robots you build, will look familiar rather than overwhelming.

docs.title: Power and Motor Components
docs.text:
Structural and motion hardware only matter once something makes them move. Power and motor components are the parts that store and convert electrical energy into rotational force. The StarterBot Kit runs on a single 12V battery, held in place by a Battery Mount and secured with a Battery Strap so it cannot shift during a match or a bumpy test drive.

The kit includes two models of Yellow Jacket motor, a type of DC gearmotor that combines an electric motor with an internal gearbox. The gearbox trades rotational speed for torque (twisting force), and the two ratios included in the kit sit at opposite ends of that trade-off.

Motor Gear Ratio Speed Torque Typical Use Yellow Jacket 19.2:1 Lower ratio Faster rotation Lower torque Driving wheels for quick movement Yellow Jacket 50.9:1 Higher ratio Slower rotation Higher torque Mechanisms needing more twisting force, like an intake roller

In addition to the two DC motors, the kit includes Speed Servos, a different kind of motor that rotates to a specific commanded angle rather than spinning continuously. Servos mount inside a Compact ServoBlock, a housing that also holds a wheel hub, so the servo can be geared to drive a wheel directly. You will meet servos again in a later chapter on control systems, but for now it is enough to recognize a servo as the small, boxy motor bolted inside its own block housing, distinct from the larger cylindrical Yellow Jacket gearmotors.

docs.title: Fasteners and Hardware
docs.text:
Every structural and motion part in the kit stays together because of fasteners: the screws, nuts, and washers that clamp parts to one another. Fasteners are easy to overlook because they are small, but a build with the wrong fastener in the wrong hole will fail, either falling apart during a match or binding so tightly that a shaft cannot spin.

The StarterBot Kit uses three sizes of socket head screw (8mm, 10mm, and 12mm), named for the length of the screw's shaft, and driven with a hex key that fits into a hexagonal socket in the screw's head. Paired with each screw is typically a locknut, a nut with a nylon insert that grips the screw's threads so vibration cannot loosen it over time, and often a washer, a flat disc that spreads the clamping force over a wider area so the aluminum channel is not dented or cracked.

Here is a quick reference for matching each fastener to its role in the build:

  • 8mm socket head screw — shortest length, used to join thin stacks of parts such as two U-channels
  • 10mm socket head screw — medium length, used for block mounts and bearing plates
  • 12mm socket head screw — longest length, used where several parts stack together, such as a motor mount plus a channel
  • Locknut — threads onto a screw and resists loosening from vibration
  • Washer — spreads clamping force and protects the aluminum surface
  • Hex key — an L-shaped tool that fits the socket in each screw head; the manual specifies which size hex key to use for each screw

Warning

A locknut that spins too easily by hand has lost its nylon grip and should be replaced. A locknut that requires heavy force from the very first turn is being cross-threaded. Both situations are worth stopping to fix before continuing the build.

docs.title: Assembly Instructions Reading
docs.text:
Now that you can identify every category of part, the next skill is learning to read a technical assembly manual, the same skill an aircraft mechanic, furniture installer, or robotics engineer relies on daily. The StarterBot manual presents 40 numbered steps, each showing an illustration of the parts needed, an arrow or highlight showing where they attach, and a callout list naming each part and how many are required.

Reading an assembly manual is not the same as reading a paragraph of text top to bottom. Instead, experienced builders repeat a small cycle for every single step, checking their work before moving on rather than plowing ahead and hoping for the best. Because this cycle repeats identically at every one of the 40 steps, it is worth slowing down to see it as its own process, separate from any single step's specific parts.

docs.title: Diagram: Reading an Assembly Step Workflow
docs.text:
Reading an Assembly Step Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: assembly-reading-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Teach the repeating cycle a builder follows for every numbered step in a technical assembly manual, using the StarterBot manual as the concrete example.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) and Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, demonstrate, sequence

Learning objective: Students will explain the purpose of each stage in the read-verify cycle and apply it while working through real StarterBot assembly steps.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart, five process nodes in a loop, rendered top to bottom with an arrow returning from the last node back to the first.

Steps (each is a clickable node with a click directive opening an infobox): 1. "Read the Step" — Hover/click text: "Look at the step's illustration and instructions before touching any parts. Note the step number and any orientation arrows." 2. "Identify Parts" — Hover/click text: "Match each callout in the parts list to a real part in your sorted trays, confirming both the name and the quantity, such as '2x 8-Hole U-Channel.'" 3. "Gather Tools" — Hover/click text: "Set out the correct hex key size and any other tool the step calls for before starting, rather than searching mid-step." 4. "Perform the Step" — Hover/click text: "Assemble the parts exactly as shown, matching the illustrated orientation, such as which face of a U-channel points outward." 5. "Verify" — Hover/click text: "Compare your assembled result to the manual's picture. Check that screws are snug, nothing spins that should be fixed, and nothing is fixed that should spin."

Connections: Step 1 to Step 2 to Step 3 to Step 4 to Step 5, then Step 5 loops back to Step 1 for the next numbered step, with the loop-back arrow labeled "Next Step."

Color coding: Blue for information-gathering steps (Read, Identify, Gather), green for the hands-on step (Perform), gold for the checkpoint step (Verify).

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click directives bound to a JavaScript function that displays the hover text above in a styled infobox beneath the diagram.

Two habits separate a fast, frustration-free build from a slow, error-prone one: reading the entire step before touching a single part, and verifying each step before moving to the next. Skipping verification is how a shim gets left out three steps before it becomes impossible to reach.

docs.title: Guided Robot Assembly
docs.text:
With the reading cycle established, the StarterBot manual's 40 steps group naturally into a handful of larger construction phases. Recognizing these phases helps you understand where you are in the build and what the current step is building toward, rather than experiencing the manual as 40 disconnected instructions.

  1. Frame construction — U-channels are joined using block mounts and standoffs to form the rectangular base and side rails of the chassis, establishing the skeleton every other part attaches to.
  2. Shaft and bearing subassemblies — 8mm REX Shafts are threaded through bearings pressed into the frame, with shims and collars used to set exact spacing, and hubs added to prepare each shaft to receive a wheel, gear, or sprocket.
  3. Chain-and-sprocket and gear drivetrain — sprockets and gears are bolted to the hubs on their shafts, plastic chain links are snapped into closed loops, and the loops are looped over paired sprockets to transmit motor rotation to the wheels.
  4. Drop-center bearing plates — these plates are bolted across the frame to hold the drivetrain shafts in precise alignment so nothing binds or wobbles once the frame is closed up.
  5. Battery mount — the Battery Mount and Battery Strap are installed in a protected, centrally balanced location on the chassis.
  6. Intake roller mechanism — a gear-driven roller subassembly is built separately and then bolted onto the front of the chassis.
  7. Wheels — Gecko Wheels are mounted through servo-driven Compact ServoBlocks, and Omni Wheels and Hogback Wheels are bolted onto their prepared shafts, completing the rolling chassis.

Notice that phases 2 through 4 all revolve around getting shafts to spin smoothly and stay aligned: this is the mechanical heart of the robot, and it is worth double-checking spacing and tightness in these steps even if the manual does not explicitly say to pause and verify.

docs.title: Robot Subassembly Build
docs.text:
A subassembly is a smaller group of parts built and tested as its own unit before it is attached to the main chassis. Manuals for anything mechanically complex, from furniture to aircraft to robots, rely heavily on subassemblies because it is far easier to fix a mistake in a small group of six parts sitting on a workbench than to fix the same mistake after it has been buried inside a fully assembled machine.

The StarterBot manual has you build several subassemblies before they ever touch the main frame: a shaft-bearing-hub subassembly, a sprocket-and-chain drivetrain subassembly, a battery mount subassembly, an intake roller subassembly, and a wheel-and-ServoBlock subassembly for each Gecko wheel. Recognizing which parts belong together as a subassembly, before the manual tells you explicitly, is a skill that becomes more valuable as robots grow more complex in later chapters.

To check how well you can sort real StarterBot parts into their correct subassembly group, work through the matching activity below. It reuses the same part names from the Bill of Materials you explored earlier in this chapter, but now asks you to group them by subassembly rather than by hardware category.

docs.title: Diagram: StarterBot Subassembly Matching Quiz
docs.text:
StarterBot Subassembly Matching Quiz

Type: microsim sim-id: parts-matching-quiz Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Reinforce the concept of a subassembly by having students drag individual StarterBot part names into the correct subassembly bin.

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) and Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, classify, apply

Learning objective: Given a shuffled list of StarterBot part names, students will correctly group each part into the subassembly it belongs to (shaft-bearing-hub, drivetrain, battery mount, intake roller, or wheel/ServoBlock).

Canvas layout: - Left side (60% width): a shuffled stack of draggable part-name tiles (for example "8mm REX Bearing," "10-Tooth Sprocket," "Battery Strap," "30-Tooth Gear," "Compact ServoBlock") - Right side (40% width): five labeled drop bins, one per subassembly, stacked vertically

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop: each part tile can be dragged from the left stack into any bin on the right - "Check My Work" button: highlights correctly placed tiles in green and incorrectly placed tiles in red, and shows the correct bin name for any red tile - "Shuffle New Set" button: loads a new randomized set of 8-10 part tiles from a larger pool of StarterBot parts - "Reset" button: returns all tiles to the left stack

Default parameters: 8 part tiles shown per round, drawn randomly from a pool of 20 real StarterBot part names spanning all five subassemblies.

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled tiles and empty labeled bins with no scoring yet Stage 2: Show each tile as the student drags it, snapping into the nearest bin when released Stage 3: After "Check My Work," show a per-tile color result (green/red) and a running score such as "6 of 8 correct" Stage 4: For any red tile, show a one-line explanation of why it belongs in the correct bin, for example "10-Tooth Sprocket drives the chain loop, so it belongs in the Drivetrain subassembly."

Instructional Rationale: A drag-and-drop matching pattern is appropriate for this Remember/Apply objective because it requires students to recall each part's function well enough to place it correctly, while the immediate check-and-explain feedback corrects misconceptions before they carry into the physical build.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with mouse-drag event handling for tile objects, rectangular bin hit-detection, and a scoring routine triggered by the "Check My Work" button.

docs.title: Build Verification and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The final skill this chapter teaches is knowing how to tell whether a build step, or the finished robot, actually works. Build verification means comparing your physical result against the manual's expected outcome, rather than assuming that "it looks about right" is good enough. On a robot, a part that looks correctly placed but is one shim off, or one screw loose, can still cause a wheel to bind or a chain to skip.

Verification should happen at two levels: after each individual step, as described earlier in the reading cycle, and again after each major phase (frame, drivetrain, battery mount, intake roller, wheels) is complete. At the end of the full 40-step build, spin every wheel by hand, check that the chain loops run smoothly without derailing, and confirm the battery sits securely in its mount.

When something does not work as expected, troubleshooting is the structured process of tracing a symptom back to its likely cause. The table below lists common issues builders encounter on a StarterBot chassis, paired with the most likely cause and fix, since recognizing these patterns quickly will save you from re-checking every single screw in the robot.

Symptom Likely Cause Fix Wheel does not spin freely Bearing misaligned or shaft over-tightened by a collar Loosen the nearest collar, re-center the bearing, and re-tighten gradually Chain slips or derails Sprockets not aligned on parallel shafts, or chain loop too loose Check that both sprockets sit at the same height, and shorten the chain loop by one link if needed Screw will not tighten Wrong hex key size, or threads cross-threaded Confirm the hex key size matches the screw head; back the screw out fully and restart the threads Locknut spins freely with no resistance Nylon insert worn out or wrong-size locknut used Replace with a new locknut of the correct thread size Frame flexes or racks out of square A structural joint is missing a screw, or block mount is loose Recheck every screw at that joint against the manual's callout list Battery shifts during handling Battery Strap not fully tightened Re-tighten the strap and confirm the Battery Mount is bolted to the frame, not just resting in place

Success

If every wheel spins freely by hand, the chain runs without skipping, and the battery is locked into its mount, your StarterBot chassis has passed build verification and is ready for its first test drive.

Quick check: Why does a manual have you build subassemblies separately instead of building everything directly on the main frame? Click to reveal the answer.

Because it is far easier to spot and fix a mistake in a small group of parts on the workbench, such as a shaft-bearing-hub unit, than to diagnose the same mistake after it is buried inside the fully assembled chassis. Subassemblies also let multiple people build different parts of the robot at the same time.

You now have a complete, verified StarterBot chassis and a working vocabulary for every category of part it contains: structural hardware, motion hardware, power and motor components, and fasteners. As the goBILDA manual puts it once the build is finished, "Now that the foundation is built, it's time to shift gears into programming, driver practice, and iterative design." The next chapters take that exact hardware you just assembled and explain the electrical, mechanical, and programming theory behind why it works, using the parts sitting in front of you as the running example.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Now that students have physically built a robot, this chapter puts formal vocabulary to the experience: what robotics and automation actually mean, how the universal systems model (input, process, output, feedback) describes any robotic system, and how robots are categorized (industrial, mobile, humanoid) and applied across industries. Students will be able to describe their own StarterBot in terms of these formal concepts and explain robotics as a field, its history, and its career pathways.

docs.title: What Is Robotics?
docs.text:
You already built a robot before anyone told you what "robotics" means. That order was intentional. Now that a chain-and-sprocket drivetrain, a pair of Yellow Jacket motors, and a set of Gecko wheels sit on your workbench, the formal definitions in this chapter have something real to attach to.

Robotics is the branch of engineering and computer science concerned with designing, building, programming, and operating machines that sense their environment, make decisions, and act on the physical world. Notice that this definition has three parts, and your StarterBot already satisfies all three: it has a physical body (the U-channel frame and drivetrain you assembled), it can be given commands (through programming you will meet in the next chapter), and it acts on the world (spinning wheels, moving an intake roller). A machine that is missing any one of these three parts, sensing, deciding, or acting, is not usually considered a robot in the formal sense.

Robotics is closely related to, but distinct from, automation, the use of technology to perform tasks with reduced human intervention. Automation is a broader idea than robotics: a thermostat that turns a furnace on and off is automation, but nobody would call a thermostat a robot. Robotics is a specific way of achieving automation, one that usually involves a movable, physical machine rather than a fixed control box. Every robot performs automation, but not every automated system is a robot.

The following table clarifies this relationship using examples your class has already encountered, since a table works well here to reinforce a distinction rather than introduce a brand-new idea.

System Automated? Is It a Robot? Why Home thermostat Yes No Fixed in place, no moving body, only switches a furnace on/off Automatic sliding door Yes Debatable Senses motion and acts, but has no broader decision-making or mobility Dishwasher Yes No Follows a fixed timed cycle, does not sense or adapt to its environment StarterBot chassis Yes Yes Senses (once sensors are added), decides via program, and physically moves through space Industrial welding arm Yes Yes Senses part position, follows a programmed decision path, and physically manipulates a tool

At the heart of both automation and robotics is a control system, the combination of hardware and logic that governs how a machine responds to conditions in order to reach a desired outcome. Your StarterBot's chain-and-sprocket drivetrain is a mechanical result, but a control system is what will eventually decide when and how fast those wheels turn. Control systems can be as simple as a thermostat's switch or as complex as the balance-correcting software inside a walking humanoid robot; the rest of this chapter, and an entire later chapter of this course, builds directly on this idea.

docs.title: The Universal Systems Model
docs.text:
Every robot, no matter how simple or advanced, can be described using the same four-part framework: the universal systems model. This model states that any system, robotic or otherwise, transforms something it receives into something it produces, and that a well-designed system checks its own results and adjusts accordingly. Learning to see this pattern is more valuable than memorizing any single robot's parts list, because the same four-part lens applies to a thermostat, a StarterBot, a spacecraft, and a national power grid alike.

The four parts of the universal systems model are:

  1. System input — information or material that enters a system from the outside, such as a sensor reading, a button press, or a command from a program
  2. System process — the internal logic, calculation, or mechanism that transforms input into a planned action
  3. System output — the result the system produces and delivers to the world, such as a motor turning or a message displayed
  4. System feedback — information about the output that is returned to the system so it can check and adjust its own future behavior

Rather than memorize this list in the abstract, it helps to map each term onto a robot you already understand from the inside out. Explore the interactive model below, which uses your own StarterBot as the running example for each of the four stages.

docs.title: Diagram: Universal Systems Model on the StarterBot
docs.text:
Universal Systems Model on the StarterBot

Type: diagram sim-id: universal-systems-model Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Purpose: Teach the four components of the universal systems model (input, process, output, feedback) by mapping each stage onto the real StarterBot the students built in Chapter 1.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: classify, exemplify, explain

Learning objective: Given a description of a robotic behavior, students will correctly classify each described event as system input, process, output, or feedback, and explain how the four stages connect in a continuous loop.

Components to show: - Four large clickable nodes arranged left to right in a loop: "Input," "Process," "Output," "Feedback" - A curved arrow returning from "Feedback" back to "Input," visually closing the loop - Each node is color-coded and labeled with its formal name

Connections: Input to Process to Output to Feedback to Input, forming a continuous cycle rather than a one-way line.

Interactive elements: - Clicking "Input" opens an infobox: "Input — information entering the system. StarterBot example: a driver's joystick command, or a future distance-sensor reading." - Clicking "Process" opens an infobox: "Process — internal logic that decides what to do. StarterBot example: the onboard program deciding how fast to spin each drive motor based on the joystick value." - Clicking "Output" opens an infobox: "Output — the result delivered to the world. StarterBot example: the Yellow Jacket motors turning, driving the chain-and-sprocket drivetrain, moving the wheels." - Clicking "Feedback" opens an infobox: "Feedback — information about the output sent back into the system. StarterBot example: a future encoder reporting how far the wheel actually turned, so the program can correct its next command." - A "Play Example" button animates a token traveling around the loop once, pausing briefly at each node.

Visual style: Circular/looped network diagram, force-directed layout locked to a left-to-right circular arrangement.

Color scheme: Blue for Input, gold for Process, green for Output, orange for Feedback, with the loop-back arrow in orange to match Feedback.

Implementation: vis-network with a fixed circular layout (not force-directed, to keep the loop shape stable), click event listeners on each node opening a shared infobox panel, and a simple animated marker for the "Play Example" button.

Feedback deserves special attention because it is what separates a genuinely adaptive system from one that simply follows a script. A system with no feedback, like a wind-up toy car, runs exactly the same way every time regardless of what happens around it. A system with feedback, like a modern robot with encoders and sensors, can detect when its output did not match its intended result and correct course. You built the mechanical hardware for feedback (motors, and eventually sensors) in Chapter 1; the programming chapters ahead will show you how to write the logic that actually closes the loop.

Tip

A useful habit for the rest of this course: whenever you read about a new robot subsystem, ask "what is its input, what is its process, what is its output, and does it have feedback?" That single question will make almost every future control-system topic easier to understand.

docs.title: Defining "Robot" and Sorting Robots by Type
docs.text:
With the systems model as a foundation, it is time to settle a question this chapter has been circling: what exactly counts as a robot? A workable definition, and the one this course uses, is that a robot is a programmable, physical machine that senses its environment (or at least receives input), processes that input according to a set of instructions, and acts on the physical world through some form of movement or manipulation. This definition intentionally lines up with the universal systems model: if a machine cannot be described in terms of input, process, and output, it probably is not a robot.

Not every robot looks or works the same way, however. Robots are typically sorted into types of robots based on where they operate and what physical form they take. This course focuses on three major categories:

  • Industrial robots — robots fixed in one location, typically a factory floor, that repeatedly perform a precise physical task such as welding, painting, or assembling parts
  • Mobile robots — robots designed to move through an environment, on wheels, tracks, legs, or propellers, to reach different locations rather than staying fixed in place
  • Humanoid robots — robots built with a body plan that resembles a human's, typically including a torso, two arms, and often two legs, designed to operate in spaces and use tools built for people

Your own StarterBot is a clear example of a mobile robot: its chain-and-sprocket drivetrain and Gecko/Omni/Hogback wheel combination exist specifically so it can travel across a competition field, not stay bolted to one spot. Contrast that with the welding arm mentioned earlier in this chapter, which is bolted to a factory floor and never relocates itself: that is an industrial robot. A robot with a humanlike torso, arms, and legs designed to walk through spaces built for people falls into the third category.

Because these three categories differ along several dimensions at once, mobility, typical environment, and typical task, the diagram below lets you explore each category and compare real-world examples side by side rather than trying to hold all three definitions in your head simultaneously.

docs.title: Diagram: Robot Type Classifier
docs.text:
Robot Type Classifier

Type: workflow sim-id: robot-type-classifier Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students distinguish industrial, mobile, and humanoid robots by exploring clickable real-world examples of each category, including where the StarterBot fits.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: differentiate, classify, compare, contrast

Learning objective: Given a description or image of an unfamiliar robot, students will classify it as industrial, mobile, or humanoid, and justify the classification using the robot's mobility, environment, and task.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart styled as a three-branch classification tree, with a root node "Robot" branching into three category nodes, each of which branches further into 2-3 real-world example nodes.

Steps (each node is clickable with a click directive opening an infobox): 1. Root node: "Robot" — click text: "A programmable machine that senses, processes, and acts on the physical world." 2. Branch: "Industrial Robots" — click text: "Fixed in place, perform a repeated precise task, common in factories." 3. Example under Industrial: "Welding Arm" — click text: "Bolted to a factory floor; repeats the same weld path thousands of times per shift." 4. Example under Industrial: "Pick-and-Place Arm" — click text: "Picks parts from a conveyor and places them precisely into packaging or assembly." 5. Branch: "Mobile Robots" — click text: "Designed to travel through an environment using wheels, tracks, legs, or propellers." 6. Example under Mobile: "Your StarterBot" — click text: "Uses a chain-and-sprocket drivetrain and Gecko/Omni/Hogback wheels to travel across a competition field." 7. Example under Mobile: "Warehouse Delivery Robot" — click text: "Navigates warehouse aisles autonomously to move inventory between shelves and packing stations." 8. Example under Mobile: "Mars Rover" — click text: "Drives across uneven planetary terrain using specialized wheels, operating far from any human operator." 9. Branch: "Humanoid Robots" — click text: "Built with a body plan resembling a human, often with a torso, arms, and legs." 10. Example under Humanoid: "Warehouse Humanoid Assistant" — click text: "Designed to walk through aisles and use shelves and tools built for human workers." 11. Example under Humanoid: "Research/Disaster-Response Humanoid" — click text: "Designed to operate stairs, ladders, and doors originally built for people during search-and-rescue tasks."

Connections: Root branches to the three category nodes; each category node branches to its own example nodes. No cross-links between categories.

Color coding: Gray for the root node, orange for Industrial and its examples, blue for Mobile and its examples (with the StarterBot example highlighted in a distinct gold outline), purple for Humanoid and its examples.

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax (graph TD) with click directives bound to a JavaScript function displaying each node's text in a styled infobox beneath the diagram.

It is worth noting that these three categories are not the only way to sort robots, and some robots blend categories, for example a mobile robot with two arms bolted on for manipulation. For this course, however, industrial, mobile, and humanoid cover the vast majority of robots you will encounter in industry, research, and competition, and they give you a shared vocabulary for describing any new robot you meet.

docs.title: Robotics Applications
docs.text:
Robots show up far beyond factories and competition fields. Robotics applications refers to the wide range of industries and tasks where robots are put to practical use, and recognizing this breadth helps explain why robotics careers, covered later in this chapter, span so many different fields.

Consider how differently the three robot types you just learned show up across industries:

  • Manufacturing — industrial robotic arms weld car frames, place electronic components on circuit boards, and package finished products at speeds and precision no human could sustain for an entire shift
  • Agriculture — mobile robots and automated harvesters drive through fields to plant seeds, apply fertilizer precisely, and pick fruit without bruising it
  • Healthcare — surgical robots give surgeons finer control and steadier hands during delicate procedures, while mobile robots deliver medications and supplies through hospital hallways
  • Logistics and warehousing — fleets of mobile robots move shelves and packages through massive distribution centers, coordinating with each other to avoid collisions
  • Space exploration — mobile rovers and robotic arms operate in environments too distant, radioactive, or otherwise dangerous for a human crew
  • Disaster response — mobile and humanoid robots search collapsed buildings, inspect damaged nuclear facilities, and handle suspected explosives from a safe distance

Every one of these applications, no matter the industry, is still built from the same universal systems model you learned earlier in this chapter: something senses or receives input, something processes that input, something acts as output, and increasingly, something checks that output through feedback.

docs.title: Robotics Careers
docs.text:
The breadth of robotics applications you just read about translates directly into breadth of robotics careers, the range of jobs available to people who design, build, program, maintain, and manage robotic systems. It is a common misconception that "robotics" means only writing code; in reality, the field draws on mechanical, electrical, and software skills in roughly equal measure, along with several career paths that do not involve hands-on building at all.

The table below organizes common robotics career paths by the primary skill set each one relies on, since a table is well suited to comparing several distinct roles along a shared set of categories.

Career Path Primary Focus Example Task Robotics/mechanical engineer Physical design and mechanisms Designing a new drivetrain or gripper mechanism Robotics software/controls engineer Programming and control systems Writing the code that closes a feedback loop for stable movement Electrical/electronics engineer Circuits, sensors, and power systems Designing sensor wiring and power distribution for a robot Robotics technician Assembly, maintenance, and troubleshooting Diagnosing and fixing a robot that has stopped functioning correctly on a production line Robotics field service specialist On-site installation and repair Traveling to a factory to install and calibrate a new industrial robot Robotics project manager Planning and coordinating teams Scheduling a multi-discipline team building a new mobile robot product

Every skill you practiced in Chapter 1, reading a Bill of Materials, following an assembly manual, verifying a finished build, maps directly onto entry-level work as a robotics technician. The formal vocabulary in this chapter maps onto the engineering roles above it in the table.

docs.title: Robotics History
docs.text:
Robotics did not appear all at once; it grew out of decades of automation and control system research, each era building the foundation the next era relied on. Understanding robotics history helps explain why today's robots look and work the way they do, and it shows that the field is still changing quickly, meaning the robots you build in this course sit on a continuum rather than at some final, finished endpoint.

Rather than reading a static list of dates, explore the interactive timeline below, which highlights the milestones most relevant to the industrial, mobile, and humanoid robot categories you just learned.

docs.title: Diagram: Milestones in Robotics History
docs.text:
Milestones in Robotics History

Type: timeline sim-id: robotics-history-timeline Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students historical context for how robotics grew from early automation and control theory into today's industrial, mobile, and humanoid robots.

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) and Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: recall, identify, summarize

Learning objective: Students will recall key milestones in robotics history and summarize how each milestone connects to a robot type or concept introduced earlier in this chapter.

Time period covered: 1950s-present

Orientation: Horizontal

Events: - 1954: George Devol patents Unimate, the first programmable industrial robotic arm concept, later installed on a General Motors assembly line in 1961 - 1961: Unimate begins working on a GM factory floor, marking the first true industrial robot in commercial use - 1969: The Stanford Cart, an early mobile robot, navigates obstacles using a camera and remote computer processing - 1973: WABOT-1, developed in Japan, becomes one of the first full-scale humanoid robots able to walk and manipulate objects - 1997: Sojourner, a small mobile rover, becomes the first wheeled robot to explore the surface of Mars - 2000: Honda unveils ASIMO, a humanoid robot capable of walking, running, and climbing stairs, advancing humanoid robotics research significantly - 2011-2012: Curiosity rover lands on Mars, an advanced mobile robot carrying a full science laboratory - 2010s: Warehouse mobile robot fleets (such as those used by major online retailers) become widespread in logistics - 2020s: Advanced humanoid robots begin pilot deployments in warehouses and factories alongside industrial robotic arms - Today: FIRST Tech Challenge teams, including this class, build mobile robots like the StarterBot using the same core concepts (motors, drivetrains, control systems, feedback) as commercial and research robots

Visual style: Horizontal timeline with alternating above/below event placement to avoid crowding.

Color coding: Orange for industrial robot milestones, blue for mobile robot milestones, purple for humanoid robot milestones, gold for the final "Today" event connecting history to the student's own build.

Interactive features: - Clicking or hovering any event opens an infobox with the full description above - A "Filter" control lets students show only industrial, only mobile, only humanoid milestones, or all of them together - Zooming and panning are enabled so students can spread out densely packed decades

Implementation: vis-timeline JavaScript library with a DataSet of the above events, group filtering tied to a color/category field, and a click event handler opening a shared infobox panel.

Notice how each type of robot you learned earlier in this chapter, industrial, mobile, and humanoid, has its own distinct historical thread, and that all three threads continue to advance today, often influencing each other as engineers borrow ideas across categories.

docs.title: Robotics Ethics
docs.text:
As robots take on more tasks once done only by people, questions of robotics ethics become impossible to ignore: the study of the moral and social responsibilities that come with designing, deploying, and using robots. This is not an abstract concern reserved for advanced researchers; it is directly relevant to the applications and careers covered earlier in this chapter.

A few of the central questions in robotics ethics include:

  • Job displacement — when an industrial robot replaces a task once done by a human worker, what responsibility do companies and engineers have toward the people affected?
  • Safety — how much testing and how many safeguards are required before a mobile or humanoid robot works safely alongside people?
  • Privacy — mobile robots often carry cameras and sensors; who has access to the data they collect, and how long should it be kept?
  • Accountability — when an autonomous robot's decision causes harm, who is responsible: the programmer, the manufacturer, or the operator?
  • Access and fairness — as robotics transforms industries and creates new careers, who has access to the education and training needed to participate in those careers?

Question

Suppose a mobile warehouse robot and a human worker occupy the same aisle at the same time, and the robot must choose to either stop suddenly (risking the goods it carries) or continue on its current path (risking the worker). Who should decide the rule the robot follows in that moment, and what values should that rule prioritize?

These questions do not have a single correct answer, but engineers who understand the universal systems model from earlier in this chapter are better equipped to reason about them: every ethical question above can be traced to a specific input, process, output, or feedback decision that a human designer had to make somewhere in the system. Robotics ethics, in other words, is what happens when you ask "and what should this system's process actually decide?"

Quick check: Is a home thermostat a robot? Click to reveal the answer.

No. A thermostat is automation, technology performing a task with reduced human intervention, but it lacks the physical mobility and manipulation typically required to call it a robot. It also does not fit the three robot type categories (industrial, mobile, humanoid) covered in this chapter, since it never moves or acts on objects in the world beyond switching a furnace on or off.

You now have the formal vocabulary to describe the robot sitting on your workbench: it is a mobile robot, built from real hardware, that will eventually take input from sensors and drivers, run that input through a process you will program, produce output through its motors and drivetrain, and improve over time through feedback. The chapters ahead return to this same StarterBot again and again, first to teach you the programming that drives its process, and later to add the sensors and control logic that close its feedback loop.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Before students write a single line of robot code, this chapter builds general-purpose programming skills: algorithms, pseudocode, flowcharts, variables, data types, conditional statements, loops, functions, and debugging. Program testing and program security are also introduced. These concepts are taught independent of any particular hardware, so students can focus purely on computational thinking before applying it to their robot in the next chapter.
