docs.title: Thinking Like a Programmer: What Is an Algorithm?
docs.text:
Before you write a single line of code, you need a plan. An algorithm is a finite, ordered sequence of precise steps that solves a problem or completes a task, taking some starting information as input and producing a predictable result as output. Notice that this definition does not mention computers at all, because algorithms exist everywhere in daily life, not just inside a program.

Consider a recipe for making a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. It has a clear starting point (two slices of bread and a knife), a clear sequence of steps (open the jars, spread the peanut butter, spread the jelly, put the slices together), and a clear ending point (a finished sandwich). A computer program's algorithm works the same way, except the "ingredients" are data and the "steps" are instructions a computer can carry out.

For a sequence of steps to count as a true algorithm, and not just a vague suggestion, it generally needs to satisfy several properties:

  1. Finite — the algorithm must eventually stop; it cannot run forever
  2. Ordered — the steps happen in a specific, defined sequence
  3. Unambiguous — each step is precise enough that there is only one reasonable way to carry it out
  4. Has input and output — the algorithm starts with some given information and produces a result

Throughout the rest of this chapter, one running example will appear again and again: an algorithm that checks whether a whole number is even or odd. It is simple enough to hold in your head, yet rich enough to demonstrate every concept from pseudocode through functions. Keep it in mind as each new tool for expressing and organizing algorithms is introduced.

docs.title: Expressing Algorithms Before Writing Code: Pseudocode and Flowcharts
docs.text:
Programmers rarely jump straight from an idea to finished code. Instead, they first sketch the algorithm in a form that is easy to think through and easy to change, before worrying about the strict rules of any particular programming language. Two of the most common tools for this planning stage are pseudocode and flowcharts.

Pseudocode is a way of describing an algorithm's steps using structured, plain language that resembles real code but does not follow the exact syntax rules of any specific programming language. Pseudocode lets you focus entirely on the logic of a solution, the order of decisions and repeated steps, without getting distracted by punctuation, spelling of commands, or which language you eventually plan to use.

The pseudocode below describes the even-or-odd algorithm introduced earlier. Read it as a numbered set of plain-language instructions: it takes a number, divides it by 2, and checks whether anything is left over.

GET the number from the user
CALCULATE the remainder when the number is divided by 2
IF the remainder equals 0 THEN
    DISPLAY "The number is even"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "The number is odd"
END IF

Notice that this pseudocode reads almost like an ordinary sentence, yet it is precise enough that any programmer, regardless of which programming language they prefer, could translate it into working code. That translatability is exactly why pseudocode is such a valuable planning tool.

A flowchart is a diagram that represents an algorithm visually, using a small set of standardized shapes connected by arrows to show the exact order in which operations occur. Flowcharts use ovals for start and end points, rectangles for process steps (an action the algorithm performs), diamonds for decision points (a yes/no or true/false question that branches the flow), and arrows to connect everything in sequence. Because a flowchart is visual, it often reveals the branching structure of an algorithm, especially one full of decisions, more clearly than a written list of steps can.

Rather than only reading about what each flowchart shape means, explore the interactive diagram below, which lets you click each shape and each connecting arrow to see how it maps onto the even-or-odd algorithm you just read as pseudocode.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Flowchart
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Flowchart

Type: diagram sim-id: flowchart-anatomy Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Teach the four core flowchart shapes (start/end oval, process rectangle, decision diamond, connecting arrow) by mapping each one onto the even-or-odd algorithm introduced in this section's pseudocode.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, explain, classify

Learning objective: Given an unfamiliar flowchart, students will identify each shape by name, explain its purpose, and classify each step of the even-or-odd algorithm as a start/end, process, or decision shape.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart (graph TD) laid out top-to-bottom, mirroring the pseudocode's step order exactly.

Nodes (each node clickable with a click directive opening an infobox): 1. Start oval: "Start" — click text: "The oval shape marks where an algorithm begins. Every flowchart has exactly one start shape." 2. Process rectangle: "Get the number from the user" — click text: "A rectangle represents a process step: an action the algorithm performs, with no decision involved." 3. Process rectangle: "Calculate remainder (number divided by 2)" — click text: "Another process step. Process shapes can perform calculations, not just input/output actions." 4. Decision diamond: "Remainder equals 0?" — click text: "A diamond represents a decision point: a yes/no question that sends the flow down one of two different paths." 5. Process rectangle (Yes branch): "Display 'even'" — click text: "This process step only runs if the decision above was answered Yes." 6. Process rectangle (No branch): "Display 'odd'" — click text: "This process step only runs if the decision above was answered No." 7. End oval: "End" — click text: "The oval shape also marks where an algorithm finishes. Both branches lead back to a single end shape."

Connections: Start to Get-Number to Calculate-Remainder to the Decision diamond, which splits into a Yes arrow (labeled "Yes") to Display-Even and a No arrow (labeled "No") to Display-Odd; both branches merge into the single End oval.

Color coding: Green for the start/end ovals, blue for process rectangles, gold for the decision diamond, with the Yes arrow shown in green and the No arrow shown in orange.

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click directives bound to a JavaScript function that displays each shape's explanatory text in a styled infobox beneath the diagram.

Pseudocode and flowcharts describe the exact same algorithm in two different formats, one written and one visual, and many programmers move back and forth between them while planning. Once the logic in either format feels solid, it is time to translate it into an actual programming language.

docs.title: From Plan to Code: Programming Languages and Syntax
docs.text:
A programming language is a formal language with a defined vocabulary and grammar that a person uses to write instructions a computer can eventually carry out. Unlike the flexible plain language used in pseudocode, a programming language must follow strict, exact rules, because a computer cannot guess what a programmer "probably meant" the way a human reader often can.

Hundreds of programming languages exist, including Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, and block-based languages that let programmers snap together labeled puzzle pieces instead of typing text. Despite looking very different on the surface, most of these languages can express the exact same underlying algorithm, including the even-or-odd logic from the pseudocode above.

The table below shows that one algorithm, expressed three different ways: as pseudocode you already read, as text-based code in a Python-like language, and as the equivalent idea in a block-based language. Comparing them side by side highlights that the underlying logic never changes, only its surface appearance does.

Representation How the "IF remainder = 0" step looks Pseudocode IF the remainder equals 0 THEN Text-based language (Python-like) if remainder == 0: Block-based language An "if" puzzle piece with an equals-comparison piece snapped inside it

This strict set of rules that a language enforces, exactly how symbols, punctuation, spacing, and keywords must be arranged for a program to be considered valid, is called code syntax. Every programming language has its own syntax: Python requires a colon and consistent indentation after an if, while other languages require curly braces { } instead. A program that violates its language's syntax will not run at all, regardless of how correct its underlying algorithm is.

Tip

Almost every beginning programmer's first frustration is a syntax error, a missing colon, an extra parenthesis, a misspelled keyword. This is completely normal. Learning a programming language's syntax is a lot like learning the grammar rules of a new spoken language: frustrating at first, automatic with practice.

docs.title: Storing Information: Variables and Data Types
docs.text:
Every useful program needs somewhere to keep track of information while it runs, whether that is a number a user typed in, a score, or a sensor reading you will meet in the next chapter. A variable is a named storage location in a program's memory that holds a value, and that value can change while the program runs, which is exactly why it is called "variable" rather than "constant."

Returning to the even-or-odd example, the number a user provides needs somewhere to live while the program works with it. A programmer might create a variable named number to hold that value, and a second variable named remainder to hold the result of dividing by 2. Giving variables clear, descriptive names, number rather than a meaningless label like x1, makes code dramatically easier for other programmers, or your future self, to read and understand later.

Not every variable can hold just any kind of value, however. A data type is a classification that tells the programming language what kind of value a variable holds and what operations can legally be performed on it. A variable storing a whole number behaves differently, and supports different operations, than a variable storing a sentence of text.

The table below summarizes the four data types you will encounter most often, along with an example value for each, reinforcing the definition you just read rather than introducing anything new.

Data Type What It Stores Example Value Integer A whole number, positive or negative, with no decimal point 7, -3, 1000 Float (decimal) A number that includes a fractional, decimal part 3.14, -0.5 String A sequence of text characters "even", "StarterBot" Boolean Exactly one of two values: true or false True, False

In the even-or-odd example, the variable number would typically use the integer data type, since the algorithm is only designed to work with whole numbers. If a data type mismatch occurs, for example trying to divide a piece of text by 2, the program will usually fail with an error, which is one reason data types matter even though they can feel like an invisible detail at first.

A few practical guidelines make variables easier to use correctly:

  • Choose a name that describes what the variable stores, such as remainder instead of r
  • Pick the data type that matches the kind of value the variable will actually hold
  • Avoid reusing the same variable name for two unrelated purposes within one program
  • Give a variable an initial value before using it in a calculation

docs.title: Controlling the Flow: Conditional Statements and Loop Structures
docs.text:
So far, the even-or-odd algorithm has moved through its steps in a straight, single-file line. Most useful algorithms are not that simple; they need to make decisions and repeat work. Two structures make this possible: conditional statements and loop structures.

A conditional statement is an instruction that tells a program to execute certain steps only if a specified condition is true, and optionally execute different steps if that condition is false. The even-or-odd pseudocode you read earlier already contains one: the IF the remainder equals 0 THEN ... ELSE ... structure is a conditional statement, branching the program down one of two paths depending on the result of a calculation.

A loop structure is an instruction that repeats a set of steps multiple times, either a fixed number of times or for as long as a specified condition remains true. Suppose you wanted to check every number from 1 through 10 for even or odd, instead of just one number typed in by a user. Repeating the entire even-or-odd conditional ten separate times by hand would be tedious and error-prone; a loop structure lets the algorithm repeat the same logic automatically.

The pseudocode below combines a loop structure and a conditional statement to check ten numbers in a row. Read it as: repeat the following steps once for each number from 1 to 10, and within each repetition, make the same even/odd decision as before.

FOR each number from 1 to 10
    CALCULATE the remainder when the number is divided by 2
    IF the remainder equals 0 THEN
        DISPLAY number, "is even"
    ELSE
        DISPLAY number, "is odd"
    END IF
END FOR

Notice that the conditional statement inside this loop is identical to the one from the single-number version; the loop structure is simply what allows that same decision-making logic to run automatically ten times instead of once. This pattern, a loop that contains a conditional statement, is one of the most common building blocks in programming.

Rather than only reading pseudocode, it helps to physically arrange these building blocks yourself and watch the resulting algorithm run step by step. The MicroSim below lets you drag conditional and loop blocks into a workspace, connect them in order, and press "Run" to see the resulting algorithm execute visually.

docs.title: Diagram: Algorithm Block Builder
docs.text:
Algorithm Block Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: algorithm-block-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students construct a simple algorithm by dragging and connecting conditional and loop blocks, then watch the assembled algorithm execute step by step against a small list of numbers.

Bloom Taxonomy: Create (L6) and Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: construct, arrange, execute, demonstrate

Learning objective: Students will arrange loop and conditional blocks into a working sequence that correctly classifies a list of numbers as even or odd, and will trace execution to demonstrate how a loop structure repeats a conditional statement.

Canvas layout: - Left side (60% width): a palette of draggable blocks: "Start Loop (repeat for each number in list)," "If remainder = 0," "Display 'even'," "Display 'odd'," "End If," "End Loop" - Right side (40% width): a workspace where dragged blocks snap into a vertical sequence, plus a "Run" button, a "Reset" button, and a small output console

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop: blocks can be dragged from the palette into the workspace and reordered - Dropdown: choose the input list (default: the numbers 1 through 5) - Button: "Run" — executes the assembled block sequence one step at a time - Button: "Step" — advances execution by a single instruction, highlighting the active block - Button: "Reset" — clears the workspace back to an empty sequence

Default parameters: - Input list: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] - Palette blocks start unplaced; a "Load Example" button can populate a correct default sequence for first-time users

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the current number being processed from the input list, highlighted in the console Stage 2: Show the calculated remainder for that number Stage 3: Show which branch (even/odd display block) executed, with that block highlighted in the workspace Stage 4: Show the accumulated output console listing every number processed so far and its classification Final: Show the completed output list matching all numbers in the input list

Behavior: - If blocks are assembled correctly (loop containing a complete if/else/end-if inside a start-loop/end-loop pair), "Run" animates through the list, highlighting the active block and updating the console after each step - If blocks are missing a required piece (for example, no "End If"), clicking "Run" displays an infobox explaining which structural piece is missing, without crashing - Correct assembly is confirmed with a green checkmark and a message: "Your loop successfully repeated the conditional check for every number in the list."

Instructional Rationale: A Create-level objective requires students to actively construct a working sequence rather than passively view one. Drag-and-drop block assembly, paired with step-through execution showing concrete data at each stage, lets students build understanding of how a loop structure repeats a conditional statement without requiring them to know any language's exact code syntax yet.

Implementation: p5.js for canvas rendering and drag-and-drop detection; blocks stored as an array of typed objects; a simple step-based interpreter executes the array against the input list and reports state after each step.

Conditional statements and loop structures are two of the most powerful tools in any programmer's toolkit, precisely because so many real-world problems boil down to "make a decision" and "repeat something," combined in different arrangements.

docs.title: Organizing Code: Functions
docs.text:
As algorithms grow larger, repeating the same block of logic by copying and pasting it everywhere becomes messy and hard to maintain. A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task, can accept input values called parameters, and can return a result, and can be called from other parts of a program whenever that task needs to happen again.

The even-or-odd logic used throughout this chapter is a perfect candidate to become a function, since it might be needed in many different places within a larger program. The pseudocode below wraps that logic inside a function named checkEvenOdd, which accepts one input (a number) and displays whether it is even or odd.

FUNCTION checkEvenOdd(number)
    CALCULATE the remainder when number is divided by 2
    IF the remainder equals 0 THEN
        RETURN "even"
    ELSE
        RETURN "odd"
    END IF
END FUNCTION

Once defined, this function can be called, or invoked, from anywhere else in the program simply by name, for example checkEvenOdd(7), without rewriting the underlying logic each time. Functions offer several concrete benefits to a program's design:

  • Reuse — the same logic can be called many times from different places without duplicating code
  • Organization — breaking a large algorithm into named functions makes the overall program easier to read
  • Easier testing — a small, isolated function is much simpler to test thoroughly than one giant block of code
  • Abstraction — a function lets other parts of a program use its result without needing to know exactly how it works internally

You will use functions constantly once you begin writing real code, and in the next chapter, individual robot behaviors, like driving forward or checking a sensor, will often be organized as their own functions.

docs.title: Where You Write Code: Programming Platforms and IDEs
docs.text:
Every program needs somewhere to actually be written, translated, and run. A programming platform is the combination of hardware and software environment where a program is written, is translated into a form the hardware understands, and ultimately runs. A programming platform might be an ordinary desktop computer, a web browser running JavaScript, or, as you will discover in the next chapter, a microcontroller platform built specifically to run inside a robot.

Within a programming platform, most programmers do not simply type code into a bare text file. A programming IDE, short for Integrated Development Environment, is a software application that combines a code editor, tools that automatically highlight syntax errors, and a way to run or test the program, all within one convenient application. An IDE dramatically speeds up the process of writing, checking, and running code compared to switching between several separate, disconnected tools.

The table below compares what a plain text editor offers against what a full programming IDE typically adds, since a table is well suited to comparing two options across a shared set of features.

Feature Plain Text Editor Programming IDE Write code Yes Yes Highlight syntax errors automatically No Yes Suggest code as you type (autocomplete) No Usually Run or test the program with one click No Yes Built-in tools for finding bugs No Yes

Choosing to write code inside a proper IDE, rather than a plain text editor, is one of the simplest ways to reduce frustrating syntax errors before a program is ever run. The next chapter introduces the specific programming platform and IDE you will use to write real code for your StarterBot, building directly on the vocabulary from this section.

docs.title: Making Sure Code Works: Debugging, Testing, and Security
docs.text:
Writing an algorithm and translating it into correctly formatted code is only the beginning; real programs almost never work perfectly on the first attempt. The remainder of this chapter covers three closely related practices that professional programmers rely on constantly: debugging, program testing, and program security.

Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors, commonly called bugs, in a program's code so the program behaves as its algorithm intended. A bug can be a syntax error that stops the program from running at all, or something more subtle: a program that runs without crashing but produces the wrong answer, often because of a small mistake in a conditional statement or loop structure.

Rather than only reading a description of debugging, it helps to practice spotting a real bug yourself. The interactive exercise below shows a broken version of the even-or-odd function from earlier in this chapter, with one line highlighted, and challenges you to identify the mistake before revealing the explanation.

docs.title: Diagram: Spot the Bug
docs.text:
Spot the Bug

Type: infographic sim-id: spot-the-bug-even-odd Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Build debugging skill by presenting a broken version of the chapter's running even-or-odd function and letting students judge what is wrong before the fix is revealed.

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: judge, critique, justify, assess

Learning objective: Given a short block of pseudocode containing a single logic error, students will judge which line is incorrect, justify why it produces the wrong output, and assess the corrected version against the original algorithm's intent.

Layout: A code panel on the left displaying the buggy pseudocode with line numbers; a control and infobox panel on the right.

Buggy code shown (line 3 highlighted in red by default): 

FUNCTION checkEvenOdd(number)
    CALCULATE the remainder when number is divided by 2
    IF the remainder equals 1 THEN
        RETURN "even"
    ELSE
        RETURN "odd"
    END IF
END FUNCTION

Interactive elements: - Students click any line number to submit a guess for where the bug is located - Clicking the correct line (line 3) reveals an infobox: "Bug found: the condition checks 'remainder equals 1' but a remainder of 1 means the number is ODD, not even. The comparison value should be 0, matching the original algorithm's definition of an even number." - Clicking an incorrect line reveals an infobox explaining why that line is actually correct, reinforcing understanding of the surrounding code rather than only confirming wrong answers - A "Show Fixed Version" button reveals the corrected pseudocode side by side with the original for comparison - A "Test It" panel lets students enter a sample number and see what the buggy version outputs versus what the corrected version outputs, making the consequence of the bug concrete

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the buggy code as-is, with no annotations, so students form their own judgment first Stage 2: After a guess, show the infobox explanation tied to the clicked line Stage 3: Show the corrected code alongside the original for direct comparison Stage 4: Show a worked test case, for example input 4, producing "odd" from the buggy version and "even" from the corrected version

Instructional Rationale: An Evaluate-level objective requires students to critique and justify, not just passively observe a fix. Requiring a guess before any explanation is revealed forces active judgment, and showing feedback for both correct and incorrect line guesses reinforces understanding of the whole function rather than only the single bug.

Implementation: p5.js for the code panel rendering and clickable line numbers; a small interpreter evaluates both the buggy and corrected pseudocode against a student-entered test number for the "Test It" panel.

Finding and fixing one bug, however, does not guarantee a program is fully correct. Program testing is the practice of deliberately running a program with a variety of inputs, including unusual or extreme edge cases, to verify it produces the correct expected output before it is trusted or put into real use. A thorough tester of the even-or-odd function would not stop after trying the number 4; a complete test plan checks several different kinds of input:

  • Typical cases — ordinary numbers such as 4 or 7, to confirm the basic logic works
  • Edge cases — unusual boundary values such as 0 (which is even) or a negative number such as -2
  • Invalid input — values the algorithm was never designed to handle, such as text typed in instead of a number

Skipping edge cases and invalid input is one of the most common reasons real programs fail unexpectedly once actual users, or in a future chapter, sensors and real-world conditions, start providing input the programmer never anticipated during initial testing.

Beyond correctness, a finished program must also be trustworthy in a different sense. Program security refers to the practices and design choices that protect a program and its data from unintended misuse, unauthorized access, or malicious attack. Even a simple program that checks even or odd could be poorly secured if, for example, it crashed or behaved unpredictably whenever it received unexpected input, since predictable failure is itself a basic security concern.

Warning

Two beginner-friendly security habits are worth building now, long before you work with any sensitive data: never assume input will arrive in the exact form you expect, and always double-check any input before your program acts on it. A program that carefully validates its inputs, confirming a value really is a number before dividing it, is already practicing a basic form of program security.

Debugging, program testing, and program security are not separate, one-time chores performed after "real" programming is finished. They are ongoing habits woven throughout the entire process of building any algorithm, from its first pseudocode sketch through its final, working code.

Quick check: A loop repeats a decision-making step ten times, but the program only ever prints 'even.' What kind of concept from this chapter is most likely broken? Click to reveal the answer.

Most likely a bug in the conditional statement, for example comparing the remainder to the wrong value or always following the same branch regardless of the calculated remainder. This is exactly the kind of mistake the "Spot the Bug" exercise in this chapter trained you to look for: a program that runs without crashing but still produces the wrong output.

You now have a complete, hardware-independent toolkit for thinking like a programmer: algorithms, pseudocode, and flowcharts for planning; programming languages, syntax, variables, and data types for expressing a plan precisely; conditional statements, loop structures, and functions for controlling and organizing that logic; and programming platforms, IDEs, debugging, testing, and security for actually building and trusting real, working programs. In the next chapter, "Programming Your Robot," every one of these concepts returns, applied directly to the StarterBot sitting on your workbench.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter is where the robot comes to life. Students apply what they learned in Programming Fundamentals to the microcontroller that runs their StarterBot, learning what sensors and actuators are, the difference between open-loop and closed-loop control, and how a feedback loop and control loop work. Students will write their first robot programs: reading sensor input, commanding an actuator, and building a basic robot control loop capable of simple autonomous behavior.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 12 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Sensor
  2. Actuator
  3. Open-Loop Control
  4. Closed-Loop Control
  5. Feedback Loop
  6. Control Loop
  7. Microcontroller
  8. Robot Programming
  9. Sensor Input Programming
  10. Actuator Output Programming
  11. Robot Control Loop
  12. Autonomous Behavior

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Introduction to Robotics and Systems
  • Chapter 3: Programming Fundamentals

docs.title: Microcontroller: Your Robot's Onboard Computer
docs.text:
Every program you wrote in the last chapter, the even-or-odd checker included, ran on a laptop or desktop computer with a keyboard, a screen, and someone typing input by hand. A robot has none of those things sitting on its chassis, yet it still needs somewhere to run a program. That job belongs to a microcontroller: a small onboard computer, built directly into the robot, that loads your program, runs it continuously while the robot operates, and connects out to the robot's motors and sensors through wired ports.

Think of the microcontroller as the StarterBot's brain, in the same practical sense that the chassis you assembled in Chapter 1 is its skeleton. In FTC robotics, this role is filled by a microcontroller-based control system, such as a REV Control Hub, mounted directly on the robot. Once you load your program onto it, the control system no longer needs a laptop connected to keep running; it executes your code on its own, reading sensors and driving motors in real time, the whole time your robot is powered on and competing.

At this stage, you do not need to know how a microcontroller's internal circuitry works, that level of detail waits until a later chapter on digital logic and computing. For now, three practical facts are all you need to start programming:

  • The microcontroller stores and runs the program you write, step by step, exactly like a laptop runs a program, only smaller and built for a robot
  • The microcontroller has physical ports that motors, servos, and sensors plug into, so your code can send commands out and read values in
  • Once started, the microcontroller keeps running your program over and over, checking sensors and adjusting motors many times per second, without waiting for you to press a key

That last fact is the single biggest difference between the programs you wrote in Chapter 3 and the programs you are about to write for a robot. A desktop program usually runs once, from start to end, and then stops. A robot's program, as you will see later in this chapter, usually runs its central logic again and again for as long as the robot is active.

docs.title: Sensors and Actuators: How the Robot Senses and Acts
docs.text:
A microcontroller by itself cannot see, touch, or move anything; it only processes information. To interact with the physical world, it needs two categories of hardware plugged into its ports, and every piece of hardware on a robot falls into one or the other.

A sensor is a device that measures some physical quantity in the real world, such as distance, light, or touch, and converts that measurement into an electrical signal the microcontroller's program can read as a value. An actuator is a device that takes a command from the microcontroller's program and converts it into physical motion or force, such as spinning a wheel or rotating an arm to a specific angle. In short: sensors carry information into the program, and actuators carry commands out of the program into the physical world.

You have already met several actuators without calling them by that name. The StarterBot Kit you assembled in Chapter 1 includes two models of Yellow Jacket DC gearmotor, the 19.2:1 ratio (faster, lower torque, used for driving wheels) and the 50.9:1 ratio (slower, higher torque, used for mechanisms like the intake roller). It also includes Speed Servos mounted inside Compact ServoBlocks, which drive the Gecko wheels by rotating to a commanded angle rather than spinning continuously. Every one of these parts is an actuator: your program sends it a command, and it converts that command into real motion on the chassis in front of you.

The base StarterBot build from Chapter 1 does not include any sensors, only actuators, which is exactly why its Chapter 1 behavior was limited to spinning wheels and rollers under direct human control. Later builds in this course, and real FTC competition robots, commonly add sensors such as a touch sensor (detects physical contact, reporting a simple pressed-or-not-pressed value) or a distance sensor (measures how far away the nearest object is, usually in centimeters). Once a sensor is added to the robot, its microcontroller program gains the ability to react to the world instead of only acting on it blindly, a distinction the rest of this chapter builds directly on.

The table below reinforces the sensor-versus-actuator distinction using concrete StarterBot examples, so the difference is grounded in real hardware rather than an abstract definition alone.

Category Direction of Information StarterBot Example Sensor Real world → program (input) A distance sensor added in a later build, reporting centimeters to the nearest object Sensor Real world → program (input) A touch sensor added in a later build, reporting pressed or not pressed Actuator Program → real world (output) Yellow Jacket 19.2:1 gearmotor driving a wheel Actuator Program → real world (output) Yellow Jacket 50.9:1 gearmotor driving the intake roller Actuator Program → real world (output) Speed Servo in a Compact ServoBlock driving a Gecko wheel

Because sensors and actuators plug into different physical locations on the chassis and serve opposite roles in the flow of information, it helps to see them mapped directly onto the robot you already built. Explore the diagram below to connect each hardware category to where it actually sits on the StarterBot.

docs.title: Diagram: Sensors and Actuators on the StarterBot
docs.text:
Sensors and Actuators on the StarterBot

Type: infographic sim-id: starterbot-sensors-actuators-map Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Reinforce the sensor/actuator distinction by mapping both categories onto a simplified illustration of the StarterBot chassis, showing the actuators already installed from Chapter 1 and the sensor mounting points used in later builds.

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) and Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, locate, classify, explain

Learning objective: Given a labeled illustration of the StarterBot, students will identify which components are actuators versus sensors and explain the direction information flows for each.

Layout: A simplified top-down line illustration of the StarterBot chassis with four highlighted regions: the drive gearmotors, the intake gearmotor, the Speed Servo/Gecko wheel assemblies, and two dashed "future sensor mount" outlines near the front bumper and intake opening.

Interactive elements: - Hovering over an actuator region highlights it in orange and displays "Actuator: program sends a command out to this part" - Hovering over a dashed sensor-mount region highlights it in blue and displays "Sensor location (added in a later build): this part sends a reading into the program" - Clicking any region opens a side panel with the specific part name, its category, and a one-sentence description of what it does - A toggle switch labeled "Show Information Flow Arrows" draws small arrows on the actuator regions pointing outward from the microcontroller and on the sensor regions pointing inward toward the microcontroller

Data to be displayed: Four actuator regions (19.2:1 drive gearmotors, 50.9:1 intake gearmotor, Speed Servo/Gecko wheel assemblies, second drive assembly) and two sensor-mount regions (front bumper, intake opening) with example sensor types listed for each.

Color coding: Orange for actuators (output), blue for sensors (input), gray for structural chassis outline.

Responsive behavior: Illustration and hit regions scale proportionally to the iframe width; the side panel stacks below the illustration on narrow screens.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with a simplified line-drawing background, an array of clickable/hoverable polygon regions, and a text panel rendered in the remaining canvas space.

docs.title: Robot Programming: Applying Code to Real Hardware
docs.text:
Robot programming is the practice of writing code that controls physical hardware, sensors and actuators, through a microcontroller, rather than only manipulating numbers and text on a screen. Every tool from Chapter 3, variables, conditional statements, loop structures, and functions, still applies directly. What changes is what the code is connected to and how it behaves once it is running.

Three practical differences separate robot programming from the general-purpose programming you practiced in the last chapter:

  1. Physical units matter. A variable no longer just holds an abstract number; it might hold a distance in centimeters, a rotation in degrees, or a motor power expressed as a fraction of full strength.
  2. The program keeps running. Instead of executing once and stopping, a robot program typically loops continuously while the robot is active, checking sensors and adjusting actuators many times per second.
  3. The real world is unpredictable. A sensor reading can be noisy, a wheel can slip, and a battery can sag under load, so robot programs must tolerate imperfect, changing input in a way a simple even-or-odd checker never had to.

With those differences in mind, robot programming for the StarterBot breaks down into two concrete skills you will practice for the rest of this chapter: reading values in from sensors, and sending commands out to actuators.

docs.title: Sensor Input Programming: Reading the Real World
docs.text:
Sensor input programming is the specific skill of writing code that requests a current reading from a sensor and stores that reading in a variable so the rest of the program can use it. Just as GET the number from the user pulled a value into the even-or-odd program in Chapter 3, a robot program pulls a value in from a physical sensor instead of a keyboard.

The pseudocode below reads a value from a distance sensor mounted on a future StarterBot build and stores it in a variable named distance_value, following the same plain-language pseudocode style used throughout Chapter 3. Read it as: ask the sensor for its current measurement, save that measurement, and then display it.

READ distance_value FROM the distance sensor
DISPLAY "Distance reading: ", distance_value, "cm"

Notice that this pseudocode looks almost identical in structure to GET the number from the user from Chapter 3, except the source of the value is a physical sensor instead of a person typing at a keyboard. That similarity is intentional: sensor input programming reuses the exact same variable-and-input pattern you already learned, applied to a new kind of input source.

A single sensor reading is rarely useful on its own; robot programs typically compare a sensor value against some meaningful number to decide what to do next. The list below gives a few concrete examples of comparisons a StarterBot program might make once a sensor is installed.

  • Compare a distance reading to a stopping threshold, such as 15 centimeters, to decide whether an object is too close
  • Compare a touch sensor's value to "pressed," to decide whether the robot has bumped into something
  • Compare two distance readings taken moments apart to decide whether the robot is getting closer to or farther from an object

docs.title: Actuator Output Programming: Commanding Motors and Servos
docs.text:
Actuator output programming is the matching skill on the output side: writing code that sends a specific command to a motor or servo so it produces the intended physical motion. Where sensor input programming pulls a value in, actuator output programming pushes a command out.

Different actuators expect different kinds of commands, which is an important practical detail before you write any actuator code. A Yellow Jacket DC gearmotor is typically commanded with a power level, a fraction between full reverse and full forward, such as 0.6 for sixty percent of full forward power. A Speed Servo, by contrast, is typically commanded with a target angle in degrees, since a servo's whole design is built around rotating to and holding a specific position rather than spinning freely.

Actuator Type Command Style StarterBot Example DC gearmotor (Yellow Jacket) Power level, a fraction such as -1.0 to 1.0 Drive gearmotor commanded to run at 0.6 Servo (Speed Servo) Target angle, typically 0-180 degrees Gecko wheel servo commanded to angle 90

The pseudocode below commands both actuator types found on the StarterBot: a drive gearmotor set to a power level, and a Gecko wheel servo set to a target angle. Read it as two separate, direct commands sent out to two different physical parts.

SET drive_power TO 0.6
COMMAND left_drive_motor TO RUN AT drive_power
COMMAND wheel_servo TO MOVE TO ANGLE 90

Sensor input programming and actuator output programming are the two building blocks every robot program is constructed from. On their own, though, they describe two separate, disconnected actions. The next two sections explain what happens once those building blocks are combined, and why that combination is the single most important idea in this chapter.

docs.title: Open-Loop Control vs. Closed-Loop Control
docs.text:
Open-loop control is a control strategy in which the program sends a command to an actuator without ever checking the actuator's actual result against a sensor. The command is sent, and the program moves on, regardless of what actually happens in the physical world. Closed-loop control is a control strategy in which the program continuously checks a sensor's reading and adjusts its actuator commands based on that reading, correcting its behavior as conditions change.

An open-loop drive command might look like the pseudocode below: drive forward at a fixed power for a fixed amount of time, with no sensor involved at all.

COMMAND drive_motor TO RUN AT 0.5
WAIT 3 seconds
COMMAND drive_motor TO RUN AT 0

This open-loop code has an obvious weakness: it has no way of knowing whether the robot actually traveled the intended distance, or whether it stopped early after hitting a wall, or drifted off course because one wheel slipped on the floor. A closed-loop version of the same task would instead check a distance sensor while driving and stop only once the sensor reports the robot is close enough to its target, adjusting automatically to real conditions instead of blindly trusting a fixed time delay.

The following table summarizes the practical trade-off between the two strategies, since a StarterBot program will use both approaches at different times depending on whether a relevant sensor is available.

Control Type Uses Sensor Feedback? Adapts to Real-World Conditions? Example Open-loop control No No Drive forward for a fixed 3 seconds Closed-loop control Yes Yes Drive forward until a distance sensor reads less than 15cm

Because the difference between these two strategies is really about how information flows, whether a sensor's reading loops back to influence the actuator command or not, it is worth exploring that flow visually before moving on. Click through the two modes in the diagram below to compare how a command travels in each case.

docs.title: Diagram: Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Control Comparison
docs.text:
Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Control Comparison

Type: diagram sim-id: open-loop-vs-closed-loop-control Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students directly compare the signal-flow structure of open-loop control (command only, no feedback path) against closed-loop control (command plus a returning sensor-feedback path) using the StarterBot drive system as the concrete example.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) and Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: compare, contrast, differentiate, distinguish

Learning objective: Given a labeled diagram of each control strategy, students will differentiate open-loop from closed-loop control by identifying the presence or absence of a feedback path and explain why closed-loop control adapts to real-world conditions.

Components to show: A "Program" box, a "Drive Motor" actuator box, and a "Distance Sensor" box, arranged so command arrows and feedback arrows can be toggled on or off between them.

Interactive elements: - Two mode buttons, "Open-Loop" and "Closed-Loop," switch which diagram is displayed - In Open-Loop mode, an animated arrow travels once from Program to Drive Motor labeled "Command: run at 0.5 power," and no arrow returns; a small infobox reads "No sensor is checked. The program cannot tell whether the robot actually reached its target." - In Closed-Loop mode, the same command arrow appears from Program to Drive Motor, plus a second animated arrow looping back from Distance Sensor to Program labeled "Feedback: 12cm remaining," which then updates the next command arrow; an infobox reads "The sensor reading loops back and changes the next command, letting the program adapt." - Clicking the Program, Drive Motor, or Distance Sensor box in either mode reveals a short definition of that component's role - A "Step Through" button animates one full cycle at a time in Closed-Loop mode, so students can watch command, sensor reading, and adjusted command occur in sequence rather than all at once

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the initial command sent from Program to Drive Motor with its power value Stage 2 (Closed-Loop only): Show the Distance Sensor's current reading traveling back to Program Stage 3 (Closed-Loop only): Show the next command recalculated using that reading, with the new power value displayed Final: Show a side-by-side summary line: "Open-loop: 1 command, no adjustment. Closed-loop: command, reading, adjustment, repeating."

Instructional Rationale: A step-through animation with visible data at each stage is appropriate for this Understand/Analyze objective because students need to trace exactly where a feedback path exists and where it is missing, rather than watch a continuous, unlabeled animation that would obscure the structural difference between the two modes.

Color scheme: Blue for the Program box, orange for the Drive Motor (actuator) box, green for the Distance Sensor box, with feedback arrows drawn in green to visually tie them to the sensor.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with two pre-defined diagram layouts (open-loop and closed-loop), a mode toggle controlling which layout and arrows are drawn, and a simple step counter driving the "Step Through" animation.

Tip

Open-loop control is not automatically "wrong." Turning on an intake roller for a fixed match duration, with no sensor involved, is a perfectly reasonable open-loop design. Closed-loop control earns its added complexity specifically when a task's outcome depends on unpredictable real-world conditions, such as exactly how far away a wall happens to be.

docs.title: Feedback Loops and Control Loops: Sensing and Acting Together
docs.text:
The closed-loop example above depends on a specific pattern repeating over and over: read a sensor, decide what to do, act, and then read the sensor again to see the effect of that action. This repeating pattern has its own name at two related levels of description.

A feedback loop is the general cycle in which the outcome of an action is measured and that measurement is used to influence the next action, a concept that applies far beyond robotics, from a thermostat adjusting a furnace to a driver steering a car based on where the road appears to be heading. A control loop is the specific, repeating sequence of steps, typically sense, decide, and act, that a program executes over and over to implement a feedback loop in software. In short: a feedback loop is the underlying idea, and a control loop is how a program actually carries that idea out, one repetition at a time.

Because a control loop's three stages, sense, decide, and act, always feed into one another in the same repeating order, this cycle is often drawn as a simple looping diagram. Explore the diagram below to see how each stage connects to the next, and click each stage to review its definition before you meet the StarterBot's own control loop in the next section.

docs.title: Diagram: Sense-Decide-Act Control Loop Cycle
docs.text:
Sense-Decide-Act Control Loop Cycle

Type: diagram sim-id: sense-decide-act-loop Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Teach the three-stage sense-decide-act cycle that every control loop repeats, reinforcing the feedback loop and control loop definitions introduced just above.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, sequence

Learning objective: Given the sense-decide-act cycle diagram, students will explain the purpose of each stage and describe why the cycle must return to its starting stage rather than stopping after one pass.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart (graph TD) with three nodes arranged in a triangular loop, and a labeled arrow returning from the third node back to the first.

Nodes (each node clickable with a click directive opening an infobox): 1. "Sense" — click text: "Read the current value from a sensor, such as a distance sensor reporting how far away the nearest wall is. This is sensor input programming." 2. "Decide" — click text: "Use a conditional statement to compare the sensor reading against a target or threshold, deciding what the actuator should do next." 3. "Act" — click text: "Send a command to an actuator based on the decision just made. This is actuator output programming."

Connections: Sense to Decide, Decide to Act, and Act back to Sense, with the returning arrow labeled "Repeat" to emphasize that a control loop does not stop after one pass.

Color coding: Green for the Sense node (matches the sensor color used in the earlier open-loop/closed-loop diagram), gold for the Decide node, orange for the Act node (matches the actuator color used earlier), with the "Repeat" arrow drawn in blue.

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click directives bound to a JavaScript function that displays each node's explanatory text in a styled infobox beneath the diagram.

Notice that the "Decide" stage in this cycle is nothing more than a conditional statement, and the entire cycle repeating "over and over" is nothing more than a loop structure, both concepts you already practiced thoroughly in Chapter 3. A control loop is simply a loop structure whose body contains a sensor read, a conditional decision, and an actuator command, applied specifically to robot hardware.

docs.title: The Robot Control Loop and Autonomous Behavior
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter comes together in one final concept. A robot control loop is the specific control loop that runs continuously on a robot's microcontroller while it operates, combining sensor input programming, a decision step, and actuator output programming into one repeating cycle written directly in the robot's program. Where "control loop" describes the general sense-decide-act pattern, "robot control loop" refers to that same pattern implemented as real, running code on a specific robot's microcontroller.

The pseudocode below implements a robot control loop for a StarterBot equipped with a distance sensor, using a loop structure and conditional statement in exactly the style you practiced in Chapter 3. Read it as: keep repeating this cycle while the robot is active, checking distance on every pass and adjusting the drive motor accordingly.

SET stop_threshold TO 15
WHILE autonomous_period_active
    READ distance_value FROM the distance sensor
    IF distance_value > stop_threshold THEN
        COMMAND drive_motor TO RUN AT 0.5
    ELSE
        COMMAND drive_motor TO RUN AT 0
    END IF
END WHILE

This robot control loop drives the robot forward as long as the wall ahead is farther away than the 15-centimeter threshold, and stops the drive motor the moment the sensor reports the robot has gotten close enough. Every pass through the WHILE loop repeats the same sense-decide-act cycle from the diagram above: read the sensor, decide with the IF statement, and act with the COMMAND.

A robot control loop like this one is also what makes autonomous behavior possible. Autonomous behavior is a robot's ability to sense its surroundings and choose its own actions using its program's control loop, without a human operator continuously steering it in real time. This stands in direct contrast to driver-controlled operation, where a person continuously sends commands, for example through a joystick, and the robot has no need to decide anything for itself. In FTC competition, this distinction matters enough that matches are split into a short autonomous period, where robots run their own control loop with no driver input, and a longer driver-controlled period afterward.

To see a robot control loop's sense-decide-act cycle play out continuously rather than as a single static block of pseudocode, experiment with the simulation below. It models a simple StarterBot approaching a wall and lets you adjust the same stop_threshold value from the pseudocode above to see how it changes the robot's autonomous behavior.

docs.title: Diagram: Approaching the Wall: Closed-Loop Distance Control
docs.text:
Approaching the Wall: Closed-Loop Distance Control

Type: microsim sim-id: wall-approach-control-sim Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students experiment with a StarterBot's robot control loop by adjusting the stop-distance threshold and observing how the robot's autonomous behavior changes in response to live sensor readings.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) and Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, demonstrate, examine, distinguish

Learning objective: Given a simulated distance sensor and adjustable threshold, students will apply the robot control loop pseudocode to predict and demonstrate the robot's stopping behavior, and will distinguish the resulting motion from an open-loop, fixed-time alternative.

Canvas layout: - Top area (70% height): a side-view drawing area showing a simple robot icon on a floor, a wall on the right, and a live distance readout between them - Bottom area (30% height): control panel with sliders, buttons, and a small pseudocode panel highlighting the currently executing line

Visual elements: - Robot icon (blue rectangle with wheels) positioned on the left, able to move right toward the wall - Wall (gray rectangle) fixed on the right edge of the drawing area - A dashed vertical line marking the current stop_threshold distance from the wall - Live numeric readout of distance_value updating every animation frame - A pseudocode panel showing the robot control loop from this section, with the currently executing line highlighted as the simulation runs

Interactive controls: - Slider: stop_threshold, adjustable from 5cm to 40cm, default 15cm - Button: "Run Closed-Loop" — starts the robot moving using the robot control loop pseudocode shown above - Button: "Run Open-Loop (3s Timer)" — starts the robot moving using the open-loop pseudocode from the earlier section, ignoring the sensor entirely, for direct comparison - Button: "Reset" — returns the robot to its starting position - Checkbox: "Slow Motion" — reduces simulation speed so individual loop iterations are easier to observe

Default parameters: - stop_threshold: 15cm - Robot starting distance from wall: 200cm (simulated units) - Drive power when moving: 0.5

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the robot at its starting position with the initial distance_value displayed and no motion yet Stage 2: Show the robot moving, with distance_value counting down each frame and the corresponding pseudocode line highlighted Stage 3: Show the moment distance_value crosses the stop_threshold line, with the robot decelerating to a stop Stage 4 (Open-Loop mode only): Show the robot continuing to move, and potentially colliding with or overshooting the wall, since no sensor check occurs Final: Show a summary comparing final stopping distance in Closed-Loop mode (always near the threshold) versus Open-Loop mode (varies or overshoots, since it depends only on a fixed time)

Behavior: - In Closed-Loop mode, the robot always stops at approximately the slider's stop_threshold value, regardless of starting distance, since the control loop re-checks the sensor every frame - In Open-Loop mode, the robot always runs for a fixed simulated time regardless of the slider value, which the simulation highlights by graying out the threshold line during this mode - Moving the stop_threshold slider mid-run in Closed-Loop mode immediately changes where the robot stops on its next check, visually demonstrating that the control loop is reading a live value rather than a value baked in at the start

Instructional Rationale: An Apply/Analyze objective calling for prediction and comparison is best served by parameter exploration paired with a directly contrastable open-loop mode, rather than a single fixed animation. Letting students change the threshold and immediately see the consequence, and then compare against an open-loop run of the same task, makes the abstract sense-decide-act cycle concrete and lets students distinguish adaptive from non-adaptive control by observation rather than by definition alone.

Implementation: p5.js for canvas rendering and the animation loop; robot position updated each frame based on the selected mode's logic; a synchronized text panel re-renders the active pseudocode line using the same variable names shown in this section's control loop example.

Success

Once you can write a robot control loop, you have everything you need for basic autonomous behavior: a sensor reading feeding a decision, and a decision driving an actuator, repeating on its own without a driver's joystick. Every later chapter on sensors, control systems, and advanced robot programming builds directly on this one repeating pattern.

Quick check: A student writes a program that commands the drive motor to run for exactly 3 seconds and never reads any sensor. Is this open-loop or closed-loop control, and what concept from this chapter would you add to make it closed-loop? Click to reveal the answer.

This is open-loop control, since the command is sent without ever checking a sensor's reading, and the robot has no way to adjust if conditions differ from what was expected. To make it closed-loop, you would add sensor input programming, for example reading a distance sensor, and wrap the motor command in a conditional statement inside a loop structure that keeps checking the sensor and adjusts or stops the motor based on its reading, forming a robot control loop.

You now have a working vocabulary and pseudocode pattern for programming a real robot: the microcontroller that runs your code, sensors and actuators as the two categories of hardware it connects to, the sensor input and actuator output programming skills that read and command that hardware, and the open-loop, closed-loop, feedback loop, and control loop concepts that describe how a program can react to the world instead of only acting on it blindly. The robot control loop and autonomous behavior introduced at the end of this chapter are the exact building blocks every later chapter on sensors, control systems, and advanced robot programming will expand on, using the same StarterBot sitting on your workbench.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: With a working, programmable robot in hand, students now learn how to improve and extend it. This chapter covers the full engineering design process: defining problems, setting design constraints and criteria, brainstorming, sketching, prototyping, iterating, testing, and documenting a design, including trade-off analysis and reverse engineering. Students then apply this process to manufacture custom parts for their robot using additive manufacturing and 3D printing, and practice team-based design and engineering notebook documentation along the way.
