docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

docs.title: The Engineering Design Process
docs.text:
Every custom part on a competition robot starts as a problem, not a drawing. The engineering design process is a repeatable, structured cycle that engineers use to move from a problem statement to a working solution, then loop back around as they learn more. Unlike a single flash of inspiration, the process is deliberately iterative: it expects you to revisit earlier steps as new information appears, instead of marching through a fixed sequence one time and declaring victory.

Picture a real problem that will run through this entire chapter. Your FTC team has been driving the goBILDA StarterBot you assembled in Chapter 1 and programmed in Chapter 4, and two things keep going wrong during practice matches. Game pieces bounce off the front of the intake instead of feeding into the rollers, and the distance sensor your team zip-tied near the intake keeps twisting out of alignment after every match. Nothing in the stock StarterBot kit solves either problem, so your team decides to design and 3D print a custom part: a combined intake guide and sensor mount you will call the Guide-Mount for the rest of this chapter.

The engineering design process typically includes the following stages, though real teams move back and forth between them rather than only moving forward:

  1. Define the problem
  2. Establish design constraints and criteria
  3. Brainstorm possible solutions
  4. Create concept sketches
  5. Build a prototype
  6. Test the prototype
  7. Iterate on the design
  8. Document the final design and specifications

Notice that testing and iteration point back toward brainstorming and sketching rather than toward some final finish line. A prototype that fails a test does not mean starting over from nothing; it means the team learned something and cycles through the relevant earlier steps again with better information. Before diving into each stage in detail, explore the interactive cycle below to see how the Guide-Mount project will move through every stage.

docs.title: Diagram: Engineering Design Process Cycle Explorer
docs.text:
Engineering Design Process Cycle Explorer

Type: workflow sim-id: engineering-design-cycle-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students a big-picture mental map of the engineering design process before each stage is studied in depth, using the running Guide-Mount bracket example.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, summarize, interpret

Learning objective: Given the eight stages of the engineering design process arranged in a circular workflow, students will explain what happens at each stage and identify which stages loop back to earlier ones.

Layout: Eight labeled nodes arranged in a circle in the order Define Problem, Set Constraints/Criteria, Brainstorm, Sketch, Prototype, Test, Iterate, Document. Curved arrows connect each node to the next going clockwise. Two additional curved "return" arrows, drawn in a different color, loop from Iterate back to Brainstorm and from Test back to Prototype, visually showing that the process is not strictly linear.

Interactive elements: - Clicking any node opens an infobox describing what the team does at that stage, written using the Guide-Mount bracket example (for example, clicking "Test" shows: "The team mounts the printed Guide-Mount prototype on the StarterBot and runs ten practice intake cycles, recording how many game pieces feed cleanly into the rollers.") - Hovering a return arrow displays a short tooltip explaining why the loop exists (for example, hovering the Test-to-Prototype arrow shows "A failed test sends the team back to revise and reprint the prototype, not back to square one.") - A "Play Walkthrough" button auto-advances through all eight nodes in order, pausing two seconds on each with its infobox open, so students can watch one full pass of the cycle - A "Reset" button closes all infoboxes and returns to the unclicked state

Data to be displayed: Eight stage names, one Guide-Mount-specific description per stage, and two loop-back explanations.

Color scheme: Forward-progress arrows in blue, return/loop arrows in orange, active node highlighted in gold when its infobox is open.

Responsive behavior: Circular layout recalculates node positions and radius based on the iframe's current width so labels remain legible on narrow screens.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with node positions computed from a fixed angular step, arrow curves drawn with bezier control points, and a text infobox drawn below the circle that updates based on which node was last clicked.

docs.title: Problem Definition
docs.text:
The first stage of the process, problem definition, means writing a clear, specific statement of exactly what needs to be solved before anyone sketches a single idea. A vague complaint like "the intake doesn't work very well" is not a problem definition; it describes a symptom, not the actual problem an engineer can design against. A strong problem definition names the specific failure, the conditions under which it happens, and why it matters.

Your team's problem definition for this chapter might read: "During competition matches, roughly one in three game pieces that touch the front bumper bounce away instead of entering the intake rollers, and the zip-tied distance sensor loses its aim after contact, causing missed detections." Notice how specific this is compared to "the intake needs work." A precise problem definition keeps the whole team focused on the same target and prevents wasted effort brainstorming solutions to the wrong problem.

Good problem definitions generally answer four questions:

  • What exactly is going wrong, in observable, measurable terms?
  • Under what conditions does it happen (every match, only at certain angles, only after several cycles)?
  • Who or what is affected by the problem?
  • Why does solving it matter to the team's goals?

docs.title: Design Constraints and Design Criteria
docs.text:
Once a team agrees on the problem, it needs rules for judging any solution before brainstorming begins. Design constraints are fixed limits that any acceptable solution absolutely must satisfy; a design that violates a constraint is disqualified, no matter how clever it is otherwise. Design criteria, by contrast, are the qualities used to judge and rank solutions that already meet every constraint, so a team can decide which acceptable design is actually the best one.

For the Guide-Mount, a constraint might be "must bolt to existing StarterBot channel holes without drilling new holes in the chassis," because FTC competition rules and the team's limited tools make redrilling impractical, not just undesirable. A criterion, on the other hand, might be "should be as lightweight as possible," because a lighter bracket is preferred, but a slightly heavier one that still fits and functions is not automatically disqualified.

The table below reinforces this distinction with concrete Guide-Mount examples, so the difference between an absolute limit and a preference is grounded in the running project rather than left abstract.

Category Question it answers Guide-Mount example Design constraint What MUST the design satisfy to be acceptable at all? Must mount using existing goBILDA U-channel hole spacing Design constraint What MUST the design satisfy to be acceptable at all? Must not block the intake roller's rotation Design criterion What makes one acceptable design BETTER than another? Should minimize total mass added to the robot Design criterion What makes one acceptable design BETTER than another? Should be quick to remove for maintenance

docs.title: Brainstorming and Concept Sketching
docs.text:
With constraints and criteria in hand, the team moves to brainstorming, a divergent-thinking activity where the goal is generating as many possible solution ideas as possible without judging or eliminating any of them yet. Brainstorming works best when teams defer criticism until later; judging ideas too early tends to shut down the unusual suggestions that sometimes turn out to be the best ones.

Effective brainstorming sessions generally follow a few shared rules:

  • Defer judgment: no idea gets criticized during the session itself
  • Go for quantity: more ideas increase the odds that a strong one appears
  • Build on others' ideas rather than only proposing your own
  • Encourage wild ideas, since a rough idea can often be refined later

For the Guide-Mount, a fifteen-minute brainstorm might produce ideas ranging from a simple angled ramp, to a curved funnel wall, to a two-piece clamp that grips the existing channel and cradles the sensor in a rigid pocket. Once the list is long enough, the team moves to concept sketching: quickly drawing rough, low-detail pictures of the most promising ideas so they can be compared side by side. A concept sketch is not a technical drawing; it is a fast, approximate picture meant to communicate the basic shape and function of an idea in a minute or two, not to specify exact dimensions.

docs.title: Prototyping
docs.text:
A concept sketch shows what an idea might look like, but it cannot tell you whether the idea actually works on the real robot. Prototyping closes that gap by building a physical, working (or partially working) model of a design so the team can test it quickly and cheaply before committing to a final version. Prototypes exist on a spectrum from rough to refined, and skipping straight to a refined prototype often wastes time on ideas that fail for simple, avoidable reasons.

Teams typically move through prototype fidelity in stages:

  1. Low-fidelity prototype: cardboard, tape, and hot glue mocked up in minutes, testing rough shape and fit only
  2. Medium-fidelity prototype: a 3D-printed part in a fast, low-detail print setting, testing real fit and basic function
  3. High-fidelity prototype: a carefully printed, dimensionally accurate part, close to or identical to the final design

For the Guide-Mount, the team's first prototype is a piece of cardboard taped to the chassis in the shape of the angled ramp idea, just to confirm the geometry does not collide with the intake rollers before spending any filament. Only after the cardboard mock-up survives a few test cycles does the team move on to an actual 3D-printed version.

docs.title: Design Iteration and Design Testing
docs.text:
Design testing means evaluating a prototype against the constraints and criteria established earlier, using a real robot and real conditions rather than guesswork. For the Guide-Mount, testing means mounting each printed prototype on the StarterBot and running repeated intake cycles with practice game pieces, recording how many pieces feed cleanly into the rollers and whether the sensor holds its aim after contact.

Design iteration is what happens next: using the test results to revise the design, then testing the revised version again. Iteration is not a sign that the first attempt failed completely; it is the expected, normal way a design improves. The table below shows how the Guide-Mount actually improved across two rounds of testing and iteration.

Test round Result Iteration made Round 1 (angled ramp) 6 of 10 pieces fed cleanly; sensor still shifted slightly on hard contact Added a rigid pocket around the sensor and steepened the ramp angle Round 2 (ramp + sensor pocket) 9 of 10 pieces fed cleanly; sensor held aim through all 10 cycles Design accepted; minor edge rounded to reduce piece bounce further

Iteration can loop a design through testing several times before it is considered finished, and a team should budget time for at least one full iteration cycle rather than assuming the first printed version will be the last.

docs.title: Trade-Off Analysis and Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
Sometimes two candidate designs each satisfy every constraint, yet one scores higher on some criteria and lower on others; a thinner bracket might be lighter but less durable, while a thicker one might be stronger but heavier and slower to print. Trade-off analysis is the structured comparison engineers use to decide between such options by scoring each candidate against weighted criteria, rather than choosing by gut feeling alone.

A simple trade-off analysis assigns each criterion a weight based on importance, scores each design option, and multiplies weight by score to get a total. The weighted decision matrix below compares three Guide-Mount shapes the team actually considered, using a 1-5 scale where higher is better.

Criterion (weight) Angled ramp Curved funnel Two-piece clamp Print time (x2) 5 (fast) 3 (medium) 2 (slow) Feed reliability (x3) 4 5 3 Ease of removal (x1) 4 3 5 Weighted total 34 34 24

Notice that the angled ramp and curved funnel tie overall, even though they score differently on individual criteria; a trade-off analysis often narrows a field to a couple of strong finalists rather than a single obvious winner, leaving room for the team to break the tie using practical factors like available print time before competition.

Before finalizing a shape, many teams also practice reverse engineering: studying an existing part or design closely to understand how and why it works, in order to inform a new design. Your team reverse engineers the stock goBILDA U-channel by measuring its hole spacing and pattern rather than guessing, so the Guide-Mount's mounting tabs align perfectly with existing holes instead of requiring new ones drilled into the chassis. Reverse engineering an existing, proven part is often faster and more reliable than designing mounting geometry from scratch.

docs.title: Design Specifications and Bill of Materials
docs.text:
Once trade-off analysis and reverse engineering point to a final shape, that shape needs to become a precise, buildable description. Design specifications are the exact, measurable technical details a finished design must meet, translated directly from the team's constraints and criteria into numbers: overall dimensions, hole spacing, wall thickness, maximum mass, and required material.

A specification for the Guide-Mount might state: overall length 65mm, mounting tab spacing matching the standard goBILDA hole pitch, minimum wall thickness 2mm for strength, maximum mass 12 grams, and clearance of at least 3mm around the intake roller shaft. Specifications like these give both the CAD designer and the 3D printer operator an unambiguous target, rather than leaving details open to interpretation late in the project.

Alongside specifications, a finished design also needs a Bill of Materials, the complete list of every item required to actually produce the part, including quantities. A 3D-printed part's BOM looks different from the kit BOM you read in Chapter 1, since it must account for filament and print time rather than pre-made components.

Item Quantity Notes PLA filament 18 grams Estimated from sliced model M3 heat-set insert 2 For sensor mounting screws M3 x 8mm screw 2 Secures distance sensor to bracket Print time 55 minutes At chosen layer height and infill

docs.title: Design Documentation and the Engineering Notebook
docs.text:
Every decision made across problem definition, brainstorming, trade-off analysis, and testing is only useful to the team later if someone wrote it down. Design documentation is the complete record of a project: sketches, test data, specifications, the Bill of Materials, and the reasoning behind key decisions, kept together so the process can be reviewed, defended, or repeated. Many FTC competitions specifically judge teams on design documentation as part of an Engineering Design or Innovate award.

The primary tool for design documentation is the engineering notebook, a dated, chronological journal, physical or digital, where a team records its work as it happens rather than reconstructing it from memory afterward. A strong engineering notebook entry for a single work session typically includes:

  • The date and names of team members present
  • The problem or task worked on that session
  • Sketches, photos, or screenshots created during the session
  • Data collected, such as test results or measurements
  • Decisions made and the reasoning behind them

Tip

Record failed prototypes and rejected ideas in the notebook too, not only successes. Judges reviewing an FTC engineering notebook are often more interested in how a team responded to a failed test than in a design that worked perfectly on the first try.

docs.title: Team-Based Design
docs.text:
None of the stages above happen in isolation on a real FTC team; they happen through team-based design, where multiple students share responsibility across roles, communicate constantly, and reach decisions together rather than leaving every choice to a single member. Brainstorming benefits from a range of perspectives, trade-off analysis benefits from multiple people scoring options independently before comparing notes, and documentation benefits from someone specifically responsible for keeping the notebook current.

A team working on the Guide-Mount might divide responsibilities roughly as follows:

  • A mechanical lead who owns the CAD model and print settings
  • A testing lead who runs intake cycles and records results
  • A notebook keeper who documents each session's decisions and data
  • A build lead who installs prototypes on the robot and checks for interference

Dividing roles does not mean working separately; it means each stage of the engineering design process has a clear owner making sure that step actually gets done, while decisions like which shape to prototype next are still made as a group. Communication matters as much as any single role: a mechanical lead who changes a dimension without telling the testing lead can waste an entire test session on an outdated prototype, and a notebook keeper who is not included in trade-off discussions cannot document the reasoning behind them accurately.

docs.title: Manufacturing Process
docs.text:
Once the Guide-Mount's specifications are locked in, the team faces one final question: how do you actually turn a digital design into a physical part? A manufacturing process is the sequence of steps that transforms raw material into a finished physical object matching a design's specifications. Manufacturing processes fall into two broad families, and understanding both helps explain why FTC teams so often choose the one covered in the next section.

Subtractive manufacturing starts with a solid block of material and removes material, using tools like drills, mills, or saws, until only the desired shape remains, the same way a sculptor carves a statue from a block of stone. Additive manufacturing, covered in detail next, instead builds an object up from nothing, adding material only where the design calls for it. Neither family is universally better: subtractive processes like CNC milling can produce very strong metal parts but struggle with hollow internal shapes and waste the material that gets cut away, while additive processes handle complex internal geometry easily and waste very little material, but usually in weaker plastics rather than machined metal. The clickable diagram below contrasts these two families directly, using the Guide-Mount bracket as the example part in both cases.

docs.title: Diagram: Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing
docs.text:
Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing

Type: workflow sim-id: additive-vs-subtractive-manufacturing Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students distinguish additive from subtractive manufacturing by contrasting how each family of processes would produce the same Guide-Mount bracket.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: differentiate, compare, contrast

Learning objective: Given the same target part, students will differentiate the additive and subtractive manufacturing workflows and explain why additive manufacturing is well suited to a one-off custom bracket like the Guide-Mount.

Diagram type: Mermaid flowchart with two parallel swimlane-style branches from a shared starting node

Nodes (all nodes must be clickable, each opening an infobox with the listed text): - Start node: "Digital Design File" — infobox: "The 3D CAD model of the Guide-Mount, created after specifications were finalized." - Subtractive branch node 1: "Solid PLA/Aluminum Block" — infobox: "Manufacturing starts with more material than the final part needs." - Subtractive branch node 2: "CNC Mill Removes Material" — infobox: "A rotating cutting tool removes material path by path until the bracket shape remains." - Subtractive branch node 3: "Finished Bracket + Scrap Material" — infobox: "Leftover material is waste; complex internal shapes may be impossible to reach with a cutting tool." - Additive branch node 1: "Sliced Layer Data" — infobox: "Slicing software divides the 3D model into thin horizontal layers, typically 0.1-0.3mm thick." - Additive branch node 2: "3D Printer Deposits Material Layer by Layer" — infobox: "Material is added only where the design calls for it, one thin layer at a time, from the bottom up." - Additive branch node 3: "Finished Bracket, Minimal Waste" — infobox: "Complex internal shapes, like the sensor pocket, print in one piece with very little wasted material."

Edges: Start node branches into both the subtractive chain and the additive chain; each chain flows through its three nodes in order. Click directives required on every node per the interactivity rule (click NodeId call showInfo("...") style handlers).

Color coding: Subtractive branch nodes shaded gray/silver (evoking metal removal), additive branch nodes shaded blue/teal (evoking printed plastic layers).

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax rendered client-side, with JavaScript click handlers registered on each node id to open a shared infobox panel below the diagram.

docs.title: Additive Manufacturing and 3D Printing
docs.text:
Additive manufacturing is the broad family of manufacturing processes that build a physical object by adding material layer by layer from a digital 3D model, rather than removing it from a larger block. Several distinct technologies fall under this umbrella. Stereolithography (SLA) cures liquid resin with a laser, and Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) fuses powdered material layer by layer, both common in industrial and professional settings. The version most accessible to FTC teams, schools, and hobbyists is 3D printing, specifically a process called Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), which melts a plastic filament and extrudes it through a heated nozzle, tracing each layer before moving up to print the next one directly on top of it.

Turning the Guide-Mount's finished CAD model into a physical part requires slicing software, a program that converts the 3D model into a set of printer instructions (G-code) and lets the team choose print settings that affect the final part's strength, weight, and print time. Two of the most important settings are layer height, the thickness of each printed layer, and infill percentage, how solid or hollow the interior of the part is filled with a repeating support pattern. Thinner layers and higher infill generally produce stronger, heavier, slower-to-print parts, while thicker layers and lower infill print faster and lighter but weaker. Explore how these two settings trade off against each other in the interactive tool below before your own team chooses settings for its first Guide-Mount print.

docs.title: Diagram: 3D Print Settings Explorer
docs.text:
3D Print Settings Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: print-settings-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students explore how layer height and infill percentage affect estimated part strength, weight, and print time for a 3D-printed bracket like the Guide-Mount.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: apply, predict, calculate

Learning objective: Given target values for print time, weight, and strength, students will adjust layer height and infill percentage sliders to produce a print setting combination that satisfies a stated design constraint, applying the relationship between print settings and outcomes.

Canvas layout: - Left side (60% width): A simplified cross-section illustration of the Guide-Mount bracket showing visible print layers (thicker or thinner based on the layer height slider) and an internal lattice pattern (denser or sparser based on the infill slider) - Right side (40% width): Two sliders and three live-updating output readouts

Interactive controls: - Slider: Layer height, range 0.1mm to 0.3mm, step 0.05mm - Slider: Infill percentage, range 10% to 100%, step 5% - Button: "Try Guide-Mount Preset" loads the team's final chosen settings (0.2mm layer height, 35% infill) - Button: "Reset to Default"

Default parameters: Layer height 0.2mm, infill 20%

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1 (defaults): Show estimated print time ("52 minutes"), estimated part weight ("14 grams"), and a qualitative strength rating bar ("Moderate") for the default settings Stage 2 (learner moves infill slider up): Recalculate and display new print time, weight, and strength rating live, e.g. moving infill from 20% to 60% increases weight from 14g to roughly 24g, increases print time from 52 to roughly 75 minutes, and raises the strength bar from "Moderate" to "High" Stage 3 (learner moves layer height slider up): Recalculate live, e.g. increasing layer height from 0.2mm to 0.3mm at fixed infill decreases print time by roughly 30% but lowers the strength rating one notch and visibly reduces the number of drawn layer lines in the cross-section Final: Learner is challenged with a target readout ("Match: under 60 minutes print time AND at least 'High' strength") and must find a slider combination that satisfies both

Interaction: Direct manipulation via sliders with immediate, continuous readout updates (no animation/particle effects); this is a parameter-exploration tool, not a step-through narrative

Instructional Rationale: An Apply-level objective calling for students to find settings meeting a constraint is best served by direct parameter manipulation with instant, concrete numeric feedback, rather than animation, so students can form and test their own hypotheses about the relationship between print settings and outcomes.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with two slider UI elements, a cross-section drawn as a stack of rectangles whose count and thickness respond to the layer height value, a dot-grid lattice pattern whose density responds to the infill value, and a simple formula-based estimate (not a physics simulation) driving the three output readouts.

With print settings chosen, the team slices the final Guide-Mount model, sends the resulting file to the school's 3D printer, and roughly an hour later removes a finished bracket that bolts directly onto the StarterBot's existing channel holes. The distance sensor sits in its rigid pocket instead of a zip tie, and the ramp guides game pieces into the intake rollers instead of letting them bounce away. The part exists because the team walked the entire engineering design process end to end: a defined problem, clear constraints and criteria, a wide brainstorm narrowed by sketching, a cardboard prototype that became a printed one, two rounds of testing and iteration, a trade-off analysis that settled the final shape, and a notebook documenting every step along the way. The same cycle you just walked through for one bracket is exactly what real FTC teams repeat, part after part, all season long.

Quick check: The Guide-Mount's Round 1 prototype only fed 6 of 10 game pieces cleanly into the rollers. Was this a wasted attempt, and which two concepts from this chapter describe what the team did next? Click to reveal the answer.

No, it was not wasted. Round 1 supplied the data needed for design testing to succeed, and the team used that data to perform design iteration, revising the ramp angle and adding a sensor pocket before testing again. A "failed" prototype that produces useful test data is a normal, expected part of the engineering design process, not a sign to abandon the project.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Having built, programmed, and modified a robot, students now dig into why its electrical system works. This chapter covers core electrical theory: voltage, current, resistance, and Ohm's Law; the difference between direct and alternating current; series and parallel circuits; electrical power; and essential electrical safety practices, including how to recognize and prevent short circuits.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

docs.title: Stepping Back to Ask "Why"
docs.text:
Over the last five chapters, you built the StarterBot, learned the vocabulary of robotic systems, wrote programs to control it, and even designed custom parts for it. At every step, you trusted that flipping a switch would send power to the Yellow Jacket motors and the servos would spin exactly when your code told them to. This chapter steps back from building and asks a more basic question: what is actually happening, invisibly, inside the wires that connect your robot's 12V battery to its motors?

Electricity is the flow of electric charge through a material, and it is the invisible force that powers every motor, sensor, and controller on your robot. You cannot see electricity directly the way you can see a gear turn or a chain move, but you can measure its effects, predict its behavior with a small set of equations, and design circuits that use it safely. This chapter builds the theoretical foundation you will lean on for the rest of the course, starting with the three quantities that describe electricity in any circuit and ending with the safety habits that keep you and your robot protected.

Here is the arc this chapter will follow:

  • The three core quantities that describe electricity: voltage, current, and resistance
  • Ohm's Law, the single equation that ties those three quantities together
  • Direct current versus alternating current, and why your robot's battery supplies one and not the other
  • How circuits, series circuits, and parallel circuits organize the paths current can take
  • Electrical power, the rate at which a circuit does useful work
  • Conductors and insulators, the materials that either allow or block current
  • Electrical ground, short circuits, circuit protection, and the safety habits that tie it all together

docs.title: The Water Analogy: Voltage, Current, and Resistance
docs.text:
Electrical quantities are difficult to picture because charge itself is invisible, so engineers often compare a circuit to a system of water flowing through pipes. Water needs pressure to push it through a pipe, it flows at some measurable rate, and the pipe itself offers some resistance to that flow depending on its width and length. Electric circuits behave the same way, with three matching quantities that you will use constantly for the rest of this course.

Voltage is the electrical pressure that pushes charge through a circuit, measured in volts (V). Just as water pressure pushes water through a pipe even when the pipe is not flowing, voltage exists across a battery's terminals whether or not a circuit is connected to it. The StarterBot's battery is rated at 12 volts, meaning it maintains 12 volts of electrical pressure across its terminals, ready to push current through the robot's motors the moment a switch closes the circuit.

Current is the rate at which electric charge flows past a point in a circuit, measured in amperes, or amps (A). In the water analogy, current is like the rate of water flow through the pipe, measured in gallons per minute. A Yellow Jacket motor spinning under load draws a measurable current from the battery, and a stalled motor (one blocked from turning) can draw a much larger current, which is one reason motor stalls are dangerous to a robot's electrical system.

Resistance is a material's opposition to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω, the Greek letter omega). A narrow pipe resists water flow more than a wide one, and in the same way, a long thin wire resists current flow more than a short thick one. Resistance is not always unwanted: some components, called resistors, are built specifically to add a controlled amount of resistance to a circuit, protecting sensitive parts from too much current.

Because these three quantities map so directly onto a water system, it helps to see them side by side before moving on to the equation that connects them.

Water System Electrical Circuit Unit Water pressure from a pump Voltage Volts (V) Rate of water flow through a pipe Current Amps (A) Narrowness of the pipe Resistance Ohms (Ω) Water flowing through the pipe Electric charge Coulombs (C)

The analogy has limits

Water is a physical substance that can pool or leak; electric charge in a simple circuit does not pool anywhere unless it is stored in a component like a capacitor or a battery. Use the water analogy to build intuition, but remember that current flows through a complete loop, not into empty space.

docs.title: Ohm's Law: The Equation That Ties It Together
docs.text:
Voltage, current, and resistance are not independent of each other; they are locked together by one of the most useful equations in all of electronics. Ohm's Law states that the voltage across a circuit equals the current flowing through it multiplied by the resistance it encounters. Written as an equation, Ohm's Law is:

\[ V = IR \]

where \( V \) is voltage in volts, \( I \) is current in amps, and \( R \) is resistance in ohms. Because this equation relates three quantities, knowing any two lets you calculate the third. Rearranging the equation gives two more useful forms:

\[ I = \frac{V}{R} \]

\[ R = \frac{V}{I} \]

Consider the StarterBot's 12V battery connected to a simple resistive load with 4 ohms of resistance. Using the first rearranged equation, the current flowing through that load would be \( I = 12 \div 4 = 3 \) amps. If a different component in the same circuit had a much higher resistance of 60 ohms, only \( I = 12 \div 60 = 0.2 \) amps would flow. Higher resistance always means less current for the same voltage, which is exactly what the water-pipe analogy predicts: a narrower pipe lets less water through at the same pressure.

Before exploring the interactive tool below, notice that Ohm's Law describes a direct relationship between current and voltage, but an inverse relationship between current and resistance. The MicroSim lets you test both relationships by adjusting each value independently and watching the circuit respond.

docs.title: Diagram: Ohm's Law Explorer
docs.text:
Ohm's Law Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ohms-law-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students manipulate voltage and resistance independently and observe the resulting current, while watching an animated circuit that visually represents the flow.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: calculate, demonstrate, solve

Learning objective: Given a voltage and resistance value, students will calculate the resulting current using Ohm's Law and verify their prediction against the simulation's animated circuit.

Canvas layout: - Top (60% of height): A simple animated circuit diagram showing a battery, two wires forming a loop, and a resistor symbol (zigzag) in the loop - Bottom (40% of height): Two sliders and a numeric readout panel

Visual elements: - Battery symbol labeled with its current voltage value - Resistor symbol labeled with its current resistance value - Small dots representing charge moving along the wire loop, with dot speed proportional to calculated current - Numeric readout box showing V, I, and R with units, updating live

Interactive controls: - Slider: Voltage, range 0-24V, default 12V (matching the StarterBot's battery) - Slider: Resistance, range 1-100 ohms, default 4 ohms - Toggle: "Show equation" overlays the live calculation, e.g. "12V ÷ 4Ω = 3A"

Default parameters: - Voltage: 12V (StarterBot battery) - Resistance: 4 ohms - Resulting current: 3A, shown with moderately fast dot animation

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the default circuit with V=12, R=4, and the calculated I=3A displayed numerically Stage 2: When the learner drags the Voltage slider, show the new V value and the recalculated I value update in real time, with dot speed changing to match Stage 3: When the learner drags the Resistance slider, show the new R value and the recalculated I value update in real time, with dot speed changing inversely Final: Learner can set any V/R combination and see the exact calculated I with the full equation shown

Behavior: Moving either slider immediately recalculates current using \( I = V / R \) and updates both the numeric readout and the animation speed of the charge dots. If current would exceed 10A, the wire flashes red and a warning label reads "Current this high would overheat a thin wire," connecting the simulation forward to the chapter's later discussion of short circuits and circuit protection.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level objectives call for parameter exploration and calculators rather than passive animation, so this MicroSim gives students direct control over two of the three Ohm's Law variables and requires them to predict the third before confirming it against the live readout.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with two HTML range sliders bound to draw() via event listeners; charge dots implemented as an array of positions animated along a fixed bezier path at a speed proportional to calculated current.

docs.title: Direct Current vs. Alternating Current
docs.text:
Ohm's Law works the same way regardless of which of two fundamentally different current types is flowing, but robots and household power rely on different ones. Direct current (DC) is electric current that flows in only one direction through a circuit, at a steady or slowly changing voltage. The StarterBot's 12V battery supplies direct current: electrons flow from the negative terminal, through the circuit, and back to the positive terminal, always in the same direction, which is exactly why the battery's voltage can be described with a single fixed number.

Alternating current (AC) is electric current that periodically reverses direction, cycling back and forth many times per second. The electricity that comes out of a wall outlet in the United States is AC, reversing direction 60 times per second. AC is efficient for transmitting power over long distances from power plants to homes, which is why household and industrial power grids use it, while battery-powered devices like the StarterBot almost always run on DC.

The two current types are suited to very different jobs, so it helps to compare them directly.

Feature Direct Current (DC) Alternating Current (AC) Direction of flow One direction only Reverses periodically Typical source Batteries, solar cells Power plants, wall outlets StarterBot example 12V battery powering motors Not used on the robot itself Common use Portable electronics, robots Long-distance power transmission

Because the StarterBot runs entirely on DC, every circuit concept for the rest of this chapter, and for the rest of this course, assumes current flowing steadily in one direction from the battery's positive terminal, through the robot's components, and back to its negative terminal.

docs.title: Electrical Circuits: Series and Parallel Paths
docs.text:
Voltage alone cannot power a motor; the charge it pushes needs a complete path to travel before it can do any work. An electrical circuit is a closed loop that provides a continuous path for current to flow from a power source, through one or more components, and back to that source. If the loop is broken anywhere, by an open switch, a disconnected wire, or a burned-out component, current stops flowing entirely, the same way water stops flowing the instant a pipe is cut.

When a circuit contains more than one component, those components can be arranged in one of two basic patterns. A series circuit connects components one after another along a single path, so the same current flows through every component in turn, and the total voltage from the source is divided among them. A parallel circuit instead connects components across separate branches, so the full source voltage appears across each branch independently, while the total current from the source divides itself among the branches.

Imagine the StarterBot's two Yellow Jacket motors wired as loads on the 12V battery. If they were wired in series, current would have to pass through the first motor before reaching the second, meaning both motors would share the same current but split the battery's 12 volts between them, likely starving both motors of the voltage they need to run at full speed. Wiring them in parallel instead gives each motor the full 12 volts across its own branch, letting both motors run at full power while the battery supplies the combined current both motors draw. This is why robot drivetrains almost always wire their motors in parallel rather than in series.

Before comparing the two circuit types side by side in an interactive tool, notice the key trade-off: series circuits share current but divide voltage, while parallel circuits share voltage but divide current.

docs.title: Diagram: Series vs. Parallel Circuit Comparison
docs.text:
Series vs. Parallel Circuit Comparison

Type: microsim sim-id: series-parallel-circuit-comparison Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students toggle between series and parallel wiring of two StarterBot Yellow Jacket motors on a 12V battery, and observe how voltage and current distribute differently in each configuration.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: differentiate, compare, contrast, distinguish

Learning objective: Given the same two motor loads wired first in series and then in parallel, students will distinguish how voltage divides in a series circuit but stays constant in a parallel circuit, and how current divides in parallel but stays constant in series.

Canvas layout: - Top toggle bar: two buttons, "Series" and "Parallel" - Main drawing area (75% of height): circuit diagram that redraws based on selected mode - Bottom readout panel (25% of height): numeric table of voltage and current at each labeled point

Visual elements: - 12V battery symbol on the left - Two motor symbols labeled "Motor A (Yellow Jacket)" and "Motor B (Yellow Jacket)", each with an assumed resistance of 4 ohms - Wires connecting battery to motors, redrawn as a single loop through both motors in Series mode, or as two separate branches in Parallel mode - Labeled measurement points (V1, V2, I-total) that update based on mode

Interactive controls: - Toggle button: "Series" / "Parallel" switches the wiring diagram and recalculates all values - Hover over any wire segment or motor: infobox shows the voltage across and current through that specific segment - Slider: Motor resistance (2-8 ohms) applied equally to both motors, to let students see the pattern hold at different resistance values

Default parameters: - Mode: Series - Battery voltage: 12V (fixed, matches StarterBot) - Motor resistance: 4 ohms each

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1 (Series, default): Show total resistance 8Ω, total current 1.5A (shared by both motors), and voltage split 6V across each motor Stage 2 (toggle to Parallel): Show each motor receiving the full 12V, each drawing 3A independently, and total current from the battery of 6A Stage 3: Learner adjusts the resistance slider and observes both modes recalculate consistently with Ohm's Law Final: Learner can articulate, using the two side-by-side numeric readouts, that series divides voltage while parallel divides current

Behavior: Clicking the mode toggle animates the wire redraw and immediately updates the readout panel and infoboxes with recalculated values using \( V = IR \) for each branch and combined resistance rules for series (\( R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 \)) and parallel (\( 1/R_{total} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 \)) circuits.

Instructional Rationale: An Analyze-level objective requires students to identify a structural pattern and its consequences, so a side-by-side toggle with live numeric readouts is more effective than an animation alone, letting learners directly compare the two configurations rather than only watching one at a time.

Implementation: p5.js canvas redrawing circuit topology based on a mode variable; resistance and current calculations performed each frame; hover detection using mouseX/mouseY against stored wire-segment bounding boxes.

docs.title: Electrical Power
docs.text:
Every circuit does work by converting electrical energy into some other form, whether that is motion in a motor, light in an LED, or heat in a resistor. Electrical power is the rate at which a circuit converts electrical energy, measured in watts (W). Power depends on both voltage and current, according to the equation:

\[ P = VI \]

where \( P \) is power in watts, \( V \) is voltage in volts, and \( I \) is current in amps. A Yellow Jacket motor drawing 2 amps from the StarterBot's 12V battery under normal driving load is converting \( P = 12 \times 2 = 24 \) watts of electrical power into mechanical motion and a small amount of waste heat.

Because power scales with both voltage and current, doubling either one doubles the power, and a motor stalled under load (drawing far more current than normal) can spike its power consumption dramatically, generating heat fast enough to damage the motor's windings if the current is not limited. Watching power in a circuit is one of the main reasons engineers care so much about current, since a fixed 12V battery means every increase in current is also an increase in power draw, and eventually in heat.

  • A slow-moving Yellow Jacket motor under light load might draw 0.5A, consuming 6W
  • A motor driving the robot at normal speed might draw 2A, consuming 24W
  • A stalled motor blocked from turning might spike to 10A or more, consuming over 120W as heat

docs.title: Conductors and Insulators
docs.text:
Not every material lets current flow equally well, and the StarterBot's parts were chosen with this difference in mind. A conductor is a material that allows electric current to flow through it easily, because its atomic structure holds some electrons loosely enough to move freely when voltage is applied. Metals are the most common conductors: the StarterBot's steel 8mm REX shafts, its aluminum U-channels, and the copper wires running from the battery to the motors all conduct current readily, which is exactly why bare wire must never be allowed to touch the aluminum frame accidentally.

An insulator is a material that strongly resists the flow of electric current, holding its electrons tightly enough that they do not move freely even under voltage. Plastic, rubber, and most ceramics are common insulators. On the StarterBot, the plastic chain links, the rubber tread on the Gecko wheels, and the colored plastic jacket wrapped around every wire are all insulators, chosen specifically to keep current confined to the metal conductors inside them and away from a student's hands or the rest of the frame.

Recognizing conductors and insulators at a glance is a practical safety skill, not just a vocabulary exercise, so the interactive diagram below lets you test your own classification against real StarterBot parts before checking the answer.

docs.title: Diagram: Conductors and Insulators Classifier
docs.text:
Conductors and Insulators Classifier

Type: infographic sim-id: conductors-insulators-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students classify familiar StarterBot materials as conductors or insulators and understand why each material was chosen for its role.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: classify, distinguish, exemplify

Learning objective: Given an image of a StarterBot component, students will classify the material as a conductor or an insulator and explain why that classification matters for the part's function.

Layout: A grid of 8 clickable tiles, each showing a labeled StarterBot part: "Steel 8mm REX Shaft," "Aluminum U-Channel," "Copper Motor Wire," "Yellow Jacket Motor Housing (metal)," "Plastic Chain Link," "Gecko Wheel Rubber Tread," "Wire Insulation Jacket," "Plastic ServoBlock Housing." Two labeled bins, "Conductor" and "Insulator," sit below the grid.

Interactive elements: - Learner drags or clicks each tile to sort it into the Conductor or Insulator bin - On drop, the tile flashes green if correctly sorted or red if incorrect, and an infobox reveals: the correct classification, why the material behaves that way (loose vs. tightly bound electrons), and why the StarterBot uses that material in that role - A "Reveal All" button shows the completed sort with all 8 explanations visible at once for review - A running score counter tracks correct-on-first-try classifications

Data to be displayed: 8 part names, their correct conductor/insulator classification, and a one-sentence rationale for each (for example, "Wire insulation jacket: Insulator. The plastic jacket keeps current confined to the copper wire inside, protecting students from shock and preventing the wire from shorting against the aluminum frame.")

Color coding: Conductor tiles resolve to a copper/orange highlight; insulator tiles resolve to a blue highlight.

Responsive behavior: Grid reflows from 4 columns to 2 columns on narrow screens, maintaining tile aspect ratio.

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level classification objective, so a sorting interaction with immediate feedback and a short rationale per item is appropriate; a continuous animation would not help students internalize the conductor/insulator distinction the way concrete, labeled examples do.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with draggable tile objects, drop-zone bounding boxes for the two bins, and a data array pairing each tile with its classification and explanation text.

docs.title: Electrical Ground
docs.text:
Every circuit needs a shared reference point that all its voltages are measured against, and that point has a special name. Electrical ground is a common reference point in a circuit, typically connected to the negative terminal of the power source, against which all other voltages in the circuit are measured. On the StarterBot, the battery's negative terminal serves this role: every voltage measurement in the robot's electrical system, whether at a motor, a sensor, or a controller, is measured relative to that shared negative connection.

Ground serves two related purposes. First, it gives every component in the circuit a consistent zero-volt reference, so that a "12V signal" and a "5V signal" both mean something specific relative to the same baseline. Second, in many electrical systems, ground provides a deliberate low-resistance path that safely carries away stray or fault current, rather than letting it build up somewhere unpredictable, such as inside a control board or through a person's body.

docs.title: Short Circuits and Circuit Protection
docs.text:
Grounding safely directs current along an intended path, but electrical faults can create unintended paths with almost no resistance at all. A short circuit occurs when current finds an unintended path of very low resistance, bypassing the intended load and allowing far more current to flow than the circuit was designed for. Recall from Ohm's Law that current equals voltage divided by resistance; when resistance drops close to zero, current spikes dramatically, generating heat fast enough to melt wire insulation, damage a battery, or start a fire.

A short circuit on the StarterBot might happen if a bare, uninsulated wire touched the aluminum frame in two places, creating an unintended low-resistance loop that skips the motor entirely. Because the frame conducts electricity well (it is aluminum, after all), this kind of accidental contact is exactly the failure mode that wire insulation and careful cable routing are designed to prevent.

Circuit protection refers to devices and design practices that limit current automatically to prevent damage from short circuits and other electrical faults. The most common circuit protection device is a fuse, a component containing a thin metal strip that melts and breaks the circuit if current exceeds a safe threshold, sacrificing itself to protect the rest of the system. Circuit breakers perform a similar job but can be reset after they trip, rather than being replaced.

Protection Device How It Works Reusable? Fuse Thin metal strip melts and breaks the circuit above a set current No, must be replaced Circuit breaker Mechanical switch trips open above a set current Yes, can be reset Polyfuse (resettable) Resistance rises sharply when overheated, self-resets when cooled Yes, resets automatically

docs.title: Electrical Safety
docs.text:
Everything covered in this chapter, from Ohm's Law to circuit protection, comes together in a handful of practical safety habits every robotics student should follow around the StarterBot's electrical system. Electrical safety is the set of practices and precautions that prevent electrical shock, fire, and equipment damage while working with circuits.

  • Disconnect the battery before working on any wiring, motor connection, or exposed terminal
  • Inspect wire insulation regularly for cuts, fraying, or exposed conductor, especially near moving parts like sprockets and chain
  • Never let bare wire touch the aluminum frame, since the frame is a conductor and can create an unintended short circuit
  • Keep the battery's connections secure so vibration during driving cannot loosen a terminal and create arcing
  • Respect fuses and circuit breakers as protection, not inconvenience; never bypass one with a piece of wire

Never bypass circuit protection

A fuse or breaker that trips repeatedly is telling you something is wrong somewhere in the circuit, likely a short circuit or an overloaded motor. Replacing a fuse with a higher-rated one, or with a plain wire, removes the one safeguard designed to stop a fire before it starts.

With voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, circuit types, power, materials, grounding, and protection all in place, you now have the theoretical toolkit to understand exactly what is happening every time the StarterBot's battery powers a motor. The next chapter builds directly on this foundation, moving from electrical theory into the specific electronic components, like resistors, capacitors, and diodes, that make up real circuit designs.

Quick check: Why do the StarterBot's two drive motors share the battery's 12 volts equally instead of splitting it? - Click to expand

Because they are wired in parallel, not in series. A parallel circuit gives each branch the full source voltage, while only the total current supplied by the battery divides among the branches, letting both motors run at full power simultaneously.
