docs.title: From Theory to Practice
docs.text:
Chapter 6 gave you the vocabulary of electricity: voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, series and parallel circuits, and the safety habits that keep a lab bench safe. That vocabulary was necessary, but abstract. You calculated current with a formula; you did not yet hold the part current flows through in your hand. This chapter closes that gap, teaching you to identify the physical components in every StarterBot circuit, read the diagrams describing how they connect, and practice hands-on skills—breadboarding, soldering, and multimeter use—that turn a diagram into a working circuit.

By the end of the chapter, you will be able to look at a real circuit board, name most of what is on it, and explain why each part is there. You will also design and simulate a simple circuit of your own before ever touching a soldering iron, which is exactly how professional engineers work: think first, build second.

docs.title: Circuit Diagram: The Blueprint of a Circuit
docs.text:
Before you can build a circuit, you need a way to describe it that does not depend on drawing every wire exactly as it will be routed in real life. A circuit diagram (also called a schematic) is a standardized drawing that represents electronic components as symbols and shows how they connect electrically, without depicting their physical size, shape, or position. Just as an architect's blueprint uses standard symbols for doors and windows regardless of what brand is installed, a circuit diagram uses standard symbols for resistors, batteries, and switches regardless of what the physical part looks like.

Reading a circuit diagram is a skill, not an instinct, and it rewards a specific strategy:

  1. Find the power source first (battery or power supply symbol) and identify its two terminals.
  2. Trace the wire from the positive terminal, component by component, following the loop.
  3. Note every component the current passes through and in what order.
  4. Confirm the loop returns to the negative terminal, completing the circuit.

A schematic only becomes useful once you can connect each symbol to a real part sitting on your workbench, so the next several sections introduce the core components one at a time, alongside the schematic symbol used to represent each one.

docs.title: Diagram: Reading a Simple LED Circuit Diagram
docs.text:
Reading a Simple LED Circuit Diagram

Type: diagram sim-id: reading-led-circuit-diagram Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand Bloom Taxonomy Verb: interpret, identify

Learning objective: Given a complete schematic of a simple battery-resistor-LED-switch circuit, students will interpret each symbol and trace the current path around the loop.

Components to show: A single closed-loop schematic containing a battery symbol (two parallel lines, long/short), a single-pole switch symbol, a resistor symbol (zig-zag or rectangle), an LED symbol (diode triangle-and-bar with two small arrows), and connecting wires drawn as straight lines with right-angle corners.

Connections: All four components are wired in a single series loop: battery positive terminal to switch, switch to resistor, resistor to LED anode, LED cathode back to battery negative terminal.

Interactive elements: - Clicking the battery symbol reveals: "Battery: the energy source. The long line is the positive terminal, the short line is the negative terminal." - Clicking the switch symbol reveals: "Switch: an open gap in the wire that closes to complete the circuit." - Clicking the resistor symbol reveals: "Resistor: limits current flow to protect the LED from too much current." - Clicking the LED symbol reveals: "LED: the arrow direction shows current can only flow one way, from anode to cathode, and light is emitted when it does." - Clicking any wire segment highlights the full current path from positive terminal back to negative terminal in yellow - A "Toggle Switch" button animates a dot traveling around the loop when the switch is closed, and freezes it at the open gap when the switch is open

Visual style: Clean schematic line drawing on a white background, standard IEEE-style symbols, thick black lines for wires

Color scheme: Black symbols and wires by default; clicked symbol and its infobox highlighted in blue; active current path highlighted in yellow when the switch is closed

Implementation: p5.js canvas with clickable bounding regions over each symbol, a state variable for switch position, and a simple animated dot along a predefined path array when current is flowing.

docs.title: The Core Components: Symbols and Functions
docs.text:
Every circuit, no matter how complex, is built from a small number of fundamental component types. This section introduces five of them: the resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor, and LED. Each has its own schematic symbol, its own job, and its own reason for appearing in the StarterBot's electronics.

A resistor is a component that opposes the flow of current by a fixed, known amount, measured in ohms, and used to limit current or divide voltage in a circuit. You already used resistance conceptually in Chapter 6's Ohm's Law calculations; a resistor is simply a physical part manufactured to provide a specific, reliable resistance value. Resistors are color-coded with bands of paint indicating value and tolerance, letting you identify a resistor's value without a multimeter once you learn the code.

A capacitor is a component that stores electrical energy in an electric field between two conductive plates, and releases that energy back into the circuit when needed. Unlike a battery, which stores energy chemically and releases it slowly over minutes or hours, a capacitor stores a much smaller amount of energy but can charge and discharge almost instantly. On a robot's control board, small capacitors smooth out sudden dips or spikes in voltage, for example when a motor first switches on and briefly pulls extra current.

A diode is a component that allows current to flow in only one direction and blocks it in the other, acting like a one-way valve for electricity. This property makes diodes useful for protecting circuits from being connected backward, and for converting alternating current into direct current in a power supply. A diode has two terminals, the anode and the cathode, and current flows only from anode to cathode, never the reverse.

Before moving on to the two remaining components, it helps to see these first three side by side, since their symbols are easy to confuse at a glance:

Component Symbol Shape Primary Function Resistor Zig-zag line or plain rectangle Limits current to a fixed, known amount Capacitor Two parallel lines with a small gap Stores energy briefly in an electric field Diode Triangle pointing into a flat bar Allows current to flow in one direction only

A transistor is a component that uses a small input current or voltage to control a much larger current flowing through it, functioning as either an electronic switch or an amplifier. Transistors are the building blocks of every microcontroller and every motor driver you will meet later in this chapter, because they let a low-power signal from a control chip switch on and off a high-power connection to a motor or a light, without the low-power signal ever touching the high-power current directly.

An LED (light-emitting diode) is a type of diode that emits visible light when current flows through it in the forward direction. An LED is a diode first and a light source second: it shares the diode's one-way current behavior, but it also converts a portion of that current directly into light rather than heat, which makes it far more efficient than an incandescent bulb. Every LED requires a resistor in series with it to limit current, since an LED's own resistance is too low to safely limit current on its own; connecting an LED directly to a battery without a resistor will typically burn it out within seconds.

Because these five components appear on nearly every circuit board, being able to recognize each one by its schematic symbol, without hesitating, is a foundational skill for everything that follows in this chapter.

docs.title: Diagram: Circuit Symbol Matching Infographic
docs.text:
Circuit Symbol Matching Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: circuit-symbol-matching Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, recognize, recall

Purpose: Help students recognize the standard schematic symbol for each of eight core components and recall its one-line function, reinforcing the vocabulary introduced in this chapter and Chapter 6.

Layout: A grid of 8 symbol tiles arranged 4 columns by 2 rows (2 columns by 4 rows on narrow screens): resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor, LED, battery, switch, relay. Each tile shows only the schematic symbol with no label.

Interactive elements: - Clicking a tile flips it over to reveal the component's name and a one-sentence function ("Resistor: limits current flow to a fixed, known amount") - A "Shuffle" button rearranges the tiles into a new random order - A "Quiz Me" mode hides all names and asks the learner to click the tile matching a spoken/displayed component name, tracking correct-on-first-try score out of 8 - Hovering an un-flipped tile in normal mode shows a faint outline highlight only, with no text, to encourage active recall before clicking

Data to be displayed: 8 component names, their schematic symbols, and one-sentence function descriptions matching the definitions given in this chapter and in Chapter 6 (battery, switch, relay recur from earlier sections)

Color coding: Neutral gray tile backs; flipped tiles colored by component family (passive components—resistor, capacitor—in blue; semiconductor components—diode, transistor, LED—in green; power and control components—battery, switch, relay—in orange)

Responsive behavior: Grid reflows from 4x2 to 2x4 on narrow screens, tiles remain square

Instructional Rationale: This is a Remember-level recall objective, so a flashcard-style matching interaction with immediate reveal is appropriate; a continuous animation or complex simulation would add no value at this level and would distract from simple symbol-to-name recall.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with an array of tile objects (symbol, name, function, family color), a flip-state boolean per tile, and click detection to toggle flip state; quiz mode swaps the click handler to score matching instead of flipping.

docs.title: Powering the Circuit: Battery and Power Supply
docs.text:
Every circuit needs an energy source, and robotics projects typically draw on one of two kinds: a battery or a power supply. A battery is a device that stores chemical energy and converts it to electrical energy on demand, delivering a roughly steady voltage until its stored energy runs low. The StarterBot's single 12V battery, introduced in Chapter 1 and referenced throughout Chapter 6, is a rechargeable battery pack built from multiple cells connected internally to reach 12 volts.

A power supply is a device that converts electrical energy from one form or voltage to another, usually converting a wall outlet's alternating current into the steady direct current voltage a circuit requires. Unlike a battery, a power supply does not store its own energy; it depends on being plugged into an external source and simply transforms that source's voltage and current into a usable form. Many robotics workbenches use a benchtop power supply during testing, since it can supply a precise, adjustable voltage without draining a battery, and it can be switched off instantly if something goes wrong.

The following table summarizes the practical differences a robotics student needs to keep in mind when choosing between them:

Feature Battery Power Supply Energy source Stores chemical energy internally Converts external outlet power Portability Portable, works untethered Requires a wall connection Runtime Limited, depletes with use Unlimited while plugged in Typical robotics use Powering the robot during operation Bench testing before final assembly

Both must ultimately connect to the rest of the circuit through a control point that lets current flow only when intended, which is the job of the next two components.

docs.title: Controlling the Flow: Switch and Relay
docs.text:
A switch is a mechanical device that opens or closes a circuit by making or breaking a physical electrical connection, controlled directly by a person's hand. The simplest switch, a single-pole single-throw (SPST) switch, has exactly two positions: fully open (no connection, no current) and fully closed (connection made, current flows). More complex switches can route current to one of several paths, but every switch shares the same basic job: a physical, human-operated gate for current.

A relay is an electrically operated switch that uses a small control current to open or close a separate, often much larger, circuit. Inside a relay, a small electromagnet pulls a mechanical arm to close (or open) a set of contacts, similar to the electromagnetic effects you may have encountered when studying motors. This design solves a problem a plain switch cannot: a microcontroller's output pins can only safely supply a tiny current, far too little to directly power something like a large motor or a household appliance, but that tiny current is more than enough to energize a relay's electromagnet, which then switches the much larger current on the relay's other side.

Relays and transistor-based motor drivers (covered later in this chapter) solve the same underlying problem—letting a weak control signal command a strong load—but they do it differently:

  • A relay uses a mechanical, moving contact, which makes an audible click and can wear out over many cycles, but can switch very high currents and works with both AC and DC loads.
  • A transistor-based motor driver has no moving parts, switches almost instantly, and is generally preferred for the fast, frequent switching a robot's drive motors need.

docs.title: Breadboard: Prototyping Without Solder
docs.text:
Now that you can identify the core components and the power sources that drive them, it is time to actually connect them into a working circuit—without committing to a permanent solder joint on your first attempt. A breadboard is a reusable prototyping board with a grid of spring-loaded holes that let components and wires be inserted and removed without soldering, allowing circuits to be built, tested, and modified quickly.

Internally, a breadboard's holes are connected in hidden strips beneath the plastic surface:

  • Each short row of five holes in the center section is electrically connected, so inserting a component's leg anywhere in that row of five connects it to everything else in that same row.
  • The long rows running along the top and bottom edges, usually marked with a red (+) and blue (-) stripe, are power rails, connected the entire length of the board, used to distribute power and ground to many components at once.
  • The center gap running down the middle of the board is not connected across, which is exactly where a chip or component that needs pins on both sides is placed.

Because no solder is involved, a mistake on a breadboard costs nothing more than the time it takes to pull a wire out and reposition it, which is exactly why breadboards are the standard first step for testing any new circuit design, including the LED-resistor-battery circuit from the diagram earlier in this chapter.

docs.title: Diagram: Virtual Breadboard Circuit Builder
docs.text:
Virtual Breadboard Circuit Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: virtual-breadboard-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply Bloom Taxonomy Verb: implement, demonstrate, construct

Learning objective: Students will apply their knowledge of series circuits, resistors, LEDs, and battery polarity by dragging components onto a virtual breadboard and wiring a circuit that successfully lights the LED.

Canvas layout: - Left/center (650px): A drawn breadboard grid with labeled power rails (red +, blue -) and numbered rows - Right (250px): A parts bin showing a battery, a resistor, an LED, and jumper wires, plus a status panel

Visual elements: - Realistic breadboard grid drawn as rows and columns of small circles, with power rails along top and bottom - Draggable component icons: battery pack, resistor, LED (with visibly longer anode leg and shorter cathode leg), and wire segments - Status light: red "Circuit Incomplete" or green "Circuit Complete — LED Lit!" indicator in the status panel

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop placement of battery, resistor, LED, and wires onto specific breadboard holes - Button: "Check Circuit" evaluates whether current can flow from battery positive, through the resistor, through the LED in the correct polarity (anode before cathode), and back to battery negative - Button: "Reset Breadboard" clears all placed components - Toggle: "Reverse LED" lets the learner intentionally place the LED backward to observe that it does not light

Default parameters: Empty breadboard, battery pre-placed connected to the power rails, resistor and LED value fixed (220 ohm resistor, standard red LED) to keep focus on wiring topology rather than value calculation

Behavior: - If the LED is missing the series resistor, wired directly across the battery rails, the sim shows the LED flashing red with a warning: "No resistor — this connection would damage a real LED with too much current." - If the LED is inserted backward, the sim shows the LED staying dark with an infobox: "Current cannot flow this direction through a diode. Try flipping the LED so the longer leg (anode) faces the resistor." - If wired correctly (resistor in series, LED in correct polarity, loop closed from positive rail back to negative rail), the LED icon lights up yellow and the status panel turns green

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective requiring learners to construct a working circuit from components they can now identify, so a drag-and-drop builder with clear pass/fail feedback is appropriate; a passive diagram would not let students test their own understanding of series wiring and polarity the way hands-on placement does.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with a data structure representing breadboard hole connectivity (which holes are electrically joined), drag events for each component, and a simple circuit-continuity check that traces from the positive rail to the negative rail through placed components.

docs.title: Soldering: Making Permanent Connections
docs.text:
A breadboard is perfect for testing, but its spring-loaded connections can loosen with vibration, which is a real concern on a robot that drives, bumps, and vibrates during operation. Soldering is the process of joining two metal parts, typically a component lead and a circuit board pad, by melting a metal alloy (solder) that cools into a strong, permanent electrical and mechanical connection. Once a circuit design has been tested and confirmed on a breadboard, soldering is how that design becomes a durable, vibration-resistant part of the finished robot.

A basic soldering procedure follows a consistent sequence:

  1. Heat the soldering iron to the correct temperature (typically 300–370°C for electronics work) and let it stabilize.
  2. Clean the iron's tip on a damp sponge or brass wool to remove old, oxidized solder.
  3. Position the component leads through the board holes and hold the iron tip against both the lead and the pad simultaneously.
  4. Feed solder wire into the joint, not directly onto the iron tip, letting heat from the joint itself melt the solder.
  5. Remove the solder and then the iron, and let the joint cool undisturbed for several seconds.
  6. Inspect the finished joint: it should look shiny and shaped like a small volcano, not dull, cracked, or blobby.

Soldering iron safety

A soldering iron tip reaches temperatures well above the boiling point of water and stays hot for minutes after being unplugged. Always return the iron to its stand when not actively soldering, keep the cord clear of the tip, and never test whether the iron is hot by touching it directly.

docs.title: Multimeter: Measuring and Testing
docs.text:
Whether a circuit lives on a breadboard or has been soldered permanently, you eventually need a way to confirm it is actually behaving the way your diagram predicted. A multimeter is a handheld instrument that measures multiple electrical properties, typically voltage, current, and resistance, selectable by a mode dial or button, used to test and troubleshoot circuits. A multimeter is the primary diagnostic tool for verifying the calculations you practiced in Chapter 6 against a real, physical circuit.

Each mode on a multimeter measures a different quantity and requires a different connection technique:

Mode Measures How to Connect Common Use Voltage (V) Potential difference between two points Probes touch two points in parallel, circuit stays connected Checking battery charge, confirming a power rail voltage Current (A) Rate of charge flow through a path Meter placed in series, circuit must be opened to insert it Confirming a motor is drawing expected current Resistance (Ω) Opposition to current in an unpowered component Probes touch two ends of a component removed from a powered circuit Confirming a resistor's actual value Continuity Whether a path is electrically connected Probes touch two points, meter beeps if resistance is near zero Checking a wire or solder joint for a broken connection

Never measure current like you measure voltage

Voltage mode is connected in parallel and current mode is connected in series, and confusing the two is one of the most common multimeter mistakes. Placing a multimeter in current mode directly across a battery's terminals, the way you would for a voltage reading, creates a near-zero-resistance path through the meter itself and can blow the meter's internal fuse or damage the battery.

docs.title: Printed Circuit Board
docs.text:
Breadboards and hand-soldered connections both work well for one-off projects and classroom prototypes, but neither scales well to a product built many times over. A printed circuit board (PCB) is a flat board made of insulating material with thin copper traces etched onto its surface, replacing individual wires with permanent, precisely placed conductive paths that connect components soldered onto the board. Where a breadboard's connections live in reusable spring clips and a hand-soldered protoboard relies on point-to-point wires, a PCB's traces are designed in software ahead of time and manufactured identically every time.

The tradeoffs among these three approaches to physically realizing a circuit follow a clear pattern:

Approach Reusable? Reliable Under Vibration? Best Suited For Breadboard Yes, fully reusable No, connections can loosen Early testing and quick iteration Hand-soldered protoboard No, permanent Yes, solid joints One-off finished projects Printed circuit board No, permanent Yes, most robust Repeated manufacturing, final products

A control board like the microcontroller you programmed in Chapter 4 is itself built on a PCB, with its resistors, capacitors, and connectors all soldered onto copper traces that were designed and manufactured long before you ever opened the box.

docs.title: Motor Driver: Controlling the StarterBot's Motors
docs.text:
Recall from Chapter 4 that a program commands a Yellow Jacket DC gearmotor with a power level, a fraction between full reverse and full forward such as 0.6, and that Chapter 1 described these same gearmotors as the drivetrain for the StarterBot's wheels. Sending a fractional power command from a microcontroller only works, however, because of a component that sits physically between the microcontroller and the motor. A motor driver is a circuit, typically built around transistors, that takes a low-power control signal from a microcontroller and uses it to switch a motor's much higher current and voltage on, off, or in reverse.

A microcontroller's output pins, like a relay's control input, can only safely supply a few milliamps of current, while a Yellow Jacket gearmotor under load can draw several amps, roughly a thousand times more. A motor driver bridges that gap using an arrangement of transistors called an H-bridge, which can do something a simple relay cannot do easily: reverse the motor's direction electronically, without any moving mechanical parts, simply by switching which pair of transistors conducts.

  • Setting the transistors one way lets current flow through the motor in the forward direction, spinning it forward.
  • Setting the transistors the opposite way reverses current through the motor, spinning it in reverse.
  • Rapidly switching the transistors on and off many times per second, a technique called pulse-width modulation, controls the effective power level, which is exactly how a program's "run at 0.6 power" command becomes a real, adjustable motor speed rather than only a full-on or full-off command.

Without a motor driver, a microcontroller could only ever fully connect or fully disconnect a motor from the battery, producing the same simple full-on behavior you first commanded in Chapter 4; the motor driver is what makes variable speed and reversible direction possible at all.

docs.title: Circuit Simulation and Circuit Design
docs.text:
Every component and skill in this chapter—reading a diagram, recognizing symbols, wiring a breadboard, soldering, measuring with a multimeter—comes together in a single overall process: designing a circuit that solves a specific problem, before ever touching a physical part. Circuit design is the process of selecting components and specifying their connections to build a circuit that meets a set of requirements, such as lighting an LED at a safe current or driving a motor at a target speed.

A well-organized circuit design process moves through a predictable sequence of stages:

  1. Define the requirement (for example, "light one LED safely from a 12V battery").
  2. Select components that can meet the requirement (an LED with a known forward voltage, a resistor sized to limit current with Ohm's Law).
  3. Draw a circuit diagram showing how the components connect.
  4. Simulate the design to confirm it behaves as expected.
  5. Build the circuit, first on a breadboard and then, once confirmed, soldered or on a PCB.
  6. Test the built circuit with a multimeter to verify it matches the simulation and the original requirement.

Step 4 depends on a tool this chapter has not yet named directly. Circuit simulation is the use of software to model a circuit's electrical behavior mathematically, predicting voltages, currents, and component states before any physical parts are purchased or assembled. Circuit simulation software, such as Tinkercad Circuits or LTspice, applies the same equations you learned in Chapter 6, including Ohm's Law, to a diagram you build on screen, then reports whether the design will work, whether a component might be overloaded, and what its actual voltage and current values would be.

Simulating a design first offers a clear practical advantage: a mistake in simulation costs nothing, while the same mistake in a physical circuit can damage an LED, a transistor, or a battery, and cost both money and time to diagnose. This is precisely why professional engineers, not just students, simulate a design before ordering parts or manufacturing a PCB.

docs.title: Diagram: LED Circuit Design and Simulation Studio
docs.text:
LED Circuit Design and Simulation Studio

Type: microsim sim-id: led-circuit-design-studio Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze, Create Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, justify, design, formulate

Learning objective: Students will design a safe LED circuit by selecting a resistor value for a given battery voltage and LED forward voltage, analyzing the resulting current with Ohm's Law before virtually building and simulating the circuit.

Canvas layout: - Top (300px): A live schematic of a battery, resistor, and LED in series, redrawn as parameter sliders change - Bottom (200px): Calculation panel and pass/fail status readout

Visual elements: - Schematic showing battery, resistor, and LED symbols matching the style from the "Reading a Simple LED Circuit Diagram" diagram earlier in this chapter - Live numeric readout of calculated current in milliamps, updating as sliders move - LED icon that visually brightens, glows normally, or flashes a burnout warning depending on calculated current

Interactive controls: - Slider: Battery voltage (3V to 12V, default 12V, matching the StarterBot's battery) - Slider: Resistor value (10 ohms to 1000 ohms, default 100 ohms) - Fixed display value: LED forward voltage (2.0V, a typical red LED) and safe current range (15–20 mA typical, danger above 30 mA) - Button: "Run Simulation" locks in current slider values and displays the calculated result with a pass/fail judgment

Default parameters: Battery voltage 12V, resistor 100 ohms, LED forward voltage fixed at 2.0V

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the circuit's known values: battery voltage, LED forward voltage, and the chosen resistor value Stage 2: Show the voltage drop calculation across the resistor (battery voltage minus LED forward voltage) Stage 3: Show the current calculation using Ohm's Law (resistor voltage drop divided by resistor value) Stage 4: Show the final current result compared against the LED's safe operating range, with a clear pass ("LED lit safely") or fail ("Current too high — LED would burn out" or "Current too low — LED will appear dim") message

Behavior: - As the resistor slider decreases toward 10 ohms, calculated current rises past the safe range and the LED icon flashes red with "burnout" warning text - As the resistor slider increases toward 1000 ohms, calculated current falls very low and the LED icon dims to barely visible - A highlighted "safe zone" band on the resistor slider shows the range of values that keep current within 15–20 mA for the current battery voltage setting

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-and-Create objective, since students must examine the relationship between voltage, resistance, and current to justify a resistor choice and formulate a working design; a parameter-exploration pattern with visible, stepwise calculations is appropriate so learners see exactly how changing one value changes the outcome, rather than only observing a final animation.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with two slider inputs, a recalculation function applying Ohm's Law on every slider change, and a schematic redraw function that updates LED brightness based on the calculated current relative to the safe range.

This design-simulate-build-test cycle is the one you will return to for the rest of this course, whether the circuit ahead lights a single LED or drives every motor on a finished robot. You now have the vocabulary, from resistor to relay, and the practical skills, from breadboarding to multimeter testing, to move confidently between a circuit diagram on a screen and a working circuit on your bench.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Students already know what a sensor and an actuator are from programming their robot. This chapter goes much deeper: precision measurement, direct and indirect measurement techniques, coordinate systems, and a tour of specific sensor types (light, temperature, distance, touch, sound, encoders, potentiometers). The chapter closes with sensor calibration, data transmission, and signal processing, preparing students to select and tune the right sensor for any task.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 14 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Precision Measurement
  2. Direct Measurement
  3. Indirect Measurement
  4. Coordinate System
  5. Light Sensor
  6. Temperature Sensor
  7. Distance Sensor
  8. Touch Sensor
  9. Sound Sensor
  10. Encoder
  11. Potentiometer
  12. Sensor Calibration
  13. Data Transmission
  14. Signal Processing

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 4: Programming Your Robot
  • Chapter 7: Electronic Components and Circuit Design

docs.title: From "It Has a Sensor" to "It Knows the Distance"
docs.text:
Back in Chapter 4, you defined a sensor as any component that converts a physical quantity—light, distance, temperature, sound—into an electrical signal your microcontroller can read. You wrote a few lines of code to read a sensor value and use it to command an actuator, the component that turns an electrical signal back into motion or another physical effect. That was enough to make a robot react to the world.

This chapter asks a harder question: how good is that reaction? A robot that merely knows "something is nearby" behaves very differently from one that knows "the wall is 14.2 centimeters away, and that reading is accurate to within 2 millimeters." The gap between those two robots is the entire subject of this chapter. You will learn how to measure precisely, how to locate objects in space using a coordinate system, how to choose among the specific sensor types your kit provides, how to calibrate a sensor so its numbers can be trusted, and how to move that data cleanly from the sensor to the microcontroller's brain.

By the end of the chapter, you will stop thinking of a sensor as a single component and start thinking of it as the first link in a measurement pipeline—one that can introduce error at every stage, and one you now have the tools to control.

docs.title: Precision Measurement: Why "Good Enough" Isn't Always Good Enough
docs.text:
Every measurement a sensor produces is an estimate, not a perfect fact. Precision measurement is the practice of obtaining sensor readings that are consistent, fine-grained, and trustworthy enough to support the decision the robot must make. Precision is not the same thing as accuracy: a sensor can report the same distance reading five times in a row (high precision) while still being wrong every time (low accuracy), because it was never calibrated against a known value.

Consider two robots approaching the same wall:

  • Robot A's distance sensor reports "close" or "far"—a coarse, two-state reading good enough to stop before a wall.
  • Robot B's distance sensor reports a number in millimeters, refreshed 20 times per second, accurate to within 1% of the true distance.

Robot A can avoid a collision. Robot B can park itself exactly 5 centimeters from a wall, follow a wall at a constant offset, or dock precisely with a charging station. The difference is not the sensor hardware alone—it is how precisely the robot is willing to measure, process, and trust the data that sensor produces.

Precision matters more as tasks get harder. A line-following robot needs enough precision to distinguish the edge of a black line from ordinary floor noise. A robotic arm stacking blocks needs enough precision to place a block within a few millimeters of its target, or the stack topples. Whenever you design a sensing system, ask what level of precision the task actually requires—overspending on precision wastes processing time and money, but underspending causes failures that are hard to diagnose later.

docs.title: Direct Measurement vs. Indirect Measurement
docs.text:
Sensors do not all obtain their readings the same way. Direct measurement occurs when a sensor's output corresponds straightforwardly to the physical quantity being measured, with little or no calculation required. Indirect measurement occurs when the physical quantity of interest cannot be sensed directly, so the robot measures a related quantity and calculates the value it actually needs.

A touch sensor is a clean example of direct measurement: pressing the switch closes a circuit, and the microcontroller reads a simple "pressed" or "not pressed" signal that directly represents the physical event. A distance sensor that uses sound, by contrast, is a classic case of indirect measurement: the sensor cannot detect "distance" as a raw physical quantity. Instead, it measures the time an ultrasonic pulse takes to travel to an object and echo back, and the robot calculates distance using the known speed of sound.

This distinction matters because indirect measurements inherit every error in the calculation used to produce them. If the speed-of-sound constant used in a distance calculation is wrong for the current air temperature, every distance reading will be off by the same proportional amount, even though the raw timing measurement was fine. The following table reinforces the distinction with sensors covered later in this chapter.

Sensor What it directly senses What is reported Direct or indirect? Touch sensor Circuit open/closed Pressed / not pressed Direct Potentiometer Wiper position (resistance) Angle or position value Direct Encoder Light or magnetic pulses per rotation Rotation count, speed Indirect (pulses converted to angle/speed) Ultrasonic distance sensor Echo travel time Distance in cm Indirect (time converted using speed of sound) Temperature sensor (thermistor) Resistance change Temperature in °C Indirect (resistance converted using a formula)

Notice that several of the sensors your robot already relies on for "simple" jobs are secretly performing a calculation behind the scenes. Keeping that calculation in mind will help you understand later, in the section on sensor calibration, why some sensors drift out of accuracy more easily than others.

docs.title: Coordinate Systems: Giving the Robot a Sense of Space
docs.text:
Knowing a distance or an angle is only useful if the robot also knows what point in space that number is measured from and in what direction. A coordinate system is a framework of reference axes and an origin point that lets a robot describe the position and orientation of itself or of objects around it using numbers. Without a coordinate system, "10 centimeters" is a meaningless fraction—10 centimeters from where, and in which direction?

Robots commonly use more than one coordinate system at the same time, and part of good sensor design is keeping straight which one a given reading belongs to:

  • A robot-centered (egocentric) coordinate system places the origin at the robot itself, usually at its center or its front sensor mount. Distances and angles are measured relative to the robot's own body—"the wall is 30 cm ahead and 10 degrees to the left."
  • A world (global) coordinate system places the origin at a fixed point in the environment, such as the corner of a room or a competition field. Positions are measured relative to that fixed point, so the robot's location changes as it moves, but the origin never does.
  • A polar coordinate system describes a point using a distance and an angle from an origin, which is a natural match for many rotating sensors, such as a distance sensor mounted on a spinning turret.
  • A Cartesian coordinate system describes a point using perpendicular axes (x, y, and sometimes z), which is a natural match for grid-based navigation and mapping.

A signpost worth remembering: every sensor reading is meaningless until you know which coordinate system it belongs to, and converting between systems (for example, from a sensor's egocentric polar reading to the robot's position on a global Cartesian map) is one of the core calculations in robot navigation, revisited in later chapters on control systems.

docs.title: A Tour of Sensor Types
docs.text: With precision, measurement type, and coordinate systems established as the underlying concepts, the rest of this chapter surveys the specific sensors most robotics kits provide. Each sensor converts a different physical quantity into an electrical signal, and each is suited to a different job.

docs.title: Light Sensor
docs.text: A light sensor detects the intensity of visible or infrared light striking it and reports that intensity as a voltage or digital value. The most common type in educational robotics kits is a photoresistor or phototransistor, whose electrical resistance changes depending on how much light reaches it. Robots use light sensors to follow a line printed on the floor (the line reflects less light than the surrounding surface), to detect whether a room is dark or bright, or to find a light source by comparing readings from two sensors mounted apart.

docs.title: Temperature Sensor
docs.text: A temperature sensor converts ambient or contact temperature into an electrical signal, typically by using a thermistor (a resistor whose resistance changes predictably with temperature) or an integrated circuit sensor that outputs a voltage proportional to temperature. This is a textbook example of indirect measurement: the sensor measures resistance or voltage, and the microcontroller applies a formula to convert that value into degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit. Robots use temperature sensors to monitor motor overheating, check whether a room is safe for entry, or trigger a cooling fan.

docs.title: Distance Sensor
docs.text: A distance sensor measures the space between the sensor and the nearest object in its detection path. The two most common technologies in educational kits are ultrasonic sensors, which time an echoing sound pulse, and infrared sensors, which measure the angle or intensity of reflected infrared light. Distance sensors are central to obstacle avoidance, wall-following, and parking behaviors, and—because most types rely on indirect measurement—they are especially sensitive to calibration error, a topic covered later in this chapter.

docs.title: Touch Sensor
docs.text: A touch sensor (also called a bump or contact sensor) detects physical contact by closing or opening an electrical circuit when pressed. It is the simplest sensor in this tour and a direct-measurement device: no calculation converts its reading into a physical quantity, because "pressed" is the physical quantity. Robots use touch sensors as bump switches on a chassis edge, as limit switches that stop an arm at the end of its range of motion, and as simple user input buttons.

docs.title: Sound Sensor
docs.text: A sound sensor converts air pressure vibrations (sound waves) into an electrical signal, usually using a small microphone element followed by an amplifier circuit. Simple sound sensors report only volume (loudness), while more advanced versions can detect specific frequencies or claps. Robots use sound sensors to respond to a clap or whistle command, to detect an alarm, or to react to the volume of ambient noise.

docs.title: Encoder
docs.text: An encoder measures the rotation of a shaft, most often a motor shaft or wheel axle, by counting pulses generated as the shaft turns, using slotted disks and light sensors or magnets and magnetic sensors. Encoders answer the question "how far, or how fast, has this wheel turned?"—information a robot needs to drive a precise distance, maintain a target speed, or estimate its own position by counting wheel rotations. This is another indirect measurement: the raw signal is a stream of pulses, and software converts pulse count into rotation angle or distance traveled using the known pulses-per-revolution of the encoder disk.

docs.title: Potentiometer
docs.text:
A potentiometer is a variable resistor whose resistance changes as a knob, dial, or lever attached to it is rotated or slid, producing an output voltage that directly represents its physical position. Because the output voltage corresponds straightforwardly to position, a potentiometer is a direct-measurement sensor. Robots use potentiometers to sense the angle of a steering mechanism, the position of a joint on a robotic arm, or as a simple manual input control for adjusting a setting like speed or volume.

The following interactive element lets you explore all seven sensor types side by side before moving on to how their readings are made trustworthy.

docs.title: Sensor Calibration: Making Readings Trustworthy
docs.text:
A sensor fresh out of the box rarely reports a physical quantity with perfect accuracy. Sensor calibration is the process of comparing a sensor's raw output against a known, trusted reference value and adjusting the sensor's readings (or the formula that converts them) so that its output matches reality as closely as possible. Calibration is what turns "the sensor reads 480" into "the sensor reads 30 centimeters," and what corrects for the fact that no two sensors of the same model behave identically.

Calibration matters for a specific, practical reason: manufacturing variation. Two distance sensors of the exact same model, purchased at the same time, may report slightly different raw values for the exact same distance, because of tiny differences introduced during manufacturing. Environmental conditions add a second layer of drift—temperature, humidity, and even battery voltage can shift a sensor's baseline reading over the course of a single class period.

A typical calibration procedure for a distance sensor follows these steps:

  1. Place a known object at a precisely measured distance from the sensor (for example, exactly 20 cm, using a ruler).
  2. Record the sensor's raw output value at that known distance.
  3. Repeat at several other known distances (for example, 10 cm, 30 cm, and 50 cm) to capture how the raw value changes across the sensor's range.
  4. Use the recorded pairs of (raw value, true distance) to build a conversion formula or lookup table.
  5. Apply that formula in code so future raw readings are automatically converted into accurate distance values.
  6. Re-calibrate periodically, especially after changing batteries or operating in a new environment.

Tip

A sensor that is precise but never calibrated will confidently report the wrong answer every single time. Precision without calibration is a trap—always calibrate against a known reference before trusting a sensor's absolute value.

The MicroSim below lets you see calibration in action by simulating a noisy distance sensor and comparing raw versus filtered, calibrated readings.

docs.title: Diagram: Sensor Noise and Calibration MicroSim
docs.text:
Sensor Noise and Calibration MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: sensor-noise-calibration-microsim Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, calculate, apply

Learning objective: Students will apply averaging and filtering techniques to a simulated noisy distance sensor and calculate how signal averaging reduces the effect of random noise on a calibrated reading.

Canvas layout: - Top (300px): A live-updating line chart plotting the last 100 simulated sensor readings against time, with the true distance shown as a flat reference line - Bottom (200px): Control panel with sliders and numeric readouts

Visual elements: - A simulated "true" object distance, shown as a solid horizontal reference line (default 30 cm) - A jagged "raw reading" line overlaid on the chart, generated by adding random noise to the true distance each frame - A smoother "filtered reading" line overlaid on the same chart, computed as a moving average of the raw readings - A numeric readout showing the current raw value and current filtered value in centimeters

Interactive controls: - Slider: "Noise Level" (0 to 10 cm standard deviation, default 2 cm) - Slider: "Averaging Window Size" (1 to 30 samples, default 1, meaning no averaging) - Slider: "True Distance" (5 to 100 cm, default 30 cm) to let students move the simulated object - Button: "Reset Chart" - Display: Root-mean-square error of the raw signal vs. true distance, and RMS error of the filtered signal vs. true distance, updated live

Default parameters: - Noise level: 2 cm - Averaging window: 1 (no filtering) - True distance: 30 cm

Behavior: As "Averaging Window Size" increases, the filtered line visibly smooths and its displayed RMS error drops toward zero, while the raw line's RMS error stays roughly constant, demonstrating that averaging reduces the effect of random noise without changing the sensor's underlying calibration.

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show raw noisy readings with high RMS error and window size 1 Stage 2: Show the same noise level with window size increased to 5, filtered RMS error visibly lower Stage 3: Show window size increased to 20, filtered RMS error near zero but responding more slowly to sudden changes in "True Distance" Final: Show a side-by-side numeric comparison of raw RMS error vs. filtered RMS error at the student's chosen settings

Instructional Rationale: Parameter exploration with live numeric feedback is appropriate for this Apply-level objective because students must manipulate the averaging window and directly observe (not just be told) the resulting drop in error, connecting the abstract idea of "filtering" to a concrete, calculable improvement in signal quality.

Implementation: p5.js for the canvas and line chart; noise generated using a Gaussian random function; moving average computed over a circular buffer sized by the "Averaging Window Size" slider; RMS error computed each frame over the visible 100-sample window.

docs.title: From Sensor to Microcontroller: Data Transmission and Signal Processing
docs.text:
A calibrated sensor reading is not automatically useful the instant it is captured—it must travel from the sensor to the microcontroller and be cleaned up along the way. Data transmission is the process of moving a sensor's signal from the sensor itself to the microcontroller that will interpret it, using an electrical connection and an agreed-upon signaling method. Signal processing is the set of techniques used to clean, filter, or transform a raw signal so that noise, drift, and irrelevant variation are reduced before the microcontroller acts on the data.

Data transmission can take several forms, and the choice affects how much signal processing is needed downstream:

  • Analog transmission sends a continuously varying voltage (for example, 0 to 5 volts) that the microcontroller must convert into a digital number using an analog-to-digital converter. Potentiometers and many light sensors use analog transmission.
  • Digital transmission sends discrete on/off pulses or structured digital messages (using protocols such as I2C or SPI) that the microcontroller reads directly as numbers, with no conversion step. Many modern distance sensors and encoders use digital transmission.
  • Pulse-based transmission sends information encoded as the timing or count of pulses, as with an ultrasonic sensor's echo pulse or an encoder's rotation pulses; the microcontroller must measure pulse timing or count pulses to extract the value.

Once a signal arrives at the microcontroller, signal processing techniques are commonly applied before the value is trusted:

  • Averaging (smoothing) combines several recent readings into one value, reducing the effect of random noise, as explored in the calibration MicroSim above.
  • Filtering removes specific unwanted patterns from a signal, such as a low-pass filter that suppresses rapid flickers while preserving slower, meaningful changes.
  • Thresholding converts a continuous value into a simple decision, such as treating any light-sensor reading below a set value as "dark."
  • Debouncing prevents a single physical event—like pressing a touch sensor—from being misread as several rapid presses due to mechanical vibration when the switch contacts touch.

The final interactive element in this chapter traces the complete path a piece of sensor data takes, from the physical world to a decision made in your robot's code.

docs.title: Diagram: Sensor-to-Microcontroller Signal Path
docs.text:
Sensor-to-Microcontroller Signal Path

Type: workflow sim-id: sensor-to-microcontroller-signal-path Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, deconstruct

Learning objective: Students will deconstruct the full path a sensor reading takes from the physical world to a robot decision, distinguishing the role of data transmission from the role of signal processing at each stage.

Purpose: Show that a sensor reading is not a single instantaneous event but a multi-stage pipeline, each stage capable of introducing or removing error.

Visual style: Left-to-right flowchart with four main nodes and one decision-style final node

Steps: 1. Node: "Physical Quantity" Hover/click text: "The real-world property being measured, such as distance to a wall, light intensity, or temperature. This is the ground truth the sensor is trying to capture."

  1. Node: "Sensor" Hover/click text: "Converts the physical quantity into a raw electrical signal (voltage, resistance, or pulses). Introduces its own manufacturing variation, which is why calibration is required."

  2. Node: "Data Transmission" Hover/click text: "Moves the raw signal from the sensor to the microcontroller, as an analog voltage, a digital message, or a stream of timed pulses. The transmission method determines what conversion the microcontroller must perform."

  3. Node: "Signal Processing" Hover/click text: "Cleans the raw value using averaging, filtering, thresholding, or debouncing, reducing the effect of noise before the value is trusted."

  4. Node: "Microcontroller Decision" Hover/click text: "The processed, calibrated value is compared against a threshold or used in a calculation, and the microcontroller commands an actuator in response."

Connections: Straight arrows from Physical Quantity to Sensor to Data Transmission to Signal Processing to Microcontroller Decision, all left to right, no branching.

Color coding: Gray for Physical Quantity (outside the electronic system), blue for Sensor and Data Transmission (hardware stages), orange for Signal Processing (software stage), green for Microcontroller Decision (outcome stage)

Interactive features: Every node is clickable (Mermaid click directive) and opens an infobox with the hover/click text above; clicking two nodes in sequence highlights the arrow between them and displays a short note on what could go wrong at that link (for example, clicking Sensor then Data Transmission highlights that an analog signal traveling a long wire can pick up electrical interference before it reaches the microcontroller).

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax (graph LR) with a click NodeId call showInfo("nodeId") directive on every node, paired with a JavaScript showInfo() function that populates a small infobox panel below the diagram with the corresponding hover/click text.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Precision measurement, direct and indirect measurement, and coordinate systems form the conceptual foundation for everything a sensor reports. The seven sensor types toured in this chapter—light, temperature, distance, touch, sound, encoder, and potentiometer—cover the great majority of sensing tasks in educational robotics, and each fits somewhere on the direct-versus-indirect spectrum you now know how to identify. Sensor calibration turns a raw, sensor-specific number into a trustworthy physical measurement, and understanding data transmission and signal processing explains what happens to that measurement on its short but important journey to the microcontroller. The next time you write read_sensor() in your robot's code, you will know exactly what has to go right before that single number can be trusted.

Quick check: Is a photoresistor-based light sensor a direct or indirect measurement device? Click to expand

Indirect. The sensor directly measures a change in electrical resistance caused by light, and the microcontroller converts that resistance value into a light-intensity reading using a known relationship—so a calculation stands between the raw signal and the reported quantity.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explains the mechanical principles behind the hardware students assembled in Chapter 1. Topics include the six simple machines (levers, pulleys, gears, wheel and axle, inclined planes, and linkages), along with bearings, fasteners, torque, friction, and mechanical advantage. The chapter concludes with structural materials and chassis design, the foundation for designing a robot frame that can withstand real-world use.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

docs.title: Seeing the Whole Machine: What Is a Mechanical System?
docs.text:
When you built the goBILDA FTC StarterBot in Chapter 1, you turned a box of aluminum channels, shafts, gears, and screws into a rolling robot. That finished chassis is a mechanical system: a collection of connected physical parts, arranged so that a force applied at one point produces a predictable motion or force somewhere else. The StarterBot's drivetrain is a mechanical system in miniature—a motor turns a shaft, the shaft drives a sprocket, the sprocket pulls a chain loop, and the chain loop spins the wheels—each part passing motion to the next in a deliberate, engineered sequence.

Every mechanical system, no matter how complex, is built from a small number of basic parts performing one of three jobs:

  • Support — holding parts in the correct position relative to one another, the job done by the StarterBot's U-channels and bearing plates
  • Transmission — carrying force or motion from one location to another, the job done by shafts, gears, chains, and sprockets
  • Conversion — changing the type, direction, speed, or strength of motion, the job done by the simple machines this chapter examines in detail

This chapter takes the StarterBot chassis apart conceptually, piece by piece, to explain the mechanical theory behind hardware your hands already recognize. By the end, the shaft, gear, and chain you assembled in Chapter 1 will make sense not just as parts you snapped together, but as engineered solutions to specific mechanical problems.

docs.title: Simple Machines: The Building Blocks of Every Mechanism
docs.text:
A simple machine is a device with few or no moving parts that changes the direction or magnitude of a force to make a task easier to perform. Engineers have relied on simple machines since antiquity, and every complex mechanism ever built—from a bicycle to a space telescope—is ultimately an arrangement of simple machines working together. This chapter groups six simple machines that appear directly in the StarterBot Kit or in robotics mechanisms you will design later: the lever, the pulley, the gear, the wheel and axle, the inclined plane, and the linkage.

Two of these deserve a quick note before you meet them individually. A gear is often treated as a specialized wheel and axle whose rim carries interlocking teeth instead of a smooth surface, and a linkage is a modern engineering extension of the lever—a connected chain of levers working together rather than a single rigid bar. Grouping them this way reflects how they actually show up in robotics: gears and linkages are everywhere in the StarterBot's drivetrain and future custom mechanisms, so they earn full treatment alongside the four classical machines.

docs.title: Lever
docs.text: A lever is a rigid bar that pivots around a fixed point, called a fulcrum, so that a force applied at one point (the effort) moves a load at another point. Levers are classified by where the fulcrum sits relative to the effort and the load: a first-class lever places the fulcrum between the two (like a seesaw), a second-class lever places the load between the fulcrum and the effort (like a wheelbarrow), and a third-class lever places the effort between the fulcrum and the load (like a fishing rod, or a robot arm's forearm segment). Any rigid StarterBot component that pivots around a shaft to lift or push something—an arm mechanism you might design in a later chapter—is functioning as a lever.

docs.title: Pulley
docs.text: A pulley is a wheel with a grooved rim that carries a rope, cable, or belt, redirecting the direction of a pulling force or, when combined into a block-and-tackle system, multiplying it. A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force, while a movable pulley (one attached to the load itself) also reduces the effort needed to lift that load. The StarterBot Kit does not include a rope-and-pulley system, but its chain-and-sprocket drivetrain is a close mechanical cousin: instead of a smooth wheel and a flexible rope, it uses a toothed wheel (the sprocket) and a flexible chain, gaining the same benefit of transmitting motion between shafts that are not directly connected—along with a guarantee against slipping, which a smooth pulley and belt cannot offer.

docs.title: Gear
docs.text: A gear is a rotating wheel with teeth cut around its rim, designed to mesh with the teeth of another gear so the two rotate together without slipping. When two gears mesh directly, tooth to tooth, they always spin in opposite directions; when a chain or an idler gear sits between them, they spin the same direction instead. The StarterBot Kit's intake roller mechanism uses exactly this principle, meshing a 30-Tooth Gear, a 20-Tooth Gear, and a 100-Tooth Gear directly against one another to transmit rotation between shafts without the flexibility—or the possibility of slack—that a chain introduces. Because the number of teeth on each gear controls how fast it turns relative to its partner, gears deserve their own deeper look later in this chapter under Gear Ratio.

docs.title: Wheel and Axle
docs.text: A wheel and axle is a simple machine made of a large-diameter wheel rigidly attached to a smaller-diameter axle (shaft) so that the two must rotate together. Turning the wheel with a small effort produces a large force at the axle, or turning the axle produces a large motion at the rim of the wheel—the exact trade-off depends on which part receives the input force. Every wheel on the StarterBot is a wheel and axle: the wheel's larger radius, compared to the 8mm REX Shaft it is mounted on, is what lets a relatively small twisting force from the motor produce enough push at the ground to move the whole robot forward.

docs.title: Inclined Plane
docs.text: An inclined plane is a flat surface set at an angle between two different heights, allowing a load to be raised using less force than lifting it straight up, at the cost of moving it a longer distance. A wheelchair ramp and a loading dock ramp are everyday inclined planes. Two other simple machines are, geometrically, an inclined plane in disguise: a wedge is an inclined plane that moves through material to split it apart, and a screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder—which is exactly why the threads on every socket head screw in the StarterBot Kit look like a spiral ramp when viewed up close. That connection resurfaces later in this chapter, when fasteners get their own detailed treatment.

docs.title: Linkage
docs.text:
A linkage is a system of rigid links connected at joints, arranged so that moving one link produces a predictable, coordinated motion in the others. Where a single lever only rotates around one fixed fulcrum, a linkage's joints are often not fixed to the frame at all, which lets a well-designed linkage trace complex paths, convert rotating motion into straight-line motion, or amplify a small input motion into a larger output motion at the far end of the chain. Robot arms, walking-leg mechanisms, and the four-bar linkages common in custom robotics designs (a topic revisited in the chapter on designing and building custom parts) are all built from linkages.

The interactive explorer below lets you click through all six simple machines side by side, review a concrete example of each, and see the formula used to calculate its mechanical advantage—the topic covered in full later in this chapter.

docs.title: Gear Ratio: Trading Speed for Torque
docs.text:
Gears rarely work alone—they mesh in pairs or chains of pairs, and the ratio between their tooth counts controls exactly how much speed is traded for how much twisting force. The gear ratio is the ratio of teeth on the driven gear to teeth on the driving gear:

\[ \text{Gear Ratio} = \frac{\text{teeth on driven gear}}{\text{teeth on driving gear}} \]

The same ratio applies to a chain-and-sprocket drivetrain like the StarterBot's, where the "driving" sprocket is mounted on the motor's output shaft and the "driven" sprocket is mounted on the wheel shaft. If the StarterBot's 10-Tooth Sprocket on the motor shaft drives a larger 30-tooth sprocket on the wheel shaft through a closed loop of plastic chain, the gear ratio is \( 30 \div 10 = 3 \), meaning the wheel shaft turns once for every three turns of the motor shaft.

A gear ratio greater than 1 (a small driving gear turning a larger driven gear) always produces this trade-off:

  • Output speed decreases by the same factor the ratio increases
  • Output torque increases by that same factor, assuming no energy is lost to friction

A gear ratio less than 1 (a large driving gear turning a smaller driven gear) produces the opposite trade-off: higher output speed, lower output torque. This is exactly the pattern behind the two Yellow Jacket motor options from Chapter 1, reproduced below as a reminder of how gear ratio shows up in a component you have already handled.

Gear ratio (internal gearbox) Output speed Output torque Typical StarterBot use 19.2:1 Faster rotation Lower torque Driving wheels for quick movement 50.9:1 Slower rotation Higher torque Mechanisms needing more twisting force, like the intake roller

Notice that the internal gearbox ratio inside each Yellow Jacket motor works by exactly the same rule as the external 30-Tooth Gear, 20-Tooth Gear, and 100-Tooth Gear meshing in the intake mechanism, or the 10-Tooth Sprocket driving a larger sprocket through the chain loop: more teeth on the driven side always means slower and stronger, fewer teeth on the driven side always means faster and weaker. The MicroSim below lets you test that rule directly using the StarterBot's own gear and sprocket tooth counts.

docs.title: Torque and Friction: The Forces at Play
docs.text: Every mechanical system ultimately does its work through two forces that show up in nearly every StarterBot subassembly: torque and friction.

docs.title: Torque
docs.text:
Torque is a twisting force that tends to cause rotation around an axis, calculated as the applied force multiplied by the distance from the axis at which that force is applied:

\[ \tau = F \times d \]

where \( \tau \) (tau) is torque, \( F \) is the applied force, and \( d \) is the distance from the pivot or axis to the point where the force is applied. This is exactly why a longer wrench makes a stuck bolt easier to turn: the force you apply stays the same, but a longer handle increases \( d \), which increases the torque delivered to the bolt. A Yellow Jacket motor's datasheet torque rating describes the same quantity—the twisting force it can deliver at its output shaft—and it is precisely this torque that the gear ratio in the previous section multiplies or divides as it passes through the drivetrain.

docs.title: Friction
docs.text:
Friction is a force that resists the relative sliding or rolling motion between two surfaces in contact, acting opposite to the direction of motion (or attempted motion). Two categories matter for the StarterBot:

  • Static friction resists the start of motion between surfaces that are not yet sliding, such as a locknut gripping a screw's threads tightly enough that vibration cannot loosen it
  • Kinetic friction resists motion that is already happening, such as an 8mm REX Shaft turning inside a bearing

Friction is not purely a nuisance—the StarterBot's wheels depend on friction against the ground to convert rotation into forward motion, and a locknut depends on friction to stay tight. But friction inside a mechanism, such as a shaft rubbing directly against an aluminum U-channel with no bearing installed, wastes energy as heat and wears down parts. That trade-off is exactly why the StarterBot Kit places an 8mm REX Bearing at every point where a shaft passes through the frame, a component covered in detail later in this chapter.

Tip

A quick way to remember the difference: static friction has to be overcome to start something moving, and it is almost always slightly stronger than kinetic friction, which only has to be overcome to keep something moving. That is why a stalled shaft can feel "stuck" for a moment before it begins turning smoothly.

docs.title: Mechanical Advantage: Why Simple Machines Help
docs.text:
Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the output force a machine produces to the input force applied to it, and it is the single number that explains why every simple machine in this chapter is worth using in the first place:

\[ \text{Mechanical Advantage} = \frac{\text{output force}}{\text{input force}} \]

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the machine multiplies force, at the cost of requiring the input to move a greater distance than the output—energy is never created for free, only traded between force and distance. A mechanical advantage less than 1 does the opposite: it trades force for speed or distance, which is exactly the case for the StarterBot's 19.2:1 Yellow Jacket motor driving a wheel meant to move quickly rather than push hard.

The table below reinforces the mechanical advantage formula for each simple machine introduced earlier in this chapter, now gathered in one place for comparison.

Simple Machine Mechanical Advantage Formula StarterBot / Everyday Example Lever effort arm length ÷ load arm length Robot arm forearm segment Pulley (or sprocket pair) number of supporting ropes, or driven teeth ÷ driving teeth Chain-and-sprocket drivetrain Gear teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driving gear 30-Tooth Gear driven by 20-Tooth Gear Wheel and Axle radius of wheel ÷ radius of axle Drive wheel on 8mm REX Shaft Inclined Plane length of slope ÷ height of slope Threads on a socket head screw Linkage varies continuously with link angles Four-bar robot arm linkage

Real mechanisms never reach their theoretical mechanical advantage exactly, because friction consumes some of the input force before it ever reaches the load. Engineers distinguish between ideal mechanical advantage (IMA), calculated from a machine's geometry alone (tooth counts, arm lengths, ramp dimensions), and actual mechanical advantage (AMA), measured from real output and input forces after friction losses are included. A well-lubricated, properly supported shaft—one running through an 8mm REX Bearing rather than grinding directly against aluminum—keeps AMA as close to IMA as possible.

docs.title: Bearings and Fasteners: The Hardware That Holds It Together
docs.text: Simple machines only work reliably when the hardware supporting them is chosen correctly. Two categories of hardware do that job throughout the StarterBot Kit: bearings and fasteners.

docs.title: Bearing
docs.text: A bearing is a component that supports a rotating shaft while minimizing friction between the shaft and its surrounding structure, typically by replacing sliding contact with rolling contact or a low-friction sleeve. The StarterBot's 8mm REX Bearing is a ring of hardened steel with an inner race that lets a shaft spin with almost no resistance, mounted wherever a shaft passes through a U-channel or a Drop-Center Bearing Plate. Without a bearing, a spinning shaft would grind directly against the aluminum frame, generating friction, heat, and wear with every rotation—exactly the kinetic friction problem described earlier in this chapter.

docs.title: Fastener
docs.text:
A fastener is a hardware component used to mechanically join two or more parts together, typically by clamping them with friction or a mechanical interlock rather than permanently bonding them. The StarterBot Kit relies on three main types working as a team:

  1. Socket head screws (8mm, 10mm, and 12mm lengths) provide the clamping force, driven by a hex key into a hexagonal socket in the screw head
  2. Locknuts thread onto a screw and use a nylon insert to grip its threads tightly, resisting the vibration that would otherwise back a plain nut off over time
  3. Washers spread the clamping force of a screw and locknut over a wider area, preventing the aluminum U-channel from denting or cracking under concentrated pressure

Recall from the Inclined Plane discussion earlier in this chapter that a screw's threads are, geometrically, an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. That is precisely why turning a screw with modest effort produces a large clamping force: the screw's threads give it a very large mechanical advantage, trading a long rotational travel distance for a strong, concentrated squeeze.

docs.title: Structural Materials
docs.text:
Structural materials are the materials chosen to form the load-bearing skeleton of a mechanical system, selected based on properties like strength (resistance to breaking), stiffness (resistance to bending), and strength-to-weight ratio (how much load a material can bear per unit of its own weight). The StarterBot's U-channels are extruded aluminum, a material chosen specifically because it combines high stiffness and strength with low weight—a critical trade-off for any robot that needs to move quickly without wasting motor torque simply hauling around its own frame.

Different robotics and engineering applications call for different structural materials, each suited to a different trade-off:

  • Aluminum — excellent strength-to-weight ratio, easy to machine and drill, used for the StarterBot's U-channels and bearing plates
  • Steel — higher strength and stiffness than aluminum but significantly heavier, used for the StarterBot's 8mm REX Shafts, where wear resistance and rigidity under load matter more than saving weight
  • Plastic (nylon or similar polymers) — lightweight and low-friction, used for the StarterBot's chain links, where flexibility and smooth sliding matter more than raw strength
  • Carbon fiber — exceptional strength-to-weight ratio at a much higher cost, common in competition-grade robotics but not included in an introductory kit like the StarterBot

docs.title: Chassis Design
docs.text:
Chassis design is the engineering process of arranging structural materials into a frame that supports every other subsystem of a robot—drivetrain, sensors, battery, and any custom mechanisms—while withstanding the forces of driving, collisions, and vibration. The StarterBot's chassis demonstrates several chassis design principles you will reuse in later custom-part design: side rails built from long U-channels for rigidity, cross braces from shorter U-channels to resist twisting, Quad Block Mounts at corners to distribute joint stress, and Drop-Center Bearing Plates positioned precisely so drivetrain shafts stay parallel and aligned.

The clickable diagram below revisits the StarterBot chassis you assembled in Chapter 1, this time asking you to identify the structural role each component plays rather than simply naming the part.

docs.title: Mechanical Design: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Mechanical design is the engineering discipline of selecting, sizing, and arranging simple machines, materials, and hardware into a system that reliably performs a specific mechanical task. It is the capstone concept of this chapter because it is not a single part you can point to—it is the process that produced every part you have studied so far. Designing the StarterBot's drivetrain meant choosing a gear ratio that balanced speed against torque, selecting aluminum for the frame to save weight without sacrificing stiffness, specifying bearings everywhere friction needed to be minimized, and choosing fastener types and sizes strong enough to survive vibration without over-engineering the whole frame into unnecessary weight.

Good mechanical design follows a recognizable pattern, whether the mechanism is a StarterBot drivetrain or a custom part you design later in this course:

  1. Define the mechanical task precisely (move a wheel, lift an arm, roll an intake mechanism)
  2. Choose simple machines that provide the needed trade-off between force, speed, and direction
  3. Select structural materials that balance strength, stiffness, and weight
  4. Specify bearings and fasteners that control friction and resist vibration at every joint
  5. Verify the design—by calculation, simulation, or physical testing—before committing to a final build
Check yourself: If a gear ratio increases from 2:1 to 4:1, what happens to output speed and torque? — Click to expand

Output speed is cut in half again, and output torque doubles again, because both scale directly with the gear ratio: a 4:1 ratio delivers twice the speed reduction and twice the torque multiplication of a 2:1 ratio, assuming friction losses stay the same.

With mechanical systems and simple machines now connected back to the hardware in your hands, the next chapter turns to a different way of transmitting force through a robot: fluid power, where pressurized air or liquid—rather than gears and shafts—does the work of moving a mechanism.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Beyond gears and motors, some robotic systems use fluid power. This chapter introduces hydraulics and pneumatics, fluid pressure, cylinders, valves, pumps, and compressors, along with fluid power safety and how to read a fluid power diagram. Students finish by designing a simple fluid power system for a given application.

docs.text:
