docs.title: From Driver's Seat to Autonomous Control: Why This Chapter Comes Now
docs.text:
Now that you understand control loops in depth from Chapter 11: Control Systems and Feedback Loops, and know what is happening inside your microcontroller from Chapter 12: Digital Logic and Computing Fundamentals, it is time to put that knowledge to work in more sophisticated robot programs. Back in Chapter 4: Programming Your Robot, your programs were short scripts written before you understood setpoints, error signals, or the PID math that makes a real feedback loop stable. This chapter revisits robot programming with all of that theory already in hand.

A real FTC competition match is split into two very different programming problems, and that split organizes this entire chapter. During the autonomous period, a fixed thirty-second window at the start of a match, the robot runs entirely on pre-written code with no human input at all. During the driver-controlled period that follows, a human operator steers the robot in real time using a gamepad, and the robot's program exists mainly to translate those button presses and joystick movements into motor commands. Every concept in this chapter falls on one side of that divide or the other, or bridges between them:

  • Human-controlled side: teleoperation and the robot interface that carries a driver's commands to the robot
  • Autonomous side: robot motion programming and path planning, which let the robot decide and execute its own movement
  • Shared, cross-cutting skills: wheeled and arm control strategies, calibration, troubleshooting, and safety programming apply to both halves of a match equally

docs.title: Teleoperation: Programming for a Human in the Loop
docs.text:
Teleoperation is the practice of controlling a robot in real time from a distance, using a human operator's input device to command the robot's actuators moment by moment. In FTC, teleoperation happens during the driver-controlled period, when a student driver holds a gamepad and a program on the robot continuously reads that gamepad's state and converts it into motor and servo commands. Unlike the autonomous programs you will meet later in this chapter, a teleoperation program never decides on its own what the robot should do next; it simply repeats a fast, faithful translation loop for as long as the match clock runs.

That translation loop follows a predictable pattern in almost every teleoperation program, regardless of what specific robot it controls:

  1. Read the current state of every input device (joystick positions, button presses, trigger values)
  2. Convert each raw input value into a meaningful command, such as a motor power level or a servo angle
  3. Send that command out to the appropriate actuator
  4. Repeat the entire cycle again immediately, often thirty to sixty times per second

Notice how closely this mirrors the sense-decide-act cycle from Chapter 4's control loops, except the "decide" step has been handed almost entirely to the human driver. The program's real job is translation and safety-checking, not decision-making, which is exactly why teleoperation code tends to be shorter and more predictable than the autonomous code you will study next.

docs.title: Robot Interface: The Bridge Between Driver and Machine
docs.text:
A robot interface is the combination of hardware and software that carries commands from a human operator's input device to the robot's microcontroller, and often carries status information back the other way. In FTC, the robot interface includes a wireless connection between a Driver Station tablet and the robot's control hub, a gamepad plugged into that Driver Station, and the software layer on the robot that reads gamepad values by name, such as gamepad1.left_stick_y for the left joystick's vertical position.

A well-designed robot interface does more than pass raw numbers through unchanged. It maps physical inputs to logical robot actions in ways that make the robot predictable and comfortable to drive. The table below reinforces this mapping using vocabulary already introduced above, showing how one common gamepad layout might be assigned to a robot's actuators.

Gamepad Input Raw Value Range Mapped Robot Action Left stick (vertical) -1.0 to 1.0 Forward/backward drive power Right stick (horizontal) -1.0 to 1.0 Turning rate Right trigger 0.0 to 1.0 Intake roller speed A button Pressed / not pressed Toggle arm servo between two preset angles

Robot interface design also includes decisions about deadzone, a small range of raw joystick values near zero that the program treats as exactly zero, so a joystick that is not perfectly centered does not cause the robot to creep forward on its own. Building a deadzone into the interface layer is a small piece of code with an outsized effect on how controllable a robot feels to its driver.

docs.title: Robot Motion Programming: Moving Without a Human at the Wheel
docs.text:
Robot motion programming is the practice of writing code that plans and executes robot movement without a human continuously supplying input, the defining skill of FTC's autonomous period. Where teleoperation translates a driver's joystick into motor commands moment by moment, robot motion programming must decide, entirely in advance or through sensor feedback alone, exactly how far to drive, when to turn, and when to stop.

This distinction is important enough that it is worth seeing the two control flows side by side before moving further into either one. The interactive diagram below lets you toggle between FTC's teleop and autonomous periods and watch how the flow of information changes completely, even though the same drive motors and the same microcontroller are involved in both.

docs.title: Diagram: Teleop vs. Autonomous Control Flow
docs.text:
Teleop vs. Autonomous Control Flow

Type: diagram sim-id: teleop-vs-autonomous-flow Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students distinguish teleoperation from robot motion programming by contrasting where the "decide" step happens in each control flow.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, compare, contrast, interpret

Learning objective: Given a toggle between FTC's teleop and autonomous periods, students will contrast the control flow of driver-issued commands with the control flow of a self-directed motion program.

Components to show: - A "Driver / Gamepad" box (visible only in Teleop mode) - A "Pre-Written Motion Program" box (visible only in Autonomous mode) - A shared "Microcontroller" box in the center - A "Drive Motors" box and a "Servos" box on the right - A "Sensors" box feeding back into the center box

Connections: - Teleop mode: an animated arrow travels repeatedly from Driver/Gamepad to Microcontroller labeled "Joystick + button state, ~50 times/sec," then onward to Drive Motors and Servos; the Sensors box is grayed out to show it is optional and rarely consulted - Autonomous mode: an animated arrow travels from Pre-Written Motion Program to Microcontroller labeled "Next planned step," then onward to Drive Motors and Servos; a second arrow loops from Sensors back into the Microcontroller labeled "Feedback used to confirm each step," shown active and highlighted

Interactive controls: - Toggle button: "Teleop Period" / "Autonomous Period," switches the entire diagram's active boxes and arrows - Clicking any box (Driver/Gamepad, Pre-Written Motion Program, Microcontroller, Drive Motors, Servos, Sensors) opens an infobox with that component's role in the currently selected mode

Style: Simple block diagram with animated flow arrows, redrawn per mode rather than shown simultaneously

Labels: "Teleop Period" and "Autonomous Period" as large mode headers above the diagram

Color scheme: Blue arrows and boxes for Teleop mode, green arrows and boxes for Autonomous mode, gray for inactive components

Implementation: p5.js, using a mode variable to control which boxes and arrows are drawn and animated; infoboxes rendered as a side panel that updates on click

Robot motion programming commonly relies on odometry, the technique of estimating a robot's position and heading by tracking wheel rotations over time, since an autonomous robot has no driver watching to correct its course. A basic autonomous motion program might command the robot to drive forward until an encoder reports 24 inches traveled, then turn 90 degrees, then drive forward again, chaining together simple moves into a complete routine.

docs.title: Path Planning: Deciding a Route Before Moving
docs.text:
Path planning is the process of computing a sequence of positions or moves that will get a robot from its current location to a goal location, ideally while avoiding known obstacles. Robot motion programming, introduced above, focuses on executing a single planned move accurately; path planning operates one level higher, deciding what the full sequence of moves should be in the first place, especially when obstacles stand between a robot and its goal.

A simple approach to path planning treats the robot's field as a grid of cells, some of which are blocked by obstacles, and searches for a connected sequence of open cells linking the start cell to the goal cell. The MicroSim below lets you experiment with exactly this kind of grid-based path planning yourself, placing a start point, a goal, and obstacles, and watching a simple search algorithm find a route around them.

docs.title: Diagram: Grid Path Planner
docs.text:
Grid Path Planner

Type: microsim sim-id: grid-path-planner Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students apply the concept of grid-based path planning by placing a start cell, a goal cell, and obstacle cells, then running a search algorithm and observing the resulting path.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: apply, demonstrate, practice, solve

Learning objective: Given a blank grid, students will place a start point, goal point, and obstacles, then apply a path-finding algorithm to produce and evaluate a valid obstacle-avoiding path.

Canvas layout: - Left (75% width): a 12x12 grid of clickable square cells - Right (25% width): control panel with mode buttons and a status readout

Visual elements: - Empty cells (white/light gray) - Obstacle cells (dark gray, set by clicking in "Place Obstacle" mode) - Start cell (green) - Goal cell (red) - Computed path cells (highlighted in blue after search runs)

Interactive controls: - Mode buttons: "Place Start," "Place Goal," "Place Obstacle," "Erase" - Button: "Find Path" — runs a breadth-first search from start to goal on the current grid - Button: "Clear Grid" - Status readout: number of steps in the found path, or "No path found" if the goal is fully walled off

Default parameters: - Grid: empty except a default start (bottom-left) and goal (top-right) - Mode: "Place Obstacle" selected by default

Behavior: - Clicking a cell in the current mode sets that cell's type - Clicking "Find Path" runs breadth-first search treating each open cell as a node connected to its four neighbors, then animates the discovered path one cell at a time - If obstacles fully block every route, the status readout reports "No path found" instead of drawing a path - Clicking "Clear Grid" resets all cells to empty except the default start and goal

Instructional Rationale: An Apply-level, parameter-exploration pattern is appropriate here because path planning is best understood by manipulating obstacles directly and observing how the computed route changes, rather than by watching a single fixed example.

Implementation: p5.js, storing the grid as a 2D array and implementing breadth-first search with a queue; animate the final path by revealing one cell per short interval

Real FTC autonomous routines rarely need a full search algorithm like the one above, since most fields have only a few known obstacles. Even so, the underlying idea, planning several moves ahead rather than reacting one step at a time, is exactly what separates a fragile autonomous program from a robust one.

docs.title: Wheeled Robot Control: Steering the Drivetrain
docs.text:
Wheeled robot control is the set of programming techniques used to command a robot's drive motors so the whole chassis moves and turns as intended. The StarterBot chassis you built in Chapter 1 uses a drivetrain of Yellow Jacket gearmotors driving Gecko wheels, and the specific wiring of that drivetrain determines exactly which control technique applies.

Two wheeled drive layouts appear most often in FTC robots, and each demands a different piece of control code. The comparison below reinforces terms already defined above and in Chapter 1, rather than introducing brand-new vocabulary.

Drive Layout Wheel Arrangement Turning Method Can Strafe Sideways? Differential (tank) drive Left-side and right-side wheel pairs, each pair driven together Left and right sides run at different powers or opposite directions No Holonomic (mecanum) drive Four mecanum wheels, each with angled rollers Combining four independent wheel powers in different ratios Yes

Differential drive is the simpler of the two to program: driving straight means commanding both sides to the same power, and turning in place means commanding the two sides to opposite powers. Holonomic drive trades that simplicity for maneuverability, since a program must calculate four separate wheel powers from just two joystick axes and a rotation input, but the payoff is a robot that can slide sideways without first turning to face a new direction. Whichever layout a robot uses, wheeled robot control code sits directly beneath both teleoperation and robot motion programming, translating whatever "move this way" command comes from above into the specific power sent to each wheel motor.

docs.title: Robotic Arm Control: Commanding Multiple Joints Together
docs.text:
Robotic arm control is the set of programming techniques used to command a multi-jointed arm so its end effector, the tool or gripper at the arm's tip, reaches a specific position and orientation. Unlike a single drive motor that only needs a power level, an arm typically has several joints, each usually driven by its own servo or gearmotor, and all of those joints must be coordinated together to produce useful motion.

Arm control programs typically work at one of two levels of abstraction, and recognizing the difference helps explain why some robot arm code looks far more mathematical than drivetrain code:

  • Joint-space control — the program commands each joint's angle directly, such as "set the shoulder joint to 45 degrees and the elbow joint to 90 degrees," leaving it to the programmer to know what combination of angles produces a useful arm position
  • Task-space control — the program specifies where the end effector should end up in real-world coordinates, such as "move the gripper to 30 centimeters forward and 20 centimeters up," and the code calculates the joint angles needed to get there using inverse kinematics, the mathematical process of working backward from a desired end-effector position to the joint angles that produce it

Most classroom and early-competition FTC arms use joint-space control because it requires no extra math beyond commanding individual servos, the same basic servo-angle skill from Chapter 11's actuator control section. Task-space control and inverse kinematics become valuable once an arm has enough joints, or the required precision is high enough, that reasoning about individual angles by hand becomes impractical.

Why Arm Control Feels Harder Than Drive Control

A drivetrain has one goal at a time: a speed and a direction. An arm often has several joints that all affect the end effector's final position simultaneously, so a small change to one joint's angle can require compensating changes in the others. This is exactly why robotic arm control is usually taught after wheeled robot control rather than before it.

docs.title: Robot Calibration: Making Sensor Values Match Reality
docs.text:
Robot calibration is the process of adjusting a robot's software so that its sensor readings and actuator commands correspond accurately to real-world physical values. A distance sensor fresh out of the box might report a value that is close to, but not exactly, the true distance in centimeters, and a drive motor commanded to "full power" on one robot might spin noticeably faster or slower than the identical motor on a teammate's robot due to manufacturing variation, wheel wear, or battery voltage.

Calibration typically happens through a short, deliberate procedure before a robot's normal program runs, following a repeatable pattern:

  1. Place the robot or sensor in a known, measured condition (for example, exactly 20 centimeters from a wall)
  2. Record what the sensor actually reports in that known condition
  3. Calculate a correction factor or offset that converts the raw reading into an accurate real-world value
  4. Store that correction factor in the program so every future reading is automatically adjusted

Skipping calibration does not necessarily make a robot's program crash, which is precisely what makes uncalibrated robots so frustrating to debug: the code runs without errors, yet the robot consistently stops two centimeters short of a wall or turns a few degrees past its intended heading, because every uncorrected reading carries the same small, silent error into every decision that program makes.

docs.title: Robot Troubleshooting: Diagnosing What Went Wrong
docs.text:
Robot troubleshooting is the systematic process of identifying why a robot is not behaving as its program intends, and narrowing down whether the root cause is in the code, the wiring, the mechanism, or the calibration. Because a robot combines software, electronics, and moving mechanical parts, the same visible symptom, such as "the arm doesn't move," can trace back to causes in any one of those three domains.

Effective troubleshooting follows a decision-tree pattern: start from an observed symptom, ask a series of narrowing questions, and arrive at a likely cause and fix rather than guessing randomly. The clickable diagram below walks through exactly that process for several common FTC robot symptoms.

docs.title: Diagram: Robot Troubleshooting Decision Tree
docs.text:
Robot Troubleshooting Decision Tree

Type: workflow sim-id: robot-troubleshooting-decision-tree Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Guide students through a systematic troubleshooting process for common robot failure symptoms, reinforcing that the same symptom can trace to code, wiring, mechanical, or calibration causes.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: differentiate, examine, distinguish, organize

Learning objective: Given a described robot symptom, students will analyze a chain of diagnostic questions to distinguish among code, wiring, mechanical, and calibration causes and identify the corresponding fix.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart, top-down, with decision diamonds and rectangular outcome nodes

Steps: 1. Start: "Symptom: Motor does not move at all" Hover text: "The commanded actuator produces no motion whatsoever." 2. Decision: "Does the motor spin when tested directly on the Driver Station's motor test screen?" Hover text: "Isolates whether the problem is electrical/mechanical versus in your program's logic." 3. Branch "No" leads to: "Check wiring and power" (outcome) Hover text: "A motor that will not spin under direct test likely has a loose connector, blown fuse, or wiring fault, not a code problem." 4. Branch "Yes" leads to Decision: "Is the motor referenced with the correct configuration name in code?" Hover text: "FTC robot configurations must match the name used in your program exactly, or the command silently fails." 5. Branch "No" leads to: "Fix configuration name mismatch" (outcome) Hover text: "Rename the motor in code or in the Driver Station configuration file so both match." 6. Branch "Yes" leads to Decision: "Is the commanded power value actually non-zero at that point in the program?" Hover text: "A logic bug, such as a condition that is never true, can prevent the command from ever being sent." 7. Branch "Yes, non-zero power is sent" leads to: "Check for a robot calibration or mechanical jam issue" (outcome) Hover text: "If a nonzero command is truly being sent and the motor still does not move, suspect a mechanical jam or a calibration offset masking real motion." 8. Branch "No, power is always zero" leads to: "Fix the program logic" (outcome) Hover text: "Trace the conditional statements and variables controlling that motor command to find why it never receives a nonzero value."

Color coding: - Blue: symptom start node - Yellow: decision diamonds - Green: outcome/fix nodes

Interactive features: Every node includes a click directive calling an infobox function that displays that node's hover text; clicking a decision diamond additionally highlights the branch path taken to reach it

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click NodeId call showInfo("nodeId") directives on every node, paired with a small JavaScript infobox panel below the diagram

Notice that the decision tree above never jumps straight from a symptom to a fix; it always passes through at least one narrowing question first. This mirrors how experienced roboticists actually troubleshoot: they isolate variables one at a time, exactly as a scientist isolates variables in a controlled experiment, rather than replacing parts at random until something works.

docs.title: Robot Safety Programming: Designing Programs That Fail Safely
docs.text:
Robot safety programming is the practice of writing robot code so that it behaves predictably and avoids harm even when sensors fail, communication drops, or an operator makes a mistake, rather than only handling the case where everything works perfectly. Every technique covered earlier in this chapter, teleoperation, motion programming, path planning, arm and wheeled control, calibration, and troubleshooting, becomes safer when it is written with this mindset from the start.

A few safety programming practices show up repeatedly across FTC robots and industrial robots alike:

  • Timeouts — if an expected sensor reading or communication signal never arrives, the program stops the robot instead of waiting forever or assuming a default value
  • Range limiting — arm and servo commands are clamped to a safe range of angles in code, so a bug elsewhere in the program cannot command a joint past its physical limit
  • Emergency stop handling — the program checks for a stop signal on every loop pass, not just at specific points, so the robot can be halted immediately at any moment
  • Fail-safe defaults — if a control signal is lost mid-match, actuators default to a safe, stopped state rather than continuing their last command indefinitely

Untested Code Is Not Safe Code

A robotic arm that has never been tested near its full range of motion, or a drivetrain that has never been tested with a dead battery mid-command, has not actually been proven safe. Safety programming is validated through deliberate testing of failure conditions, not assumed from code that merely compiles.

Robot safety programming is a fitting closing topic for this chapter precisely because it is not a separate skill practiced in isolation. It is a discipline applied on top of teleoperation, motion programming, path planning, arm and wheeled control, calibration, and troubleshooting alike, and the strongest FTC programs are the ones where every one of those techniques was written with failure, not just success, in mind from the very first line of code.

Quick check: A student's autonomous path-planning routine finds a valid path around every obstacle on the field, but the student has never tested what happens if a wheel encoder wire comes loose mid-match. Which concept from this chapter is missing? Click to reveal the answer.

Robot safety programming is missing. A correct path plan only describes the intended route; it says nothing about how the program should behave if a sensor it depends on fails partway through execution. A safety-conscious version of the same program would include a timeout or fail-safe default so a lost encoder signal stops the robot safely instead of driving on blind, incorrect assumptions.

docs.title: Integrating, Testing, and Maintaining a Complete Robotic System
Integrating, Testing, and Maintaining a Complete Robotic System
Summary
docs.text: The capstone chapter of the course, where every earlier skill comes together. Students learn to select components (sensors, actuators) and hardware platforms for a robotic design, then assemble, wire, and integrate a complete system. The chapter covers systematic testing, reverse-engineering and documentation practices, and finishes with robot performance evaluation, maintenance, and a look at current trends shaping the robotics industry.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Robotic Components
  2. Robot Chassis
  3. Robot Power System
  4. Robot Actuator Selection
  5. Robot Sensor Selection
  6. Robotic Hardware Platform
  7. Robot Assembly
  8. Robot Wiring
  9. System Integration
  10. Robot Testing
  11. Robot Reengineering
  12. Robot Documentation
  13. Robot Performance Evaluation
  14. Robot Maintenance
  15. Robotics Industry Trends

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Introduction to Robotics and Systems
  • Chapter 3: Programming Fundamentals
  • Chapter 4: Programming Your Robot
  • Chapter 5: Designing and Building Custom Parts
  • Chapter 7: Electronic Components and Circuit Design
  • Chapter 9: Mechanical Systems and Simple Machines
  • Chapter 13: Advanced Robot Programming

docs.title: The Capstone: From Kit to Original Design
docs.text:
Why This Chapter Is Different

Every chapter before this one taught you one piece of the puzzle: building with a kit, writing code, designing custom parts, wiring circuits, choosing sensors, understanding mechanisms, controlling feedback loops, and programming advanced behaviors. This chapter does not teach a new piece. It teaches you how all the pieces fit together—the process professional engineers and competitive robotics teams use to go from a blank sheet of paper to a complete, tested, working robot.

Throughout this chapter, follow a running example: a fictional FTC (FIRST Tech Challenge) team called Vertex Robotics, preparing for a new competition season called "Vertex Rising." In this game, robots must locate scattered rings on the field, pick them up, and stack them onto scoring poles at three different heights within a two-and-a-half-minute match. Vertex Robotics has outgrown the StarterBot-style kit robot from Chapter 1. This season, they are designing an original robot from scratch, and every decision they make will draw on a chapter you have already studied.

Robotic components are the categories of physical and electronic parts that combine to form any robot, regardless of its specific purpose. Before selecting a single part, a design team should inventory the categories of components their robot will need, because forgetting a category during planning is far more expensive to fix after assembly has begun.

Every robot, from a simple line-following kit robot to a competition-grade FTC machine, is built from the same broad categories of components:

  • Structural components — the chassis, frame, brackets, and fasteners that hold everything in place (covered in this chapter and Chapter 5)
  • Power components — batteries, voltage regulators, and distribution wiring that supply energy to every other subsystem (Chapter 6)
  • Actuation components — motors, servos, and pneumatic or hydraulic cylinders that create motion (Chapters 9 and 10)
  • Sensing components — sensors that gather information about the robot and its environment (Chapter 8)
  • Control and computation components — the microcontroller or computer that runs the robot's program and makes decisions (Chapter 12)
  • Software — the code that ties sensing, decision-making, and actuation together (Chapters 3, 4, and 13)

Vertex Robotics' first planning meeting is essentially this list, turned into a checklist. Before choosing any specific part, the team asks: what does each category need to accomplish for the Vertex Rising game task of finding, collecting, and stacking rings?

docs.title: Choosing a Frame: Robot Chassis and Robotic Hardware Platform
docs.text:
A robot chassis is the structural frame that physically supports and connects a robot's other components, much like a car's frame supports its engine, seats, and body panels. The chassis determines the robot's overall size, weight distribution, ground clearance, and how easily new parts can be added or removed later.

Design teams rarely start a chassis from nothing. A robotic hardware platform is a baseline combination of chassis, drivetrain, and core electronics that a team either buys as a starting kit or designs from scratch to serve as the foundation for a specific robot. Choosing a platform is one of the first and most consequential decisions in the entire design process, because it constrains almost every choice that follows.

Vertex Robotics has to decide between three broad platform strategies, each with real tradeoffs:

Platform Strategy Description Advantage Tradeoff Kit-based platform Pre-manufactured chassis rails and drivetrain (e.g., a goBILDA or REV starter kit) Fast to assemble, proven reliability Less unique, may not fit unusual mechanisms Hybrid platform Kit drivetrain with custom-designed superstructure (from Chapter 5's fabrication skills) Balances speed and originality Requires integrating two design sources cleanly Fully custom platform Every structural part designed and fabricated by the team Maximum design freedom Highest time cost and risk of structural failure

Vertex Robotics chooses the hybrid platform: a proven kit drivetrain for reliable driving, combined with a custom 3D-printed and laser-cut superstructure—designed using the same CAD and fabrication skills from Chapter 5—built specifically to collect and stack rings.

Chassis material choice matters just as much as platform strategy. Common options include aluminum extrusion (strong, reusable, moderately heavy), polycarbonate sheet (lightweight, easy to cut, less rigid over long spans), 3D-printed plastic (highly customizable, limited by printer size and strength), and carbon fiber (very strong and light, but expensive and harder to modify). Most student teams mix materials: aluminum extrusion for the main frame, with 3D-printed or laser-cut brackets for custom mounting points.

docs.title: Powering the Robot: The Power System
docs.text:
A robot power system is the complete set of components that stores, regulates, and distributes electrical energy to every powered part of the robot. Get the power system wrong, and nothing else in this chapter matters—a robot with a brilliant sensor layout and perfectly wired actuators is useless if its battery cannot deliver enough current or its wiring melts under load.

Drawing on the electrical fundamentals from Chapter 6 and the circuit design skills from Chapter 7, a complete power system typically includes:

  1. A main battery, sized to supply enough voltage and current for the robot's motors and electronics for a full match or work session
  2. A main breaker or fuse, a safety device that interrupts current flow if a short circuit or overload occurs, protecting both the robot and the people near it
  3. Voltage regulator modules, which step battery voltage down (or occasionally up) to the specific voltages different components require—a drive motor and a microcontroller rarely run on the same voltage
  4. A power distribution harness, the wiring that carries power from the battery, through the breaker and regulators, out to every actuator and sensor
  5. A battery indicator or monitoring circuit, which alerts the team when voltage drops too low to operate safely

Warning

A power system is only as strong as its weakest connection. A loose battery connector or an undersized wire gauge can cause voltage to sag exactly when a robot needs maximum power—for example, when lifting a stack of rings. Always match wire gauge and connector type to the actual current the circuit will carry.

docs.title: Selecting Actuators and Sensors for the Job
docs.text:
With a chassis and power system chosen, Vertex Robotics faces the question every design team faces next: which specific actuators and sensors actually accomplish the game task? Robot actuator selection is the process of matching a required motion—lifting, gripping, rotating, driving—to the actuator type, size, and specification best suited to produce it. Robot sensor selection is the parallel process of matching a required piece of information—distance, color, orientation, contact—to the sensor type best suited to measure it.

Neither selection happens in isolation. Actuator selection depends on the mechanical advantage available from gears, levers, and linkages (Chapter 9), and on whether the motion needs the smooth continuous force of an electric motor or the fast linear push of a pneumatic cylinder (Chapter 10). Sensor selection depends on the coordinate systems and measurement concepts from Chapter 8, and every selected sensor and actuator ultimately reports to or is commanded by the control system and code covered in Chapters 11 through 13.

For the Vertex Rising task, the team breaks their robot's job into sub-tasks and, for each one, asks what physical requirement must be met and which chapter's concepts help answer it:

  • Detecting a ring's location on the field — requires a sensor that reports distance and possibly color, drawing on Chapter 8's sensor tour
  • Driving toward and collecting a ring — requires drivetrain motors sized for torque and speed, drawing on Chapter 9's mechanical advantage concepts
  • Lifting rings to three different scoring heights — requires an actuator capable of controlled, repeatable vertical motion, potentially a motor with a lead screw or a pneumatic cylinder from Chapter 10
  • Confirming a ring is securely gripped before lifting — requires a contact or presence sensor, preventing wasted lift cycles

The interactive tool below lets you practice this same matching process: pick a robot task requirement and explore which sensor or actuator options could satisfy it, along with the tradeoffs of each choice.

docs.title: Diagram: Component Selection Decision Tool
docs.text:
Component Selection Decision Tool

Type: infographic sim-id: component-selection-decision-tool Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate Bloom Taxonomy Verb: justify, recommend, prioritize

Learning objective: Given a stated robot task requirement, students will recommend an appropriate sensor or actuator type and justify the choice by weighing at least two tradeoffs (cost, precision, speed, or complexity).

Purpose: Let students practice the real engineering decision of matching a functional requirement to a specific component family, reinforcing sensor and actuator concepts from Chapters 8, 9, and 10 in the context of full-robot design.

Layout: A left panel lists six clickable task requirement buttons: "Detect distance to an object," "Detect an object's color," "Confirm physical contact," "Lift a load to a precise height," "Rotate an arm through a wide angle," and "Drive and turn precisely." A right panel displays results after a button is clicked.

Interactive elements: - Clicking a task requirement populates the right panel with 2-3 candidate component types (e.g., for "Detect distance to an object": ultrasonic sensor, infrared distance sensor, and time-of-flight sensor) - Each candidate appears as a small card showing its name, a one-line description, and a color-coded tradeoff badge (Low/Medium/High) for Cost, Precision, and Response Speed - Hovering a candidate card highlights the corresponding sensor or actuator type if it was covered in Chapter 8, 9, or 10, with a small citation tag (e.g., "See Ch. 8") - A "Compare" checkbox lets students select two candidates to view their tradeoff badges side by side

Data to display (sample set): - Detect distance to an object: Ultrasonic sensor (Cost: Low, Precision: Medium, Speed: Medium); Infrared distance sensor (Cost: Low, Precision: Low, Speed: High); Time-of-flight sensor (Cost: Medium, Precision: High, Speed: High) - Lift a load to a precise height: Motor with lead screw (Cost: Medium, Precision: High, Speed: Low); Pneumatic cylinder (Cost: Medium, Precision: Low, Speed: High); Linear servo actuator (Cost: High, Precision: High, Speed: Medium)

Instructional Rationale: An Evaluate-level objective requires students to weigh competing tradeoffs and defend a recommendation, so a decision-support card layout with explicit tradeoff badges is more appropriate than a passive diagram—students must actively compare options before a recommendation feels justified, rather than being told a single correct answer.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with clickable button regions on the left and a dynamically redrawn card panel on the right; tradeoff data stored in a lookup object keyed by task requirement.

docs.title: Putting It Together: Robot Assembly and Robot Wiring
docs.text:
With components selected, the physical build begins. Robot assembly is the process of physically mounting, fastening, and connecting all selected components onto the chassis according to the design plan. Good assembly practice follows a deliberate order, not a random one:

  1. Mount the heaviest components (battery, main drive motors) low and near the chassis's center to keep the robot's center of gravity stable
  2. Install structural subassemblies (arms, lifts, grippers) before running any wiring through them
  3. Leave planned access points for batteries, fuses, and connectors that will need frequent attention during competition
  4. Fasten everything securely before wiring, since a part that shifts after wiring is run can stress or disconnect a wire

Once the physical structure is assembled, robot wiring is the task of routing and connecting electrical conductors between the power system, the microcontroller, and every actuator and sensor, following a planned wiring diagram rather than improvising connections in the moment. Poor wiring is one of the most common causes of robot failure in competition, precisely because problems it causes—an intermittent connection, a pinched wire—can be difficult to diagnose once covers are back on.

The workflow below walks through the decision points a team faces while wiring a robot, from the power system outward to each sensor and actuator.

docs.title: Diagram: Robot Wiring Workflow
docs.text:
Robot Wiring Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: robot-wiring-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply Bloom Taxonomy Verb: implement, execute, demonstrate

Learning objective: Students will apply a systematic wiring order (power, then control, then actuators, then sensors) and correctly branch decisions for digital versus analog sensor connections.

Purpose: Give students a repeatable mental checklist for wiring any robot safely and in the correct order, reducing the trial-and-error wiring mistakes that cause competition failures.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart with decision diamonds and process rectangles, rendered with click directives on every node

Steps: 1. Start: "Battery Connected to Main Breaker" — Hover text: "Always connect the main breaker first so power can be cut instantly if something shorts." 2. Process: "Wire Power Distribution Harness" — Hover text: "Run main power lines to voltage regulator modules before connecting any individual device." 3. Process: "Connect Microcontroller to Regulated Power" — Hover text: "The control board typically needs a different, lower voltage than the drive motors." 4. Process: "Wire Actuators to Motor/Servo Controllers" — Hover text: "Motor controllers sit between the microcontroller's signal and the actuator's power draw." 5. Decision: "Digital or Analog Sensor?" — Hover text: "Digital sensors send discrete on/off or coded signals; analog sensors send a continuously varying voltage." 6a. Process: "Wire to Digital Input Pin" (if Digital) — Hover text: "Digital signals connect directly to digital-labeled pins on the microcontroller." 6b. Process: "Wire to Analog Input Pin" (if Analog) — Hover text: "Analog signals require a pin capable of reading a range of voltages, not just on/off." 7. Process: "Label Every Connector" — Hover text: "Unlabeled wires are the number one cause of lost time during competition repairs." 8. End: "Continuity Check Before Power-On" — Hover text: "Verify no wire touches another that it should not, before the first power-on test."

Interactive features: Every node and arrow includes a Mermaid click directive that opens an infobox with its hover text; nodes are color-coded (blue for power steps, yellow for the decision diamond, green for the two branch outcomes, orange for the final safety check)

Color coding: - Blue: power and control wiring steps - Yellow: decision point - Green: branch outcomes - Orange: safety verification step

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click NodeId call showInfo("nodeId") directives for every node, paired with a small JavaScript infobox panel beneath the diagram.

docs.title: System Integration: Making the Subsystems Act as One
docs.text:
System integration is the process of combining a robot's chassis, power system, actuators, sensors, and control software so that they operate together as a single coherent machine rather than as a collection of independently functioning parts. Integration is where a robot's individual subsystems either prove they can cooperate—or reveal conflicts that assembly and wiring alone could not expose.

Integration problems are often subtle. A sensor might work perfectly on a test bench but report unreliable readings once mounted near a motor that generates electrical noise. A lift mechanism might move correctly by itself but stall when the drivetrain draws current at the same moment, starving the lift motor of voltage. Recognizing these interactions is exactly why system integration is treated as its own concept, distinct from assembly and wiring.

The diagram below shows how Vertex Robotics' subsystems connect, and lets you click each one to review its role and which earlier chapter covered it.

docs.title: Diagram: Robot System Integration Map
docs.text:
Robot System Integration Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: robot-system-integration-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, differentiate, organize

Learning objective: Students will examine how a robot's subsystems depend on one another and organize each subsystem by which earlier course chapter provides its underlying concepts.

Purpose: Reinforce that a complete robot is a network of interdependent subsystems, and connect each subsystem back to the specific chapter where students learned its underlying theory.

Node types: 1. Chassis / Hardware Platform (gray square) — Properties: material, platform type; Example: "Hybrid aluminum + 3D-printed superstructure" 2. Power System (yellow circle) — Properties: voltage, battery capacity; Example: "12V battery with two regulator modules" 3. Microcontroller / Control System (blue diamond) — Properties: processing role; Example: "Runs main control loop" 4. Actuators (orange circle) — Properties: motion type; Example: "Lift motor, gripper servo, drive motors" 5. Sensors (green circle) — Properties: measured quantity; Example: "Distance sensor, color sensor, touch sensor" 6. Software / Code (purple square) — Properties: behavior logic; Example: "Autonomous and driver-controlled routines"

Edge types: 1. SUPPLIES_POWER_TO (solid yellow arrows) — Power System → Microcontroller, Actuators, Sensors 2. MOUNTED_ON (solid gray arrows) — all component nodes → Chassis / Hardware Platform 3. SENDS_DATA_TO (dotted green arrows) — Sensors → Microcontroller 4. SENDS_COMMANDS_TO (dashed blue arrows) — Microcontroller → Actuators 5. RUNS_ON (solid purple arrows) — Software → Microcontroller

Layout: Force-directed, with Chassis positioned centrally as the node most other nodes connect to via MOUNTED_ON edges

Interactive features: - Hover a node: show its properties and a "See Chapter ___" tag (Chassis/Platform → Ch. 5 and this chapter; Power System → Ch. 6; Microcontroller → Ch. 12; Actuators → Ch. 9 and 10; Sensors → Ch. 8; Software → Ch. 3, 4, 13) - Click a node: highlight all directly connected nodes and dim the rest, and open a side panel with a one-sentence definition of that subsystem's role - Zoom: mouse wheel; Pan: click and drag background - A "Trace a Failure" button lets students click any two nodes to highlight the shortest path between them, illustrating how a problem in one subsystem can propagate to another

Legend: Node shapes/colors explained above; edge line styles explained above

Implementation: vis-network JavaScript library with a small fixed dataset (6 nodes, 8-10 edges); click and hover event listeners open a shared infobox panel; shortest-path highlighting implemented with vis-network's built-in graph traversal utilities.

docs.title: Robot Testing: Proving It Works Before It Counts
docs.text:
Robot testing is the systematic process of verifying that a robot's subsystems—and the robot as a whole—function correctly, performed in stages of increasing complexity rather than all at once. Testing everything simultaneously on a fully assembled robot makes it nearly impossible to isolate the source of a problem, so experienced teams test in a deliberate sequence:

  1. Power-on test — verify the power system delivers correct voltage to every subsystem before anything else is checked
  2. Subsystem test — verify each actuator and sensor works correctly in isolation, disconnected from the rest of the robot's behavior
  3. Integration test — verify subsystems work correctly together, running actual control code that combines sensor input and actuator output
  4. Field test — verify the fully integrated robot performs its intended task under realistic, competition-like conditions

Each stage tends to expose a different category of problem, and catching an issue early—during a power-on test rather than a field test—saves enormous time. The interactive checklist below simulates this four-stage process, letting you click through each stage to see the kinds of issues commonly discovered there.

docs.title: Diagram: Robot Testing Stage Simulator
docs.text:
Robot Testing Stage Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: robot-testing-stage-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, organize

Learning objective: Given a description of a robot malfunction, students will identify which of the four testing stages should have caught the problem and distinguish that stage's typical issues from the other three stages.

Canvas layout: - Top (100px): Four clickable stage tabs in sequence — "Power-On Test," "Subsystem Test," "Integration Test," "Field Test" - Main area (400px): Content panel showing the selected stage's checklist and common issues - Bottom (60px): "Next Stage" and "Previous Stage" buttons

Visual elements: - Each stage tab shown as a rectangle; the active stage is highlighted in blue, completed stages shown in green, upcoming stages shown in gray - Main panel lists 3-4 example issues for the active stage as cards with icons (a battery icon, a wrench icon, a circuit icon, a flag icon for field conditions)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1 (Power-On Test): Show issues such as "Battery voltage reads 0V (loose connector)," "Breaker trips immediately (short circuit)," "Microcontroller does not power on (wrong regulator voltage)" Stage 2 (Subsystem Test): Show issues such as "Servo moves in the wrong direction (wiring reversed)," "Sensor reports constant value (sensor not receiving power)," "Motor runs slower than expected (undersized wire gauge)" Stage 3 (Integration Test): Show issues such as "Lift stalls when drivetrain runs (shared power draw)," "Sensor reading becomes unreliable near running motor (electrical noise)," "Code reads old sensor value (timing/loop issue from Chapter 13)" Stage 4 (Field Test): Show issues such as "Robot performs well on smooth floor but slips on competition mat (traction mismatch)," "Battery voltage sags after ten minutes of match-length operation (undersized battery)," "Mechanism jams under match-speed operation but not slow bench testing (fit and tolerance issue)"

Interactive controls: - Click any of the four stage tabs to jump directly to that stage's content - "Next Stage" / "Previous Stage" buttons move sequentially through stages - Clicking an individual issue card flips it to reveal a one-sentence recommended fix

Instructional Rationale: An Analyze-level objective requires students to distinguish categories of failure by testing stage, so a step-through card-reveal pattern is appropriate—it lets students examine each stage's concrete issues before comparing across stages, rather than watching a continuous animation that would obscure which issue belongs to which stage.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with clickable tab regions and card objects; issue and fix data stored in an array of objects keyed by stage name; card flip implemented as a simple state toggle redrawn each frame.

docs.title: When Testing Reveals Problems: Reengineering and Documentation
docs.text:
Testing rarely goes perfectly on the first attempt, and that is expected, not a failure of the design process. Robot reengineering is the practice of revising a robot's design—its components, wiring, or software—in direct response to problems discovered during testing, rather than treating the original design as final. When Vertex Robotics' integration test reveals that their lift motor stalls whenever the drivetrain accelerates, reengineering might mean adding a dedicated power regulator for the lift, upgrading wire gauge, or reconsidering the gear ratio from Chapter 9 to reduce the current the lift motor demands.

Reengineering only works well when a team can remember what they tried before and why. Robot documentation is the ongoing written and visual record of a robot's design decisions, wiring diagrams, code versions, and test results, kept throughout the design process rather than reconstructed from memory afterward. Good documentation turns "I think we tried that already" into a quick, confident answer.

Strong robot documentation typically includes several distinct artifacts, each serving a different purpose:

Documentation Artifact Purpose Engineering notebook Chronological record of design decisions, sketches, and reasoning (often required for FTC judging) Wiring diagram Visual reference showing every electrical connection, prevents guesswork during repairs CAD files Digital models of custom parts, enabling reprinting or redesign (from Chapter 5) Code repository Version history of all programs, allowing the team to revert a change that broke something Test logs Dated records of what was tested, what failed, and what fix was applied

Tip

In FTC competitions, judges often weight the engineering notebook as heavily as the robot's on-field performance. A well-documented reengineering decision—showing the problem, the reasoning, and the result—demonstrates the engineering process itself, which is exactly what the notebook is meant to capture.

docs.title: Judging the Result: Performance Evaluation and Maintenance
docs.text:
Once a robot is built, tested, and refined, a team needs an honest answer to a deceptively simple question: how good is it? Robot performance evaluation is the process of measuring a robot's behavior against specific, ideally quantitative, criteria—rather than relying on a general impression of "it seems to work."

For Vertex Robotics, meaningful performance criteria for the ring-stacking task might include:

  • Cycle time — average seconds to collect one ring and stack it, measured across multiple attempts
  • Accuracy — percentage of scoring attempts that successfully land a ring on the intended pole
  • Reliability — number of matches completed without an unplanned mechanical or electrical failure
  • Consistency — how much cycle time and accuracy vary from attempt to attempt, not just their average

Performance evaluation only has value if it happens repeatedly, because a robot's performance changes over time even without redesign—parts wear, connectors loosen, and batteries age. Robot maintenance is the ongoing practice of scheduled and preventive upkeep tasks that keep a robot performing reliably over its working life, rather than waiting for a failure to force a repair.

A practical robot maintenance checklist, drawn from the power, wiring, and mechanical concepts covered throughout this course, includes:

  1. Fully charge and inspect batteries before each use, checking for swelling or damage
  2. Check all connectors and fasteners for looseness after transport or heavy use
  3. Inspect drivetrain components (from Chapter 9) for wear, especially gears, belts, and wheels
  4. Re-verify sensor calibration periodically, since drift accumulates over time (Chapter 8)
  5. Back up code and documentation after every significant change
  6. Replace consumable or high-wear parts proactively, before they fail during a match

docs.title: Looking Ahead: Robotics Industry Trends
docs.text:
This course began with a kit robot and formal vocabulary in Chapter 2, including a first look at robotics careers. It is fitting to close by looking outward again—at where the field of robotics is actually heading, and how the skills built across this entire course connect to it. Robotics industry trends are the current directions of change and growth shaping the robotics field, reflecting new technologies, new applications, and new demands from industries adopting robots.

Several trends are reshaping robotics right now, and each one builds directly on concepts from this course:

  • AI-powered perception — robots increasingly use machine learning to interpret sensor data (building on Chapter 8's sensors and Chapter 13's advanced programming), enabling them to recognize objects rather than just measure simple quantities
  • Collaborative robots (cobots) — robots designed to work safely alongside humans in shared spaces, requiring careful control system design (Chapter 11) to guarantee safe, predictable behavior
  • Autonomous mobile robots — robots that navigate and make decisions without constant human control, combining every layer of this course from sensing to control to software
  • Soft and flexible robotics — actuators and structures made from compliant materials rather than rigid parts, expanding the actuator selection choices covered earlier in this chapter
  • Swarm and multi-robot systems — many simple robots coordinating to accomplish a task no single robot could do alone

The timeline below traces how these trends have emerged and connects each one back to the robotics career pathways introduced in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Diagram: Robotics Industry Trends Timeline
docs.text:
Robotics Industry Trends Timeline

Type: timeline sim-id: robotics-industry-trends-timeline Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand Bloom Taxonomy Verb: summarize, exemplify, interpret

Learning objective: Students will summarize how major robotics industry trends have emerged over time and exemplify how each trend connects to a robotics career pathway.

Purpose: Situate the technical skills built throughout the course within the broader, evolving robotics industry, and connect trends back to the career pathways introduced in Chapter 2.

Time period: 2000-2026, with a forward-looking "What's Next" marker beyond 2026

Orientation: Horizontal

Events: - 2000s: Industrial robots become standard in manufacturing, largely fixed and caged from humans - 2011: First widely-adopted collaborative robot (cobot) designs allow robots to work near humans safely - 2015: Autonomous mobile robots begin widespread warehouse and logistics use - 2018: Machine learning-based perception becomes practical for real-time robotic vision - 2020s: Soft robotics and flexible actuators expand into medical and agricultural applications - 2023-2026: Multi-robot swarm coordination matures for search, agriculture, and exploration tasks - What's Next: Robots that combine AI perception, safe human collaboration, and adaptable soft actuation into single systems

Visual style: Horizontal timeline with alternating above/below event placement, "What's Next" marker visually distinct (dashed border, question-mark icon) at the far right

Color coding: - Gray: Early fixed industrial robotics (2000s) - Blue: Human-collaborative and mobile robotics (2011-2018) - Green: AI-perception and adaptive robotics (2018-2023) - Gold: Emerging and future trends (2023-2026 and beyond)

Interactive features: - Hover an event to see a one-sentence description of the trend - Click an event to expand a panel showing which robotics career pathway it connects to (e.g., "Autonomous mobile robots" links to careers in robotics software engineering and field robotics), referencing the Robotics Careers concept from Chapter 2 - Click the "What's Next" marker to reveal a prompt encouraging students to consider which trend they find most interesting as a possible career direction

Implementation: vis-timeline JavaScript library with a small fixed dataset of 6-7 timeline items; click event listeners open a shared infobox panel below the timeline.

docs.title: You Are Ready to Design
docs.text:
Look back at everything this chapter has asked you to bring together: an inventory of robotic components, a chosen chassis and hardware platform, a working power system, deliberately selected actuators and sensors, careful assembly and wiring, verified system integration, staged testing, honest reengineering, real documentation, measured performance evaluation, and ongoing maintenance. None of that was new theory—it was the deliberate combination of everything you built and learned in Chapters 1 through 13, applied to a single, original machine of your own design.

That is the actual meaning of "capstone." You did not just learn about robotics one topic at a time. You now hold a complete, repeatable process for taking a robot from an idea to a competition-ready machine, the same process used by professional robotics engineers and FTC teams around the world. Whatever comes next—a new FTC season, a FIRST Robotics Competition build, a personal project, or a first step toward a robotics career—you are ready to design it yourself.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Technology of Robotic Design
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 200 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement Vew the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 6 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 12 categories
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, robotic system design and build last
  • Balanced categories (6.2% - 9.3% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: This taxonomy organizes the 204 concepts in the Technology of Robotic Design learning graph into 14 categories, ordered to match a "build first, then work backwards" curriculum: students build a real robot kit, program it, and design parts for it before circling back to the deeper theory behind why each piece works.

docs.title: KIT — Identifying Kit Parts and Building Your StarterBot
docs.text: Hands-on orientation to a real robot kit: identifying structural, motion, power, and fastening hardware, reading assembly instructions, and guided assembly of a complete robot. (10 concepts)

docs.title: FOUND — Introduction to Robotics and Systems
docs.text: Conceptual grounding for what the students just built: what robotics and automation are, the universal systems model, and categories, applications, and history of robots. (17 concepts)

docs.title: PROG — Programming Fundamentals
docs.text: General-purpose programming concepts taught independent of any specific hardware theory: algorithms, variables, data types, control structures, functions, debugging, and program testing/security. (15 concepts)

docs.title: RBOT — Programming Your Robot
docs.text: Applying programming fundamentals directly to the robot: microcontrollers, sensors, actuators, open/closed-loop control basics, and writing the first robot control programs. (12 concepts)

docs.title: EDP — Designing and Building Custom Parts
docs.text: The engineering design process — problem definition, brainstorming, prototyping, iteration, documentation, trade-off analysis — paired with manufacturing custom parts via additive manufacturing and 3D printing. (19 concepts)

docs.title: ELEC — Electrical Fundamentals
docs.text: Core electrical theory behind the robot's power system: voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, AC/DC, circuit types, and electrical safety. (17 concepts)

docs.title: CIRC — Electronic Components and Circuits
docs.text: Physical electronic components and circuit-building skills: resistors, diodes, transistors, breadboards, soldering, multimeters, and circuit design/simulation. (17 concepts)

docs.title: SENS — Sensors and Measurement
docs.text: A deeper dive into sensing: precision measurement, specific sensor types, calibration, and signal processing, building on the basic sensors/actuators introduced in Programming Your Robot. (14 concepts)

docs.title: MECH — Mechanical Systems
docs.text: Simple machines and mechanical design concepts: levers, gears, linkages, torque, friction, and structural/chassis design. (17 concepts)

docs.title: FLUID — Fluid Power Systems
docs.text: Hydraulic and pneumatic systems: fluid pressure, cylinders, valves, pumps, and fluid power system design. (12 concepts)

docs.title: Learning Graph for TEXTBOOK_NAME
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
